bridge: The article reports Ohio State and Oregon spending more than 40 million dollars on football rosters while Maryland spends about 20 million, and quotes Iowa's Kirk Ferentz calling the widening gap the sport's single biggest issue.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: careful reporting on spending gaps inside one conference, though it shows money concentrating rather than proving the games got worse.

text: College football and basketball players need a share of the money their games bring in.
measured_by: Total dollars paid to college athletes in revenue share and NIL each academic year.
if_true: Athlete pay keeps rising toward the 5 billion dollars Opendorse projects for 2028-29.
if_false: Athlete pay is capped or clawed back by Congress or the courts and falls below 2025-26 levels.
bottom_line: The interest that drove the lawsuits and the settlement, and the one with the clearest measure.

text: Women's basketball players and gymnasts need a way to earn from their own fame while they are in college.
measured_by: Number and total value of commercial NIL deals signed by women athletes each year.
if_true: Women's deal counts and values keep growing year over year.
if_false: Women's share of athlete compensation shrinks as school revenue share crowds out brand deals.
bottom_line: A genuine gain from NIL that sits uneasily beside the small share women receive from school payrolls.

text: Swimmers, wrestlers and tennis players at Division I schools need their teams to survive the shift of money toward football.
measured_by: Number of Division I varsity teams in the NCAA's annual sports sponsorship count.
if_true: Team counts hold steady because schools find the revenue share money elsewhere.
if_false: Team counts fall year after year as departments cut sports to fund athlete pay.
bottom_line: The interest most directly harmed so far, with 41 teams cut in the first year.

text: Fans of smaller programs need a competition where their team can still win.
measured_by: Share of College Football Playoff berths and Final Four spots held by Big Ten and SEC schools.
if_true: The two richest conferences' share of postseason spots stays near its pre-2021 level.
if_false: The two richest conferences take nearly every playoff berth as their pay advantage compounds.
bottom_line: A real worry, but competitive balance was poor before NIL, so the baseline matters.

text: High school recruits need scholarship spots that are not consumed by transfers.
measured_by: Number of high school signees per FBS recruiting class.
if_true: High school class sizes stay near their 2020 level.
if_false: High school class sizes shrink as coaches fill rosters with paid transfers.
bottom_line: Often asserted by coaches, including Nick Saban, but not yet measured nationally.

text: College athletes now receive about 4.5 billion dollars a year in revenue share and NIL pay that the old rules denied them entirely.
bottom_line: The largest and best measured effect, because Opendorse's estimate rests on payments it processes, with the caveat that the firm profits from the market it is sizing.

text: Division I schools cut roughly 41 Olympic sports teams between May 2024 and July 2025 while finding money to pay football and basketball players.
bottom_line: The clearest harm so far, though the count does not net out teams added and some cuts were in the works before the settlement.

text: The Graduation Success Rate the NCAA publishes each November for Division I athletes is a fair measure of whether paid college athletes are still students.
The number of Division I varsity teams counted in the NCAA's sports sponsorship report is a fair measure of whether paying athletes has shrunk the number of athletes who get to play.
The average Nielsen audience for a regular-season FBS football broadcast is a fair measure of whether fans still care about the paid version of the game.
College football and basketball players receive substantial money from NIL deals and school revenue sharing that they could not legally receive before July 2021.

The gains to college sports from paying athletes, such as fairness, players staying in school longer and the end of the under-the-table market, outweigh the losses, such as cut Olympic teams, roster churn and wider gaps between conferences.

The changes seen in college sports since 2021, good and bad, were caused mainly by paying athletes rather than by the transfer rule changes, conference realignment and television deals that arrived at the same time.

Within the next two years, college football and basketball players will keep receiving revenue-share payments near the cap of about 20 million dollars per school set by the House v. NCAA settlement, plus NIL deals on top.
Within the next two years, more Division I schools will cut or merge Olympic sports teams such as tennis, swimming and track to pay for football and basketball rosters.

Over the next decade, college football and basketball players will become either employees or members of a union that bargains over pay, because a paid workforce without contracts has proved hard to govern.
Over the next decade, top college football programs will be concentrated in the Big Ten and SEC, which can pay the most, while many other Division I schools drop to a lower level of competition.
College athletes should be full employees of their schools with salaries, contracts and a union, because paying them has been good for college sports and paying them fully would be better.
Letting college athletes earn money from true endorsement deals with outside companies has been good for college sports, even if booster collectives and pay-for-play have not.
Paying college athletes has been good for the athletes who receive the money, whatever its effect on the rest of college sports.
Superhero movies have exhausted their audience and will not return to their 2010s box office.
bottom_line: The evidence for a weak 2025 is strong and the evidence that the audience is exhausted is weak: the same audience set the all-time domestic opening and total records for Spider-Man: Brand New Day in 2026 while letting Supergirl lose more than $85 million. The real fight is whether the genre's 2010s box office was a genre-wide habit that has broken, or a handful of event films that still earn when the film is wanted, and Avengers: Doomsday's December 2026 opening is the next reading.
hook: In 2025 no superhero movie passed $620 million worldwide for the first time in years, and then in July 2026 Spider-Man: Brand New Day opened to $360 million domestic, the biggest opening weekend of any film ever made.
question: Has the audience for superhero movies permanently shrunk, or will the genre's box office return to its 2010s heights when the right film arrives?
ask: The page most needs the year-by-year domestic gross and ticket-share table for superhero films from 2008 through 2026 from The Numbers, so the 2010s peak and the 2025 trough can be read side by side.

text: In 2018 and 2019, seven superhero films each grossed more than $1.1 billion worldwide (Avengers: Infinity War, Black Panther, Incredibles 2, Aquaman, Avengers: Endgame, Spider-Man: Far From Home and Captain Marvel), but from 2020 through 2025 only two superhero films did (Spider-Man: No Way Home and Deadpool & Wolverine), so the genre's 2010s box office was a broad bench of hits that has not come back.
bottom_line: Strong weight: it measures the whole genre rather than its single best film, which is what the belief is about, though 2020 and 2021 were cut down by pandemic theater closures and 2026 is not over yet. Source: Wikipedia, 'List of highest-grossing superhero films', 2026.

text: Captain Marvel grossed $1.131 billion worldwide in 2019, but its 2023 sequel The Marvels grossed $206.1 million, the lowest of any Marvel Cinematic Universe film, which shows that the general audience that turned out for a superhero in the 2010s did not return for the same character four years later.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: an 82 percent drop for the same heroine is hard to explain by quality alone, but The Marvels also had weak reviews and expected viewers to have watched Disney+ series first. Sources: Wikipedia, 'The Marvels' and 'List of highest-grossing superhero films', 2026.

text: Joker grossed $1.079 billion worldwide in 2019, but its 2024 sequel Joker: Folie à Deux opened to $37.7 million domestic against the original's $96.2 million and finished at $207.5 million worldwide on a budget of $190 million to $200 million, so even a proven comic book hit could not bring its 2010s audience back.
bottom_line: Minor to moderate weight: the collapse is real and documented, but the sequel was a musical that broke with what fans of the first film wanted, so it may show a misjudged film more than a tired audience. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Joker (2019 film)' and 'Joker: Folie à Deux', 2026.

text: Disney chief executive Bob Iger said at The New York Times DealBook Summit on November 29, 2023 that 'the quantity, in our case, diluted quality, and Marvel suffered greatly from that,' an admission from the genre's largest producer that its own volume of superhero releases wore down the audience.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it is the strongest insider confirmation that fatigue was real, but Iger blamed too many and too rushed films, which a studio can fix, so it supports a slump more than a permanent ceiling. Source: CNBC, 'Bob Iger says The Marvels had little supervision and Disney has made too many sequels', 2023.

text: The Marvel story that held the 2010s audience together ran 22 films from Iron Man in 2008 to Avengers: Endgame in 2019 and then ended, so the moviegoers who followed it got a finished story and have had no equally strong reason to keep buying tickets for every new superhero film.
bottom_line: Minor to moderate weight: it is a reasonable account of why 2019 was a peak that is hard to repeat, but it is an argument from logic rather than measured fact, and Avengers: Doomsday is built to recreate exactly that pull. Source: Wikipedia, 'Avengers: Endgame', 2026.

text: The four superhero films released in 2025 grossed $618.7 million (Superman), $521.9 million (The Fantastic Four: First Steps), $415 million (Captain America: Brave New World) and $382.4 million (Thunderbolts*) worldwide, so none reached half of Avengers: Infinity War's $2.048 billion from 2018.
bottom_line: Box office grosses are public records tracked by several independent services, so the finding is reliable; what it shows is a weak year, not a permanent ceiling.

text: Superhero films accounted for 31 percent of American movie tickets sold in 2021 and 17 percent in 2023, a fall of 14 points in two years.
bottom_line: A large and well-sourced drop, though 2021 was inflated by a pandemic release calendar that left superheroes with little competition.

text: A survey reported in 2023 found 41 percent of American adults said they do not like superhero movies, up from 36 percent in 2021.
bottom_line: One survey series reported second-hand; the direction matters more than the exact figure, and there is no reading after 2023.

text: Supergirl, released June 26, 2026 with a net production budget of $170 million to $186 million and $120 million in marketing, grossed $72.4 million domestic and $126.4 million worldwide, leaving Warner Bros. a projected loss of $85 million to $125 million.
bottom_line: Reliable figures that show a well-funded new hero cannot count on the general audience, though they also fit the rival explanation that weak reviews sank it.

text: Avengers: Doomsday will open below $260 million domestic, under the low end of its September 2026 tracking, because the demand that made Endgame has thinned.
No superhero film other than a Spider-Man or Avengers title will open above $125 million domestic in 2027 or 2028.

A finding that Spider-Man: Brand New Day's audience was mostly adults over 30 who had seen earlier Spider-Man films, with few first-time superhero viewers, would show the record came from a loyal base rather than a renewed general audience.

A finding that Marvel's 2027 and 2028 non-Avengers releases each opened below $80 million domestic despite reviews above 80 percent on Rotten Tomatoes would show that quality alone no longer brings the audience back.
The superhero box office peak of 2018 and 2019 reflected demand for the genre itself, not a one-time run of well-liked films and a once-only story payoff.

A few record-breaking superhero films, such as Spider-Man: Brand New Day, do not count as a return to 2010s box office, because the belief is about the genre's typical year rather than its single best film.
The overall number of people going to movie theaters will not grow back to its 2019 size, so even a well-liked superhero film draws from a smaller pool than the 2010s hits did.

Steven Spielberg told the Associated Press in September 2015, while promoting Bridge of Spies, that there will be a time when the superhero movie goes the way of the Western, because such cycles have a finite time in popular culture.
Nia DaCosta, director of The Marvels, told Total Film in 2023 that she thinks superhero fatigue absolutely exists.
Superhero Film Fatigue Is Up From Last Year, Even Among Marvel Fans, Saleah Blancaflor, 2022
bridge: Morning Consult's surveys found the share of American adults who do not enjoy superhero movies rose from 36 percent in November 2021 to 41 percent in July 2022, and 31 percent of Marvel fans said they were getting a little tired of so many of them.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it is a real survey trend among general audiences, but it was taken before the 2024 and 2026 hits and cannot say whether the dislike lasted.

text: Deadpool & Wolverine grossed $1.338 billion worldwide in 2024, the most of any R-rated film ever, during the period commentators called the depth of superhero fatigue.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it shows the audience will return for a film it wants, though a single novelty pairing of two stars is not proof the whole genre can recover.

text: The 2025 films all faced an unusual problem of Chinese and other overseas markets shrinking for Hollywood generally, so a lower worldwide number does not by itself show that the American audience was tired.
bottom_line: Minor weight: it narrows what the 2025 numbers prove, but the belief can be tested on domestic figures alone, where 2025 was also weak.

text: Spider-Man: Brand New Day opened to $360 million domestic on the weekend of July 31, 2026, passing Avengers: Endgame's $357.1 million record, and had grossed $953 million in the United States and Canada and $2.498 billion worldwide as of October 2, 2026, making it the highest-grossing film ever in the domestic market.
bottom_line: The single strongest fact on the page: a verified record that directly contradicts the word 'exhausted', though one film is not a whole genre.

text: Avengers: Doomsday reached $50 million in advance ticket sales 100 days before its December 18, 2026 release, with 70 percent of those tickets sold for premium Infinity Vision showings, and was tracking for a $260 million to $300 million opening weekend.
bottom_line: Pre-sales are a real measure of demand, but tracking is a forecast and the actual opening will replace it in December 2026.

text: Deadpool & Wolverine grossed $1.338 billion worldwide in 2024, the highest total ever for an R-rated film and the second-highest of any film that year.
bottom_line: Reliable and relevant: it shows the audience returned at 2010s scale in the middle of the supposed slump.

text: Superman opened to $125.0 million and The Fantastic Four: First Steps opened to $117.6 million domestic in July 2025, and Superman finished as the third highest-grossing film of 2025 in the United States and Canada with $354.2 million.
bottom_line: Solid figures that show two superhero films were among the year's top ten even in the genre's weak year.

text: A finding that Avengers: Doomsday grossed more than $800 million domestic, within sight of Endgame, would show the genre's ceiling is intact when the film is one people want.
A finding that superhero films took 25 percent or more of American tickets sold in 2026 or 2027 would show the general audience returned to its 2010s habits, not just the fans.
Moviegoers judge each superhero film on its own quality, so a run of better superhero films can bring back 2010s box office totals.
The weak superhero grosses of 2023 to 2025 came mostly from Marvel releasing too many films and streaming series at once, a problem Disney has since cut back.
Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige said in July 2025, pointing to the success of Superman, that it is clearly not superhero fatigue, and blamed Marvel's slump on making too many films and series.
DC Studios co-chief James Gunn said in 2025 that he does not believe in superhero fatigue and that audiences have mediocre movie fatigue instead.
'Spider-Man' Beats 'Avengers: Endgame' as 'Brand New Day' Climbs to $360 Million, the Biggest Opening Weekend in Box Office History, 2026
bridge: Variety reported that Spider-Man: Brand New Day opened to $360 million in the United States and Canada, passing the $357 million record Avengers: Endgame set in 2019.
bottom_line: Strong weight: the single largest opening ever, set by a superhero film in 2026, is hard to square with an audience that has given up on the genre.

text: 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Poised To Cross $900 Million At Domestic Box Office, Tim Lammers, 2026
bridge: Forbes tracked Spider-Man: Brand New Day's run toward $900 million domestic by the end of August 2026, showing the film held its audience for weeks rather than burning out on opening weekend.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it shows staying power, not just fan turnout, though it is still one film's run rather than a genre-wide total.

text: Kevin Feige on Marvel Studios' Future, Focusing on Lower Budgets, Less TV and More Robert Downey Jr.: 'Look at "Superman," It's Clearly Not Superhero Fatigue', 2025
bridge: Marvel's president argued in July 2025 that the studio's slump came from making well over 100 hours of stories in half the time it took to make 50, so supply rather than audience demand was the problem.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the oversupply explanation fits the timing, but it comes from the executive with the strongest interest in saying the audience is still there.

text: Moviegoers who do not follow comic book characters need a steady supply of big-screen films made for them.
measured_by: Number of films opening above $100 million domestic each year that are not superhero titles
if_true: The count rises as studios move tentpole budgets to other genres, as 2026's Odyssey and Project Hail Mary suggest.
if_false: The count stays flat because studios keep the biggest release dates and budgets for superhero titles.
bottom_line: A broad interest that is real but mild, since these viewers already have more non-superhero hits in 2025 and 2026 than in 2019.

text: Independent filmmakers and mid-budget directors need studios to spend on scripts that are not franchise sequels.
measured_by: Number of wide releases a year with budgets between $30 million and $100 million from original screenplays
if_true: The count rises as studios fill freed release dates and budgets with original films.
if_false: The count stays low because franchise films keep the money and the dates.
bottom_line: A real interest, though studios may fill freed dates with other franchises rather than originals.

text: Movie theater owners and their workers need a dependable calendar of event films that fill large-format screens.
measured_by: Annual domestic box office from superhero films as reported by The Numbers
if_true: Superhero ticket sales settle below $1.5 billion a year, leaving theaters short of the event films that drive premium pricing.
if_false: Superhero ticket sales return to $2.5 billion or more in years with an Avengers or Spider-Man release.
bottom_line: The clearest interest against the belief: theaters just had their best-ever opening weekend from a superhero film.

text: Visual effects artists and production crews need a steady flow of large-scale shoots to keep working.
measured_by: Number of superhero films in production each year with budgets above $150 million
if_true: The count falls to two or three a year, shrinking work across effects houses.
if_false: The count stays at four to six a year, the 2016 to 2019 average.
bottom_line: A strong interest for a workforce that has already absorbed the cuts Disney announced in 2024.

text: Comic book fans need their favorite characters adapted with theatrical budgets and care.
measured_by: Number of theatrical superhero releases a year across all studios
if_true: The number falls toward two or three a year, mostly Avengers and Spider-Man titles.
if_false: The number stays near five or six a year, with room for new characters like Supergirl.
bottom_line: A devoted interest that keeps the floor under the genre but cannot by itself restore the 2010s ceiling.

text: If studios stop expecting superhero films to earn like 2019, they will avoid losses like Supergirl's projected $85 million to $125 million by budgeting mid-tier characters at mid-tier levels.
bottom_line: A real but uncertain benefit, since one Supergirl-sized miss a year is a rough guess and a well-made cheaper film can also miss.

text: If the industry treats the superhero boom as over, fewer films will be built around a decade of shared continuity, so a newcomer can watch a movie without homework.
bottom_line: A plausible benefit that is hard to count, since Marvel has said it is already spacing releases out.

text: If superhero production falls, the visual effects studios that staff up for these films will lose a large share of their work, since each tentpole carries hundreds of effects artists for a year or more.
bottom_line: A serious cost for a specific workforce, though no public count of jobs tied to the genre exists.

text: If the industry concludes the audience is gone, characters with long comic histories will go unadapted or be handed to streaming at lower budgets, as Marvel already did with much of its 2021 to 2023 slate.
bottom_line: A modest cost spread across a devoted group, and a reversible one if a cheaper film finds its audience.

text: The median domestic opening weekend of superhero films that are not Avengers or Spider-Man titles is a fair measure of whether the genre draws an audience beyond its two biggest brands.
Superhero movie box office totals since 2020 have stayed well below their levels of the late 2010s.
The fall in superhero movie grosses is caused mainly by audiences tiring of the genre rather than by weaker films, pandemic viewing habits or shrinking overseas markets.
Superhero movie box office totals will stay below their 2010s levels for the rest of this decade.
If studios accept that the superhero audience is exhausted, Disney, Warner Bros. and Sony will move more of their 2027 and 2028 summer and holiday release dates from superhero films to other genres.
If studios accept that the superhero audience is exhausted, they will approve fewer superhero films with budgets above $200 million and cancel or delay planned spinoffs within a year or two.
Over the next decade, superhero films would fall to a small share of American ticket sales, much as the Western faded after the 1960s.
Over the next decade, Hollywood studios would stop building interconnected film universes across dozens of titles and put their biggest budgets into standalone films and other kinds of adaptations.
Superhero movies are a dying genre that will fade from theaters the way the Western did, and no superhero film will earn $1 billion worldwide again.
Superhero movies no longer earn reliably big grosses, though standout superhero films can still match or beat the biggest hits of the 2010s.
Marvel Studios' films as a group will not return to their 2018 and 2019 box office totals, even if individual superhero films from Sony or DC do very well.
Hollywood's reliance on sequels and remakes has made movies worse.
bottom_line: The evidence is strong that Hollywood leans on sequels and remakes far more at the top of the box office than a generation ago, that mid-budget films have largely left theaters, and that sequels tend to rate a little below the films they follow. It is thin on whether movies as a whole got worse, because most films made are still originals, critic scores have risen, and remakes were just as common in the studio era; the real fight is whether "movies" means the handful of hits most people see or everything that gets made.
hook: In 1984 original screenplays earned 73 percent of the North American box office; by 2023 they earned 30.6 percent, even though they were still more than half of the films being made (Stephen Follows, 2025).
question: Has Hollywood's reliance on sequels and remakes made movies worse, or only made the biggest hits more familiar?
ask: This page most needs a study comparing the critic and audience scores of each year's highest-grossing films across decades, adjusted for changes in who does the rating.

text: Sequels now take a far larger share of the North American box office than they did a generation ago, so the films most moviegoers actually see are mostly continuations of earlier films.
bottom_line: Strong evidence of reliance (Stephen Follows counts sequels at 11.7 percent of the domestic box office in the 1990s and 41.7 percent on average in 2014 to 2023), but it shows what people buy tickets for, not that the films got worse.

text: Movie sequels are rated lower on average than the original films they follow, so a release slate built on sequels is a slate of weaker films.
bottom_line: Real and consistent (about 0.8 IMDb points in Alex Bass's 1,200-pair study), but part of the drop is expected regression after an unusually good first film, so it deserves moderate weight.

text: Hollywood studios' spending on franchise films has crowded mid-budget dramas and comedies out of theaters, and that middle tier once produced many of the most admired American films.
bottom_line: Well documented for theaters (Paramount and Warner Bros. went from 27 to 37 mid-budget releases a year to five), but many of those films moved to streaming rather than vanishing, which limits how much this proves about movies overall.

text: Studios that build their business around franchises choose and shape stories by what extends a brand and sets up the next installment, which pushes big films toward formula.
bottom_line: A plausible and widely voiced mechanism, but it is hard to measure directly, so it deserves weight only as far as score data backs it.

text: When the biggest budgets go to sequels and remakes, new writers and directors lose the path to wide audiences that earlier generations used to build careers on original work.
bottom_line: Likely true for theatrical careers, but the claim depends on whether streaming and television now serve as that path instead.

text: Sequels took 11.7 percent of the North American box office in the 1990s, an average of 41.7 percent from 2014 to 2023, and 45.8 percent in 2023.
bottom_line: Solid measure of how much Hollywood's revenue rests on sequels; it measures reliance, not quality.

text: Original screenplays earned 73 percent of the North American box office in 1984 but only 30.6 percent in 2023, even though their share of films made barely moved (60.4 percent to 55.9 percent).
bottom_line: Shows audiences' money has shifted heavily toward derivative films, which supports the reliance half of the belief but cuts against the idea that originals stopped being made.

text: In a study of about 1,200 original films and their sequels, the original had a median IMDb rating of 6.9 and the sequel a median of 6.1.
bottom_line: A clear and consistent gap, but it compares each sequel only with an original selected for being successful, so regression to the average explains part of it.

text: Theatrical releases budgeted between $20 million and $80 million (in 2026 dollars) fell from a peak of 127 in 2008 to 47, 52 and 62 in 2021, 2022 and 2023, and Paramount and Warner Bros. together went from 27 to 37 such films a year in 1995 to 2007 to five in both 2022 and 2023.
bottom_line: Strong evidence that theaters lost mid-budget films, though the same analysis finds many of them moved to streaming and that dramas and comedies were the main losses.

text: The average Metacritic score of the 10 highest-grossing films of 2027 in North America will be at least 10 points below the average score of that year's original wide releases.
Annual movie ticket sales in the US and Canada will stay below 1 billion in every year from 2026 through 2028 while sequels keep taking more than 40 percent of the domestic box office.
A study matching films by budget, genre and year finds that sequels and remakes score lower with both critics and audiences than comparable original films, not just lower than their own originals.

A study finds that as a Hollywood studio's share of franchise releases rose, the critic scores of its remaining original releases also fell, showing franchises drained talent or money from other films.
The quality of movies made in different decades can be compared fairly, and the comparison is not just nostalgia for the films a person grew up with.
The films given wide theatrical release are the right measure of how good movies are, since they are the films most people actually see.
Money and screens that studios give to sequels and remakes would otherwise go to original films that would on average be better.
Martin Scorsese wrote in The New York Times in November 2019 that franchise films are "sequels in name but they are remakes in spirit" and that they are crowding other kinds of films out of theaters.

Film writer Mark Harris argued in GQ in February 2011 that Hollywood had stopped telling new stories and was turning out sequels, adaptations, remakes and reboots chosen for their brands rather than their quality.
I Said Marvel Movies Aren't Cinema. Let Me Explain., Martin Scorsese, 2019
bridge: Scorsese argues that franchise films are "sequels in name but they are remakes in spirit," made to satisfy market research, and that they are pushing other kinds of films out of theaters.
bottom_line: Carries the authority of a major filmmaker and states the crowding-out mechanism clearly, but it is one artist's judgment rather than evidence, so moderate weight.

text: The Big Picture: The Fight for the Future of Movies, Ben Fritz, 2018
bridge: Fritz, a Wall Street Journal film reporter, uses studio interviews and leaked Sony documents to show how the major studios moved their money into franchise films and left most adult dramas to others.
bottom_line: Strong reporting on how studio strategy changed, which supports the reliance half of the belief; it says less about whether the films themselves got worse.

text: Hollywood remade films at least as often in its 1930s to 1950s studio era, the period many people call its golden age, as it does today.
bottom_line: Strong: a count of 986 Hollywood remakes from 1915 to 2020 found the belief that today's films are unusually derivative comes from paying attention only to recent data.

text: Most new American films are still original stories, and sequels were under 5 percent of US releases in 2023, so judging all movies by the few biggest hits mistakes the top of the box office for the whole of filmmaking.
bottom_line: Strong against the broad version of the belief, though weaker against the narrower claim that the films most people see have gotten worse.

text: Movie sequels look worse than the originals partly because studios only make sequels to unusually successful or well-liked films, so a drop afterward is the expected pull back toward average, not proof of worse filmmaking.
bottom_line: Sound statistical point that the sequel-rating gap cannot rule out, which takes real weight away from comparisons of sequels with their own originals.

text: Franchise profits steady Hollywood studios' finances, and that steady income lets studios take chances on original films they could not otherwise afford.
bottom_line: Research confirms sequels became a key way studios manage risk after about 2000, but there is little direct evidence that franchise money is actually spent on originals, so moderate weight.

text: Many sequels and remakes rank among the most admired films of their time, from The Godfather Part II to Mad Max: Fury Road and Dune: Part Two, so being a sequel or remake does not make a film worse.
bottom_line: Shows sequels can be excellent, but a handful of standouts does not settle whether the average film got worse.

text: Original and adventurous filmmaking has largely moved to streaming services, prestige television and independent distributors, so the range of good films people can watch has not shrunk even though the top of the box office has narrowed.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it depends on whether the belief is about theatrical movies only, and streaming originals are harder to compare on quality.

text: A count of 986 Hollywood remakes made between 1915 and 2020 found that the popular belief in the unusual derivativeness of today's American cinema comes from availability bias, with remaking far more pervasive in the 1930s to 1950s studio era.
bottom_line: Strong evidence against the idea that remaking is new, though it covers remakes rather than sequels, which did grow.

text: Sequels made up under 5 percent of movies released in the US in 2023, and they were about twice as common among releases in the late 1980s as in the 2010s.
bottom_line: Strong evidence that the typical film being made is not a sequel; it does not address the quality of the films most people see.

text: The average Rotten Tomatoes critics' score for wide releases rose from 46 percent in 2009 to 62 percent in 2019, the same decade in which sequels' share of the box office climbed.
bottom_line: Points against declining quality, but the article itself credits much of the rise to changes in which critics Rotten Tomatoes counts, so it deserves limited weight.

text: Sinners, an original film by Ryan Coogler made for $90 million, earned about $280 million in North America in 2025 and was the seventh-highest-grossing release of the year.
bottom_line: Shows original films can still be made and widely seen, but one hit among the top ten (where eight were sequels, remakes or reboots) is an exception as much as a rebuttal.

text: At least two sequels or remakes will be nominated for Best Picture at both the 2027 and 2028 Academy Awards.
The average Metacritic score of the 10 highest-grossing films of 2027 in North America will be within 5 points of the average score of that year's original wide releases.
A year-by-year count shows that well-reviewed original films reaching at least 1,000 North American theaters were as common in 2015 to 2025 as in 1990 to 2005.
An analysis finds that the critic and audience scores of each year's highest-grossing films have held steady since the 1980s even as sequels and remakes took over the top of the box office.
Whether a film is a sequel or remake says nothing about its quality by itself; each film has to be judged on its own.
Films released on streaming services, by independent distributors and abroad count as movies just as much as films in wide theatrical release.
Audiences who buy tickets to sequels and remakes are getting something they value, so their choices are not evidence that the films are worse.
The Hollywood Sequel: History and Form, 1911-2010, Stuart Henderson, 2014
bridge: Henderson traces sequels through every era of Hollywood, including the studio years from 1929 to 1954, which shows that making continuations of earlier hits is an old practice, not a recent break.
bottom_line: The most thorough history of the film sequel, and strong against the idea that reliance on sequels is new, though it does not settle whether today's degree of reliance is worse.

text: A statistical approach to Hollywood remake and sequel metadata, Agata Hołobut, Jan Rybicki and Miłosz Stelmach, 2024
where_found: Digital Scholarship in the Humanities, Vol. 39, No. 2 (Oxford University Press)
bridge: The authors count 986 Hollywood remakes made from 1915 to 2020 and track their yearly share of releases, which tests whether recycling old films is a new habit or an old one.
bottom_line: Peer-reviewed counting from IMDb data that weighs against the claim that remakes are a modern disease, but it measures how often films are remade, not how good they are.

text: Blockbusters: Hit-Making, Risk-Taking, and the Big Business of Entertainment, Anita Elberse, 2013
bridge: Elberse, a Harvard Business School professor, argues from ten years of studying entertainment companies that betting big on a few titles with strong hit potential is the most profitable strategy, which explains franchise reliance as a sound business choice rather than a failure.
bottom_line: Good evidence that franchise reliance is rational for studios, but profit is not quality, so it weighs only against the claim that the strategy is a mistake, not against the claim that films got worse.

text: Screenwriters with original ideas need studios willing to buy and produce scripts that are not tied to an existing brand.
measured_by: Number of original (non-sequel, non-remake) films given a wide release each year.
if_true: The count keeps falling as studios put their budgets into sequels and remakes.
if_false: The count holds steady, and franchises are not what is limiting original writers.
bottom_line: A concrete interest the data partly supports, since theatrical mid-budget releases have fallen sharply.

text: Moviegoers who want new stories need original films playing in theaters near them.
measured_by: Share of screens and showtimes at local theaters given to original films each year.
if_true: The share shrinks and original films play only briefly or in big cities.
if_false: Original films keep a steady share and can find audiences when they are good, as Sinners did.
bottom_line: Matters most to regular moviegoers; streaming softens it for people willing to watch at home.

text: Directors of dramas and comedies need studio budgets between $20 million and $80 million to make films for wide release.
measured_by: Number of theatrical releases budgeted between $20 million and $80 million each year (Stephen Follows's count).
if_true: The count stays well below the 2008 peak of 127 as franchise films absorb studio money.
if_false: The count recovers, or the loss is fully made up by streaming budgets.
bottom_line: Well measured and clearly down for theaters, which is the strongest concrete harm on this side.

text: Studio employees and shareholders need dependable hits that keep film studios profitable.
measured_by: Film studios' annual operating income from theatrical releases.
if_true: Cutting sequels would not hurt income much if the films were worse, since worse films should eventually draw less.
if_false: Sequels keep earning reliably, and cutting them would cost studios and their workers real money.
bottom_line: A heavy interest, since sequels have been central to studio profits since about 2000.

text: Fans of long-running film series need new chapters of the stories and characters they already love.
measured_by: Ticket sales and audience ratings for new installments of established series.
if_true: Fan ratings of new installments drift down as series go on.
if_false: Fans keep rating new installments highly and buying tickets for them.
bottom_line: A large and real group whose choices are a main reason studios make sequels.

text: Hollywood studios that cut back on sequels and remakes would release more mid-budget dramas and comedies in theaters.
bottom_line: A rough estimate of recovering part of the drop from 127 such releases in 2008 to 62 in 2023; it assumes the money freed up would go to that tier.

text: Screenwriters would sell more original scripts if Hollywood studios relied less on existing brands.
bottom_line: Likely direction but no reliable count of original script sales to estimate from.

text: Hollywood studios that cut back on sequels would give up their most predictable source of profit.
bottom_line: Sequels averaged 41.7 percent of the domestic box office in 2014 to 2023, and research ties them to how studios manage risk, so this cost is large.

text: Movie theaters would lose some of their surest crowd-drawers if studios made fewer sequels, remakes and reboots.
bottom_line: Eight of 2025's top ten were sequels, remakes or reboots, so theaters depend heavily on them in an industry still selling far fewer tickets than in 2019.

text: Fans of film franchises would get fewer new installments of the series they follow.
bottom_line: A real loss to the many people who buy those tickets, though hard to put a number on.

text: The average Metacritic score of each year's 20 highest-grossing films in North America, tracked from 1985 to today and compared with the average for all wide releases that year, is a fair measure of whether reliance on sequels and remakes has lowered the quality of the movies most people see.

The number of original films each year that open in at least 1,000 North American theaters and earn a Metacritic score of 75 or higher is a fair measure of whether sequels and remakes are crowding good original films out of theaters.

The gap between the average Letterboxd rating of sequels and remakes and that of original films with similar budgets released in the same year is a fair measure of whether franchise films are worse filmmaking rather than just more common.
Sequels and remakes make up a much larger share of Hollywood's biggest releases and box office than they did a generation ago.
American movies, taken as a whole or at least the films most people see, are worse now than they were before sequels and remakes became dominant.
The rise of sequels and remakes caused the drop in quality, rather than both being driven by something else such as streaming or changes in how people watch films.
Hollywood studios that cut back on sequels and remakes would greenlight more mid-budget original dramas and comedies for theatrical release within a year or two.
Hollywood studios that shift money from franchises to original films would see their yearly box office swing more widely, because original films are harder to predict.
Over a decade, more new American directors would build careers on original theatrical films instead of moving to television or to franchise work.
Over a decade, a larger share of the films that critics and audiences rank among the best of their year would be original stories that played widely in theaters.
Sequels and remakes have ruined Hollywood, and almost no franchise film made since 2000 is worth watching.
Hollywood's reliance on sequels and remakes has narrowed the range of films that get a wide theatrical release in the United States.
The highest-grossing Hollywood films each year are less original than the highest-grossing films of a generation ago.
Die Hard is a Christmas movie.
bottom_line: The facts are not in dispute: Die Hard is set on Christmas Eve and full of Christmas detail, yet it opened in July 1988 and was sold as an action film. The fight is over what makes a Christmas movie, a film set at Christmas or one about it, and on that audiences are split almost evenly, with the 'yes' side growing, especially among younger viewers.
hook: Die Hard opened in American theaters on July 15, 1988, yet a YouGov poll in December 2025 found the people who have seen it split 44% to 45% over whether it is a Christmas movie.
question: Is Die Hard a Christmas movie?
ask: The page most needs a year-by-year count of Die Hard's December share of US streaming minutes, set beside accepted Christmas films and beside 1980s action films with no Christmas setting.

text: Die Hard takes place entirely on Christmas Eve, and its story starts because John McClane flies to Los Angeles to spend Christmas with his wife and children.
bottom_line: Strong weight: the holiday is the reason the hero is in the building at all, which is more than a backdrop.

text: Die Hard's emotional story, a separated husband winning back his wife Holly in time for Christmas morning, is the same family reunion story that traditional Christmas films tell.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the reunion arc is real, but family reunions also drive many films that nobody calls Christmas movies.

text: Die Hard builds its scenes from deliberate Christmas material, including a dead gunman in a Santa hat with the note 'Now I have a machine gun. Ho-ho-ho.' and 'Let It Snow! Let It Snow! Let It Snow!' playing over the ending.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the Christmas details are written into the plot and jokes on purpose, though decoration alone does not settle what a film is about.

text: A summer release date does not stop a film from being a Christmas movie, since 20th Century Fox also opened Miracle on 34th Street in May 1947.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it removes the July 1988 release as a knockout objection, though it does not prove the positive case.

text: The studio that owns Die Hard has promoted it as a Christmas film since at least 2017, with a Christmas picture book, a 2018 holiday trailer and a December 2023 return to theaters.
bottom_line: Modest weight: the owner's own marketing shows how the film is now sold, but marketing follows money and can come after the fact.

text: In YouGov's December 2025 US poll, 44% of people who had seen Die Hard called it a Christmas movie and 45% said it is not, up from 39% who called it one in YouGov's December 2020 poll of viewers.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the trend toward 'yes' is real across two polls, but the 2025 result is still a tie, not a majority.

text: The share of Britons calling Die Hard a Christmas film rose from 30% in YouGov's December 2017 poll to 37% in its December 2022 poll.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it shows the same drift toward 'yes' in a second country, though 'no' still led in both years.

text: The word 'Christmas' appears 18 times in the Die Hard screenplay, and its four Christmas songs place it in the top 0.8% of films for holiday music.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it measures how much Christmas is on screen, not whether the story is about Christmas; the same analysis counted 'gun' 73 times.

text: Purchases and redemptions of Die Hard on Movies Anywhere rose 1,089% in December 2018 and 942% in December 2019 compared with other months.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a December spike shows people treat it as holiday viewing, but the samples were a few thousand users on one service.

text: A YouGov US holiday movie poll will show more people who have seen Die Hard calling it a Christmas movie than saying it is not.
US Google searches for Die Hard will peak during Christmas week in 2026 at more than five times their July 2026 level.
A follow-up survey found that viewers who called Die Hard a Christmas movie in their twenties still called it one ten years later and watched it mainly in December.
Production records from 1987 showed that Die Hard's makers chose the Christmas Eve setting to give the story its family reunion theme, not just for television reruns.
A film's genre can be decided by how audiences come to use the film, not only by what its makers intended when they made it.
A film that is set on Christmas Eve and uses Christmas songs, jokes and imagery on purpose has enough holiday content to count as a Christmas movie, even if its main story is about something else.
A Christmas movie does not have to be gentle or suitable for children, any more than a horror movie has to be frightening to everyone.
Yes, Die Hard is a Christmas Movie: A Semantic, Syntactic, Pragmatic Approach to Resolve the Debate Over Die Hard's Genre Status, Nathan Scoll, 2023
where_found: Comparative American Studies: An International Journal, vol. 20, no. 3-4 (Taylor and Francis)
bridge: The article applies Rick Altman's genre theory to argue that Die Hard became a Christmas movie through how audiences and the market use it, whatever its makers first intended.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a peer-reviewed genre argument rather than a joke, though it rests on accepting that audience use defines genre.

text: Die Hard's plot would work almost unchanged on any other night of the year, so Christmas is the film's setting rather than its subject.
bottom_line: Strong weight: this is the core of the 'set at Christmas, not about Christmas' case, and few of the film's turning points depend on the date.

text: A Christmas movie is one that evokes the spirit of Christmas, such as goodwill, generosity and peace, and Die Hard is an R-rated film built around killing.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it states a reasonable traditional definition, but it would also exclude darker films many people accept as Christmas movies.

text: Calling every film set at Christmas a Christmas movie would sweep in films like Eyes Wide Shut and Batman Returns, which would make the label useless for choosing what to watch.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the slippery-slope worry is fair, but supporters can answer that Die Hard uses Christmas far more than those films do.

text: The studio's Christmas marketing of Die Hard since 2017 is a campaign built on an internet joke, not evidence of what the film is.
bottom_line: Modest weight: true that the campaign rides a joke, but jokes that change how people watch a film can change its genre too.

text: In YouGov's November 2023 US poll, 50% of people who had seen Die Hard said it is not a Christmas movie and 39% said it is.
bottom_line: Strong weight against stating it as fact: in all three YouGov US polls from 2020 to 2025, 'not a Christmas movie' led, if only by a point in 2025.

text: In YouGov's December 2017 UK poll, 50% of Britons said a film set at Christmas but not about Christmas is not a Christmas film, against 31% who said it is.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it shows most people use the 'about, not just set at' rule, which is the rule Die Hard has trouble meeting.

text: YouGov's next US holiday movie poll will again find more people who have seen Die Hard saying it is not a Christmas movie than saying it is.
The December spike in US Google searches for Die Hard will shrink, with its 2028 Christmas-week peak smaller relative to its July level than its 2025 peak was.
YouGov polls showed the share of Die Hard viewers calling it a Christmas movie falling for two years in a row.
Streaming data showed that Die Hard's December viewing rise is no larger than that of 1980s action films with no Christmas setting.
A Christmas movie must be about Christmas itself, its meaning or its spirit, and not merely take place during the holiday.
How a studio first made and sold a film is better evidence of its genre than how audiences joke about it decades later.
The 'Christmas movie' label is useful only if it stays narrow enough to tell families what kind of film they are choosing.
No, 'Die Hard' Isn't a Christmas Movie, Most People Say, Morning Consult, 2018
where_found: Morning Consult (poll conducted with The Hollywood Reporter)
bridge: A survey of 2,200 U.S. adults taken November 15 to 18, 2018 found 62% said Die Hard is not a Christmas movie and 25% said it is.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a large poll showing the public rejected the label in 2018, though it asked all adults, including people who never saw the film.

text: Die Hard is NOT a Christmas movie, say Americans, Jamie Ballard, 2020
bridge: Among 1,500 U.S. adults, 44% said Die Hard is not a Christmas movie and 34% said it is; among people who had seen it, the split was 51% to 39%.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it counts only viewers in its sharper figure, which makes it a fairer test of the label than polls of all adults.

text: Bobby Bermea: 'Die Hard' - NOT a Christmas movie, Bobby Bermea, 2023
bridge: Bermea argues that Christmas stories like A Christmas Carol teach compassion and nonviolent answers, while Die Hard solves its problems with violence, so its holiday setting and songs are surface decoration.
bottom_line: Modest weight: a clear statement of the 'spirit of Christmas' definition, but one columnist's opinion rather than evidence about how the film is used.

text: Families who watch Die Hard every December need their tradition counted as real holiday viewing.
measured_by: The share of Die Hard viewers in YouGov's December polls who call it a Christmas movie.
if_true: The share rises past half and the tradition is treated as ordinary holiday viewing.
if_false: The share stays below half and the tradition remains a running joke rather than a recognized custom.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the tradition exists either way, but the label decides whether it counts as a real one.

text: TV and streaming programmers need December titles that draw viewers who skip sentimental holiday films.
measured_by: Die Hard's December streaming minutes and rentals compared with its average month.
if_true: December viewing keeps rising and programmers schedule it alongside holiday classics.
if_false: December viewing stays flat and programmers treat it as ordinary catalog action.
bottom_line: Modest weight: programmers already profit from the December spike whatever the label says.

text: Moviegoers who dislike sentimental holiday films need a Christmas movie of their own.
measured_by: How often Die Hard appears on published lists of best Christmas movies.
if_true: Die Hard holds a regular place on mainstream Christmas movie lists.
if_false: Die Hard drops off mainstream lists or appears only as a joke entry.
bottom_line: Modest weight: a real want, but one many other dark holiday films could also meet.

text: Parents of young children need the 'Christmas movie' label to signal viewing that is safe for the whole family.
measured_by: The share of films on mainstream Christmas movie lists rated G or PG.
if_true: The share falls as R-rated films like Die Hard join the lists.
if_false: The share stays high and the label keeps meaning family viewing.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the label is widely used as a family filter, though ratings do that job more reliably.

text: Fans of traditional Christmas films need the genre to keep meaning stories about goodwill and family.
measured_by: The share of Christmas movie lists and holiday programming given to films whose stories are about the holiday.
if_true: The share falls as films merely set at Christmas take more slots.
if_false: The share holds and the genre keeps its traditional meaning.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the genre's meaning matters to many viewers, but traditions have always grown by adding titles.

text: Film critics and teachers need genre labels that sort films by what they are about.
measured_by: Agreement among critics' and film reference guides' genre listings for films set at Christmas.
if_true: Reference guides start listing films by setting date, and agreement on the label drops.
if_false: Reference guides keep listing films by subject, and agreement holds.
bottom_line: Modest weight: precision matters to classifiers, but everyday genre talk has never been precise.

text: Treating Die Hard as a Christmas movie gives families with mixed tastes one holiday film that action fans and holiday fans will both sit down for.
bottom_line: Real but hard to count; the December viewing spikes suggest many households already use it this way.

text: Treating Die Hard as a Christmas movie earns its owner extra December revenue from streaming, rentals and theater re-releases every year.
bottom_line: Likely real, given the December 2023 theatrical return and December purchase spikes, but no public dollar figure exists.

text: Counting Die Hard as a Christmas movie gives people who dislike sentimental holiday films a way to join in the season's shared viewing.
bottom_line: Modest: it matters to the people it helps, but they can watch the film in December whatever it is called.

text: Parents who pick from Christmas movie lists may show young children Die Hard, an R-rated film with graphic violence and strong language.
bottom_line: Real but limited, since the R rating is printed on every listing and most parents check it.

text: Holiday screens, airtime and promotion given to Die Hard go to a 1988 catalog title instead of newer holiday films.
bottom_line: Small: Die Hard's December screenings are a handful against hundreds of holiday films each season.

text: The share of people who have seen Die Hard who call it a Christmas movie in YouGov's national December polls is a fair measure of whether audiences have adopted it as one.
The share of Die Hard's yearly viewing that falls in December is a fair measure of whether people treat it as a Christmas movie in practice.
The number of Die Hard's plot turning points that depend on the date being Christmas Eve is a fair measure of whether Christmas is the film's subject or only its setting.
Die Hard's story is set on Christmas Eve and uses Christmas as a deliberate part of its plot, music and jokes.
Whether a film counts as a Christmas movie is settled by its setting and by how audiences use it, rather than by whether its theme is the meaning of Christmas.
Enough viewers now treat Die Hard as holiday viewing for the Christmas movie label to describe a real, lasting practice rather than an internet joke.
If Die Hard is accepted as a Christmas movie, more streaming services and TV channels will schedule Die Hard in their December holiday lineups next to traditional Christmas films.
If Die Hard is accepted as a Christmas movie, more mainstream 'best Christmas movies' lists published each December will include Die Hard as a serious entry rather than a joke pick.

If Die Hard is accepted as a Christmas movie, the 'Christmas movie' label will come to cover R-rated action and horror films set at the holiday, splitting the category into family and adult kinds the way 'animated movie' has split.

If Die Hard is accepted as a Christmas movie, the share of Die Hard viewers in national polls who call it a Christmas movie will pass half within a decade as younger viewers who already lean that way grow older.
Die Hard is the greatest Christmas movie ever made.
Any film set at Christmas is a Christmas movie, whatever its story is about.
Die Hard can reasonably be watched as a Christmas movie by people who enjoy it that way.
Die Hard is an action movie set at Christmas that many viewers now treat as holiday viewing.
The Sopranos is the best television drama ever made.
bottom_line: Among all-time polls of American critics and television writers, The Sopranos is ranked first among dramas more often than any rival, but audience ratings favor Breaking Bad, one major list put Mad Men ahead, and almost every list is American. The fight is really about what "best" means (most influential, most consistent, or most loved), and no poll has yet asked the same broad group to rank the leading dramas against stated criteria.
hook: The Sopranos premiered in 1999 to fewer than 4 million viewers and went on to win 21 Emmys, including the first Outstanding Drama Series award ever given to a cable show (Television Academy).
question: Is The Sopranos the best television drama ever made, or have Breaking Bad, The Wire, Mad Men or a drama from another country done it better?
ask: The page most needs an all-time ranking from outside the United States, or a survey of viewers who have seen the leading dramas in full, that compares The Sopranos with its rivals under stated criteria.

text: The Sopranos proved that a weekly television series could carry the depth of a novel or a serious film, and most acclaimed dramas made since have built on that proof.
bottom_line: Heavy weight: the influence is widely acknowledged, though being first is a separate claim from being best, which the opposing side presses.

text: The Sopranos has been ranked first among dramas in more all-time polls of critics, actors and television writers than any other series.
bottom_line: Heavy weight, because these are the people best placed to compare dramas; the limit is that nearly all of these polls are American.

text: James Gandolfini's performance as Tony Soprano made a violent, selfish man sympathetic without excusing him, a balance few lead performances in television drama have matched.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: his three Emmys back it up, but ranking performances against each other is a matter of judgment.

text: The Sopranos mixed crime story, family comedy, psychotherapy and dream imagery in one series, a range of tones that later dramas rarely attempt.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: range is a real strength, though some viewers count tonal focus as a virtue rather than a lack.

text: The Sopranos kept its writing and acting at a high level across six seasons and 86 episodes, a longer stretch than many acclaimed dramas sustain.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: length makes consistency harder, but critics disagree about whether the later seasons held up.

text: The next edition of Rolling Stone's or Variety's all-time list of the greatest TV shows will rank The Sopranos first among dramas.
If the Writers Guild of America polls its members again on the best-written television series, The Sopranos will again place first.
A survey of viewers who have watched The Sopranos, Breaking Bad and The Wire in full finds that most of them rank The Sopranos first.
A poll of television critics from outside the United States, with The Sopranos eligible, ranks The Sopranos first among all dramas.
Some television dramas are better than others in ways that can be argued for with reasons, not merely felt.
The judgment of critics, actors and television writers is a better guide to which drama is best than audience star ratings.
How much a drama achieved, including how far it pushed what television could do, counts toward how good it is.
The Sopranos Sessions, Matt Zoller Seitz and Alan Sepinwall, 2019
bridge: Two veteran television critics who first reviewed The Sopranos while it aired go through all 86 episodes and argue that the series holds up under close study, scene by scene.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it is the most detailed critical case for The Sopranos, but its authors set out to celebrate the show rather than to weigh it against rivals.

text: No shared yardstick exists for ranking television dramas against each other, so calling any one series the best ever states a taste rather than a fact.
bottom_line: Heavy weight as a caution about the word "best", though it cuts against every rival claim equally and does not by itself favor another show.

text: The Wire portrays the institutions of a whole city (police, schools, docks, newspapers, City Hall) with a breadth that The Sopranos, centered on one family, does not attempt.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a 2021 BBC Culture poll of 206 critics chose The Wire as the best series of the 21st century, but The Sopranos was not eligible for that poll.

text: The Sopranos' final two seasons contain slow, wandering stretches that weaken its claim to consistent excellence across its whole run.
bottom_line: Light to moderate weight: some viewers fault the late seasons and others count them among the best, so this is a dispute about taste.

text: All-time television rankings are drawn almost entirely from American, English-language shows, so dramas made in other countries have rarely been weighed against The Sopranos at all.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the polls cited for The Sopranos really are mostly American, which limits what "ever made" can honestly claim.

text: Variety's 2023 list of the 100 greatest TV shows of all time ranked I Love Lucy first, Mad Men second and The Sopranos third, placing Mad Men above The Sopranos among dramas.
bottom_line: Moderate: it is a major list that did not put The Sopranos first among dramas, though it is a single exception among the six all-time rankings found, and it was chosen by one magazine's staff.

text: A drama other than The Sopranos will be the top-ranked drama in most all-time television polls published between 2026 and 2030.
A drama that premiered after 2010 will be ranked above The Sopranos in at least one major all-time television poll by Rolling Stone, Variety, the BBC or the Writers Guild of America.
A new all-time poll of more than 200 critics, with The Sopranos eligible, ranks another drama first by a clear margin.
A study of interviews with the creators of later acclaimed dramas finds that they name other series more often than The Sopranos as their model.
Ranking television dramas against each other mostly reflects personal taste and the moment a viewer first saw them.
A later drama that improves on an earlier one deserves more credit for quality, even if the earlier one deserves more credit for influence.
A claim about the best drama "ever made" has to account for dramas made outside the United States and in languages other than English.
The 100 greatest TV series of the 21st century, BBC Culture, 2021
bridge: A poll of 206 critics from many countries ranked The Wire first among series of the 21st century, so the critics' consensus about a top drama is not settled in favor of The Sopranos.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it is a large international poll, but The Sopranos premiered in 1999 and was not eligible, so it shows a rival is strong rather than that The Sopranos is weaker.

text: Film and television students need a short, agreed list of landmark dramas to study.
measured_by: Share of university television studies courses that assign episodes of The Sopranos.
if_true: The share stays high and The Sopranos remains the default case study for the modern drama.
if_false: Courses split their time among several dramas with no single default.
bottom_line: A real need, though it is met by a short list of several dramas as well as by a single number one.

text: Television writers need proof that long-form character drama can stand beside the novel and the film.
measured_by: How television dramas place in critics' polls that mix films and series, and in Writers Guild of America member polls.
if_true: A television drama keeps being ranked alongside the greatest films and novels.
if_false: The case for television's standing rests on several shows rather than one clear landmark.
bottom_line: Moderate: the status of television writing no longer depends on one show, but The Sopranos is still the example most often cited.

text: Viewers with little free time need a reliable answer about which long drama series are worth dozens of hours.
measured_by: Share of viewers who start The Sopranos and finish all 86 episodes, compared with rival dramas.
if_true: Viewers who start The Sopranos on a recommendation mostly finish it.
if_false: Many of those viewers drop The Sopranos and finish a rival drama instead.
bottom_line: Moderate: a good recommendation saves real time, but completion rates are rarely published.

text: Fans of Breaking Bad and The Wire need their shows judged by the same yardsticks as The Sopranos, not by which came first.
measured_by: Where Breaking Bad and The Wire place relative to The Sopranos in rankings that publish their criteria and scores.
if_true: The Sopranos still comes out ahead when the criteria are stated in advance.
if_false: Breaking Bad or The Wire ties with or passes The Sopranos once the criteria are stated.
bottom_line: Strong as a fairness point; TV (The Book) already found a tie when the criteria were spelled out.

text: Television makers outside the United States need their dramas counted in all-time rankings.
measured_by: Share of non-American dramas in all-time top 100 television lists.
if_true: The share stays low and the question is settled among American shows.
if_false: International dramas enter the lists and compete with The Sopranos for the top place.
bottom_line: Moderate: the gap in the lists is real, but it says more about who votes than about which show is best.

text: Showrunners making dramas today need room for a new series to be called the best without being measured against a fixed idol.
measured_by: Whether dramas premiering after 2010 reach the top three of major all-time television polls.
if_true: Newer dramas rarely break into the top three, and The Sopranos holds the top place.
if_false: Newer dramas reach the top three and sometimes pass The Sopranos.
bottom_line: Moderate: a reputation can harden into a habit, though new shows have passed older ones on several lists already.

text: Treating The Sopranos as the benchmark gives new viewers a dependable first choice when they want to see what television drama can do.
bottom_line: Real but modest: a clear recommendation saves time, though a reader who would prefer another drama is steered wrong.

text: Recognizing The Sopranos as the best drama ever made strengthens the case that television deserves the serious study given to novels and films.
bottom_line: Moderate: a shared reference helps teaching, though the series is already widely taught whether or not it is ranked first.

text: Holding up The Sopranos as the peak of the form encourages networks and streaming services to keep funding slow, character-driven dramas.
bottom_line: Uncertain: buyers fund shows for many reasons, and a single show's reputation is one input among many.

text: Naming The Sopranos the best drama ever made draws attention away from dramas made outside the United States, which all-time lists already rarely include.
bottom_line: Moderate: the lists are already lopsided, and a fixed number one can make that harder to correct.

text: Treating The Sopranos as the fixed peak pushes new dramas toward copying its antihero formula instead of trying new forms.
bottom_line: Light to moderate: the antihero wave after 2000 is real, but how much of it followed from ranking The Sopranos first is hard to show.

text: Crowning The Sopranos on the strength of being first undervalues later dramas that may have done the same things better.
bottom_line: Moderate: credit for coming first is a fair factor but not the only one, and tie-breaking toward the older show is a real habit of critics.

text: The Sopranos' rank among dramas in all-time television polls published from 2026 onward, counting only polls with at least 50 voters, is a fair measure of whether experts judge it the best drama ever made.
The Sopranos' average audience rating compared with other dramas on the largest rating sites is a fair measure of how highly viewers who watched it value it.
The share of acclaimed later dramas whose creators name The Sopranos as their main model is a fair measure of how far The Sopranos set the standard for the form.
Television dramas can be meaningfully ranked against each other by standards that viewers and critics could share.
The Sopranos ranks above Breaking Bad, The Wire and every other drama on the standards that matter most.
The pool of dramas The Sopranos has been compared against is wide enough to support the words "ever made".
Streaming services that carry The Sopranos would promote it as the first recommendation for new viewers looking for a classic drama.
Television writing and film courses would keep The Sopranos as their main case study for the modern serialized drama rather than rotating among several shows.
New dramas over the next decade would continue to be judged by critics in terms of how they compare with The Sopranos.
The Sopranos would keep placing first in all-time television polls taken ten or more years after its 2007 finale, as newer dramas are added to the ballot.
The Sopranos is the greatest work of art ever made for television in any genre, comedy included.
No television drama made since The Sopranos ended in 2007 has come close to equaling it.
The Sopranos is among the three or four best American television dramas ever made.
The Sopranos is the most influential television drama ever made, whether or not it is the best.
Taylor Swift is the most important popular musician of the twenty-first century so far.
bottom_line: On commercial measures Taylor Swift's case is stronger than anyone's: the biggest tour ever, the biggest album week ever, six IFPI global titles and first place on Billboard's 25-year chart. The evidence thins on influence over how music sounds and on reach beyond English-speaking countries, where Beyoncé, the leading rappers and Bad Bunny have real claims, so the fight is mostly about whether "most important" means biggest or most influential.
hook: In June 2023 the Federal Reserve's Beige Book reported that May had been Philadelphia's strongest month for hotel revenue since the pandemic began, "in large part due to" the crowds at Taylor Swift's three concerts in the city.
question: Is Taylor Swift the most important popular musician of the twenty-first century so far?
ask: The page most needs a careful count of which artists today's newer hit-makers name as their main influences, because that would test influence on how music is made, the one part of the claim that sales figures cannot settle.

text: Taylor Swift holds the biggest commercial records of the century, including the highest-grossing concert tour ever and the largest one-week album total in United States chart history.
bottom_line: Strong weight on the 'popular' half of the claim, since these records measure how many people chose her music, but sales alone do not settle 'important.'

text: Taylor Swift has stayed at or near the top of popular music for about twenty years, across country, pop and indie-folk, which almost no star of any era has managed.
bottom_line: Considerable weight, because importance over a 25-year span should reward lasting at the top, not one peak; rivals like Beyoncé and Drake also have long runs, so it does not settle the question alone.

text: Taylor Swift is the principal writer of her own songs, and her four Album of the Year Grammys, a record, show that working musicians and industry voters rate her songwriting craft, not just her sales.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because Grammy voting is a real peer judgment but has well-known blind spots, and Bad Bunny's 2026 win shows the award can point elsewhere too.

text: Taylor Swift's reach spread beyond music into the wider economy and politics: the Federal Reserve noted her concerts' effect on Philadelphia hotel revenue, and one Instagram post in 2023 drove more than 35,000 voter registrations at Vote.org.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, since effects outside music are a fair sign of cultural importance, though these are single episodes rather than lasting changes.

text: Billboard's chart-based ranking of the Top Artists of the 21st Century, built from Billboard 200 and Hot 100 performance from January 1, 2000 through December 31, 2024, places Taylor Swift at No. 1, ahead of Drake at No. 2 and Rihanna at No. 3.
bottom_line: Strong evidence for the commercial side of the claim, limited to United States charts.

text: IFPI named Taylor Swift its biggest-selling global recording artist of the year for 2014, 2019, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, making her the first artist to win the title six times.
bottom_line: Strong evidence that her commercial lead is worldwide and lasting, since IFPI counts sales and streams across many countries and services.

text: Taylor Swift won the Album of the Year Grammy for Fearless, 1989, Folklore and Midnights, becoming in 2024 the only artist with four wins in that category, ahead of Frank Sinatra, Stevie Wonder and Paul Simon with three each.
bottom_line: Moderate evidence of peer esteem, since Grammy voters are industry members, though the award is often criticized for favoring commercial hits.

text: Taylor Swift will be named IFPI's biggest-selling global recording artist for at least one of the years 2026, 2027 or 2028.
Billboard's next chart-based ranking of the century's top artists, covering at least through 2029, will still place Taylor Swift at No. 1.
A large survey of professional songwriters finds that Taylor Swift is the living songwriter they most often name as an influence on their own work.
How many people choose a musician's records, concerts and streams over many years is a fair part of what makes that musician important, not just a measure of marketing.
Songwriting and changes to how the music business treats artists count toward a musician's importance as much as changes in how music sounds.
Twenty-five years of evidence is enough to rank the musicians of the twenty-first century so far, even if later generations judge differently.

Sam Lansky wrote in Time's December 2023 Person of the Year cover story that Taylor Swift sits in rarefied company as a pop star alongside Elvis Presley, Michael Jackson and Madonna, and that as a songwriter she has been compared to Bob Dylan, Paul McCartney and Joni Mitchell.
Taylor Swift Is TIME's 2023 Person of the Year, Sam Lansky, 2023
bridge: Time made Taylor Swift the first person from the arts to be its Person of the Year, and Sam Lansky's cover story places her alongside Elvis Presley, Michael Jackson and Madonna as a pop star and calls her the last shared culture left in a split-up world.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because it is a serious magazine's considered judgment about one year at her peak, not a measured comparison across the whole century.

text: Heartbreak Is the National Anthem: How Taylor Swift Reinvented Pop Music, Rob Sheffield, 2024
bridge: Rolling Stone critic Rob Sheffield argues across a full book that Taylor Swift changed what pop songwriting does, which is the strongest case that her importance is artistic and not only commercial.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, since it is a detailed argument from an experienced critic, but its author writes openly as a fan and it does not weigh her against rivals in the same depth.

text: Commercial size is not the same as importance, and the most important musician of an era is the one who changes what music sounds like, which Taylor Swift has generally done less than she has refined sounds others started.
bottom_line: Strong weight, because this is the main definitional dispute; it is weakened by the fact that songwriting style, which she has shaped, is also part of how music sounds.

text: Hip-hop became the most-listened-to genre in the United States during this century, so its leading figures, such as Kanye West, Drake and Kendrick Lamar, did more to shape the era's music than any pop star did.
bottom_line: Strong weight, since genre-level change is a fair test of importance, though it splits the credit among several rappers rather than naming one person above Swift.

text: Beyoncé has the stronger claim to being the century's most important musician because she combined huge sales with bolder artistic moves, which is why Billboard's editors ranked her first among 21st-century pop stars.
bottom_line: Considerable weight, because an expert panel weighing the whole 25 years preferred her, though one magazine's staff list is a single judgment, and the same list put Swift second.

text: Taylor Swift's dominance is strongest in English-speaking countries, while Bad Bunny was Spotify's top global artist in four of the six years from 2020 to 2025 and won the first Album of the Year Grammy for a Spanish-language album in 2026.
bottom_line: Substantial weight against a worldwide claim, though IFPI's global sales chart, which counts more than one streaming service, still put Swift first in 2025.

text: Taylor Swift's record sales figures are generally inflated by marketing tactics such as many collectible vinyl and CD variants of one album, so they measure fan devotion more than broad influence.
