text: Parents of young children need clear limits on video game designs built to maximize spending and play time, without those designs being shielded as art.
measured_by: Number of enforceable consumer protection rules on game spending features that survive court challenge.
if_true: Courts and lawmakers give game designs more deference as artistic expression, and fewer limits survive.
if_false: Lawmakers can regulate game monetization like other consumer products.
bottom_line: A serious interest, though it bears more on how games are regulated than on whether they are art.

text: Novelists, filmmakers and other artists working in older forms need scarce arts grants and museum space not to be split with a much richer game industry.
measured_by: Share of public arts grant dollars and museum exhibition days going to game projects.
if_true: The share going to games rises, and older forms get less.
if_false: Arts funding stays focused on forms that lack a large commercial market.
bottom_line: A real but modest interest, since the amounts at stake are small next to game industry revenue.

text: Teachers need class time for literature and film that has stood the test of time rather than for commercial entertainment products.
measured_by: Hours of literature and film instruction per school year in secondary schools.
if_true: Some of those hours shift to games.
if_false: Classroom time stays with established literature and film.
bottom_line: A reasonable concern about scarce time, though it assumes no game has earned a place in that time.

text: Treating video games as an art form on a level with film and literature would make game projects eligible for arts grants, festival recognition and serious criticism on the same terms as films and books.
bottom_line: Plausible and partly happening already through the National Endowment for the Arts, but the size of the gain is unmeasured.

text: Treating video games as art would push museums, libraries and archives to preserve old games before the machines that run them stop working.
bottom_line: A real benefit, since art status is what usually unlocks preservation budgets, though the number of games at risk has not been counted here.

text: Treating video games as art would let teachers use well-made games to teach storytelling, history and moral reasoning to students who already play them.
bottom_line: Reasonable given that Pew found 85% of U.S. teens play video games in 2024, but no study here shows games teach these skills as well as books do.

text: Treating video games as art on a level with film and literature would make it easier for game companies to defend designs built to maximize spending and play time as protected expression.
bottom_line: A real concern because the Brown decision already struck down a game sales law, though the art question and the consumer protection question can be separated in law.

text: Treating video games as art would split scarce arts grants and museum space between older art forms and a game industry that already earns far more than they do.
bottom_line: Moderate: the funding pool is small and the game industry is large, but how much money would actually move has not been measured.

text: Treating video games as art would let games take class time that schools now give to novels, plays and films with a long record of teaching value.
bottom_line: Speculative: few schools teach games now, so the displacement is a risk rather than an observed effect.

text: How a panel of art, film and literary critics rates acclaimed video games against acclaimed films and novels, judged on the same artistic-merit scale, is a fair measure of whether games stand on a level with film and literature.
The share of U.S. adults who say video games can be art as much as films and books, tracked over time in a national poll, is a fair measure of whether the public grants games equal standing.

The number of video games entering the permanent collections of major art museums each decade, compared with the number of films, is a fair measure of whether cultural institutions treat games as equals of film.
Video games can express ideas and produce serious aesthetic experiences in the way films and novels do.
At least some video games match the artistic achievement of the best films and novels, not just the average ones.
Different art forms can be placed on a common scale of artistic standing, so that one medium can be said to be on a level with another.

If video games are accepted as an art form on a level with film and literature, more general-interest newspapers and magazines would review notable games in their arts sections alongside films and books within a year or two.

If video games are accepted as an art form on a level with film and literature, public arts councils would open more grant programs to game developers on the same terms as independent filmmakers and writers within a year or two.

Over a decade, accepting video games as an art form on a level with film and literature would put selected games on high school and university reading lists in literature and media courses the way films entered them in the late twentieth century.

Over a decade, accepting video games as an art form on a level with film and literature would lead national archives and libraries to preserve historically important games in playable form, as film archives preserve old movies.
The best video games are already greater works of art than the best films and novels, because interactivity gives games a power that older art forms lack.
Video games will become the leading art form of the twenty-first century, the way film was the leading art form of the twentieth.
Some video games are works of art, even if the medium as a whole has not yet matched the best of film and literature.
Video games can be an art form, but they should be judged by standards of their own rather than compared with film and literature.
Violent video games do not make the people who play them more violent.
bottom_line: The evidence is strong that violent video games do not turn players into people who commit serious violence, and fairly strong that any effect on everyday physical aggression is small; it is still disputed whether that small effect is real or an artifact of weak methods and publication bias. Much of the fight is about wording: researchers who find harm usually measure aggression, while this belief speaks of violence.
hook: In 2020 the American Psychological Association revised its resolution on violent video games to say that attributing violence to violent video gaming is not scientifically sound, while still listing a link to aggressive behavior.
question: Do violent video games make the people who play them more violent, or is the link too small, or too badly measured, to matter?
ask: This page most needs a preregistered long-term study, or a row citing one, that follows children for more than a year and measures real physical violence rather than lab tasks or questionnaires.

text: The best-designed long-term studies of violent video games find effects on youth aggression too small to tell apart from zero.
bottom_line: Heavy weight, because a 2020 meta-analysis of 28 longitudinal samples found the effect shrank to about r = 0.01 in the studies that followed the most good research practices.

text: Lab experiments that claimed violent video games raise aggression appear to have been inflated by publication bias, since studies with null results were less likely to be published.
bottom_line: Moderate to heavy weight, because a 2017 reanalysis in Psychological Bulletin found that bias-adjusted experimental effects on aggressive behavior were very small, though it did not show them to be zero.

text: Most research labeled as showing that violent video games cause aggression measures mild acts like blasting a stranger with noise or answering a questionnaire, not acts of real violence that hurt someone.
bottom_line: Heavy weight on the wording of this belief, because even the American Psychological Association's 2020 resolution says the research has not focused on lethal violence and that blaming violence on games is not scientifically sound.

text: Violent video games became far more popular over decades in which violent crime among young Americans generally did not rise along with them, which is hard to square with games making their players more violent.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because crime trends have many causes and a population trend cannot rule out a small effect on individual players.

text: Time spent playing video games at home is time not spent in the street settings where most youth violence happens, so violent video games may take more violence away than they add.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because an economics working paper by Cunningham, Engelstätter and Ward found this kind of displacement effect, but it rests on one line of crime-data analysis.

text: People who are already aggressive tend to seek out violent video games, so the link between playing them and aggression is generally explained by who chooses the games rather than by what the games do.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because longitudinal studies that control for earlier aggression cut the link down sharply, though some small link usually remains.

text: A meta-analysis of 28 longitudinal samples covering about 21,000 young people found an overall link of r = 0.059 between aggressive game play and later aggression, and r = 0.012 (95% confidence interval -0.010 to 0.034) in the studies that followed the most good research practices.
bottom_line: Strong evidence for the belief, because it pools the long-term studies that matter most, though one of its authors is a long-standing critic of the harm hypothesis.

text: Adults randomly assigned to play Grand Theft Auto V daily for two months showed no significant changes in aggression, empathy or impulsivity compared with adults who played The Sims 3 or no game, either right after the period or two months later.
bottom_line: Strong design but limited reach, because it was one modest-sized trial of adults rather than children.

text: In a preregistered study of 1,004 British 14 and 15 year olds, recent violent video game play was not linked to the aggressive behavior their caregivers reported, and no tipping point of heavy play was found.
bottom_line: Good evidence, because the analysis plan was fixed before the data were seen, though it is a single snapshot rather than a long-term study.

text: Preregistered longitudinal studies of violent video games published after 2026 will mostly find no statistically reliable link between violent game play and later physical aggression once earlier aggression is controlled.
No new meta-analysis restricted to high-quality studies will find an effect of violent video games on physical aggression as large as r = 0.10.

A preregistered, multi-lab study following thousands of children for several years finds no link between violent video game play and later physical aggression or arrests after controlling for earlier aggression and family factors.

A long-term randomized trial with children, run with parental consent and age-appropriate violent games, finds no difference in observer-rated physical aggression between the violent-game and nonviolent-game groups.
A link between violent video games and aggression that is too small to tell apart from zero in well-run studies should be treated as no meaningful link at all.
Lab measures such as blasting a stranger with noise or finishing word puzzles tell us little about whether a person will actually hurt someone.
When people who play violent video games are more aggressive, it is mostly because aggressive people choose those games, not because the games changed them.

Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, writing for the majority in Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association (2011), said the psychological studies California relied on do not prove that violent video games cause minors to act aggressively.
Psychologist Christopher J. Ferguson of Stetson University has argued in many studies and in the 2017 book Moral Combat that violent video games do not make the people who play them more violent.

Psychologist Patrick M. Markey of Villanova University has argued, in Moral Combat and in published crime-data research, that the release of popular violent video games is not followed by rises in violent crime.
Moral Combat: Why the War on Violent Video Games Is Wrong, by Patrick M. Markey and Christopher J. Ferguson (2017)
bridge: Two researchers who study media effects walk through the lab studies, crime trends and mass-shooting claims and argue that violent games do not turn players into violent people.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because it gathers the skeptical case clearly for ordinary readers, but it is written by advocates of one side of the research fight.

text: Do longitudinal studies support long-term relationships between aggressive game play and youth aggressive behaviour? A meta-analytic examination, by Aaron Drummond, James D. Sauer and Christopher J. Ferguson (2020)
bridge: This pooled analysis of long-term studies found the link between aggressive game play and later youth aggression was very small and shrank further in the best-run studies.
bottom_line: Heavy weight, because it looks at the long-term question this belief is about, though its authors are known skeptics and other pooled analyses reach somewhat larger numbers.

text: Violent video game engagement is not associated with adolescents' aggressive behaviour: evidence from a registered report, by Andrew K. Przybylski and Netta Weinstein (2019)
bridge: In a large sample of British teenagers, with the analysis plan fixed before the data were seen, playing violent games was not linked to aggression as rated by the teenagers' caregivers.
bottom_line: Moderate to heavy weight, because a preregistered design guards against cherry-picking, but it is one survey taken at one point in time.

text: Every major meta-analysis of violent video games, including those by critics of the research, finds at least a small positive link between playing them and later aggressive behavior.
bottom_line: Heavy weight, because Mathur and VanderWeele's 2019 reanalysis concluded that all the warring meta-analyses agree that violent games increase aggressive behavior in most settings, while agreeing the effects are almost always small.

text: Studies that follow children for months or years and control for how aggressive they already were still find that playing violent video games predicts more physical aggression later.
bottom_line: Heavy weight, because a 2018 PNAS meta-analysis of 24 such studies found a link that survived controls and showed no sign of publication bias.

text: Hitting, pushing and biting are violent acts even when they fall short of crime, so research showing violent video games raise physical aggression in children does show those children becoming more violent.
bottom_line: Moderate to heavy weight, because the dispute here is partly about what counts as violent, and the American Psychological Association notes the aggressive behaviors studied include hitting and pushing.

text: A small increase in aggression spread across the hundreds of millions of people who play violent video games can add up to many extra fights and injuries even if no single player is changed much.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because the arithmetic is sound but no study has counted the extra injuries it implies.

text: Violent video games reward players for repeatedly practicing attacks on human-looking targets, which gives them a plausible way to make aggression feel more normal in a way that watching films does not.
bottom_line: Light to moderate weight, because the mechanism is plausible but long-term trials such as the two-month Grand Theft Auto V study have not detected it.

text: The American Psychological Association's own task force reviewed the research and concluded that violent video game use is a risk factor for aggressive behavior and reduced empathy.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because a professional body's review counts for something, but the same task force found too few studies to judge any link to crime or delinquency.

text: A meta-analysis of 98 independent studies with 36,965 participants found that violent video games increase aggression and decrease prosocial behavior, with effects showing up in experimental, correlational and longitudinal studies.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because it is large, but it mixes lab measures of aggression with real behavior and predates the bias reanalyses.

text: A large preregistered longitudinal study of children will find that heavier violent video game play predicts more teacher-reported or parent-reported physical aggression a year later, after controlling for earlier aggression.
A randomized trial lasting at least a month will find that people assigned to play violent video games show more observed physical aggression than people assigned to nonviolent games.

A preregistered long-term study finds that heavy violent video game play predicts later assault arrests or school fights even after controlling for earlier aggression, home violence and peer delinquency.
A randomized trial lasting months finds a dose-response pattern in which more hours of violent video game play produce more observed physical aggression than the same hours of nonviolent play.
Pushing, hitting and other everyday physical aggression count as people becoming more violent, even when nobody is seriously hurt.
A small average effect on each player still matters when it is spread across hundreds of millions of people who play violent video games.
The pooled results of many lab and long-term studies of violent video games are more trustworthy than the reanalyses that say publication bias inflated them.

Psychologist Craig A. Anderson of Iowa State University, lead author of a 2010 Psychological Bulletin meta-analysis, has concluded that exposure to violent video games is a causal risk factor for aggressive behavior in the people who play them.
Psychologist Brad J. Bushman of Ohio State University has argued in his research and public writing that playing violent video games increases aggression in players.

Supreme Court Justice Stephen Breyer, dissenting in Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association (2011), wrote that the research gave California's legislature a reasonable basis to conclude that violent video games can harm children.

Violent video game effects on aggression, empathy, and prosocial behavior in Eastern and Western countries: A meta-analytic review, by Craig A. Anderson, Akiko Shibuya, Nobuko Ihori, Edward L. Swing, Brad J. Bushman, Akira Sakamoto, Hannah R. Rothstein and Muniba Saleem (2010)
bridge: This large pooled analysis concluded that playing violent video games is a causal risk factor for more aggressive behavior and thoughts and for less empathy, in both Eastern and Western countries.
bottom_line: Heavy weight as the most cited study on this side, though later reanalyses argued its experimental effects were inflated by publication bias.

text: Metaanalysis of the relationship between violent video game play and physical aggression over time, by Anna T. Prescott, James D. Sargent and Jay G. Hull (2018)
where_found: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
bridge: Pooling long-term studies that controlled for earlier aggression, the authors found that violent game play still predicted later physical aggression.
bottom_line: Heavy weight, because it addresses the strongest objection (that aggressive kids pick violent games) and still finds a link, though the link is small.

text: Finding common ground in meta-analysis "wars" on violent video games, by Maya B. Mathur and Tyler J. VanderWeele (2019)
bridge: Two outside statisticians reanalyzed the rival pooled studies and found they agree that violent games raise aggressive behavior in most settings, while also agreeing the effects are almost always small.
bottom_line: Heavy weight, because the authors were not party to the fight, though their finding is about aggression and says little about serious violence.

text: Game developers and studio workers need their work kept free of blame for violence it did not cause.
measured_by: Number of lawsuits, bills and official statements blaming video games for real violence.
if_true: Such lawsuits, bills and statements lose their factual basis and should decline.
if_false: Some regulation and liability becomes justified by real harm.
bottom_line: A real interest, though it is also the interest of the companies that profit from the games, so it deserves scrutiny.

text: Families of people killed in shootings need lawmakers to focus on causes of violence the evidence supports.
measured_by: Share of public statements and bills after mass shootings that address supported risk factors rather than media.
if_true: Attention spent on video games after shootings is shown to be wasted and can be redirected.
if_false: Video games become one legitimate target among several for prevention.
bottom_line: A serious interest, backed by the American Psychological Association's warning that blaming games draws attention from other factors.

text: Parents of young children need to know whether the games their children play make them more aggressive.
measured_by: Children's physical aggression as reported by parents and teachers over time.
if_true: Children's aggression does not depend on whether their games are violent.
if_false: Children who play more violent games show somewhat more aggression over time.
bottom_line: A strong interest, because parents make these choices daily and even a small effect matters to them.

text: Pediatricians need sound guidance on which media habits harm children's development.
measured_by: Whether professional guidance on violent media matches the best available long-term studies.
if_true: Guidance warning about violent games should be softened to match the evidence.
if_false: Guidance warning about violent games is confirmed and should be followed.
bottom_line: A moderate interest, because doctors need accurate advice whichever way the evidence falls.

text: If violent video games do not make players more violent, lawmakers who stop blaming them after mass shootings can spend that attention on causes of violence the evidence supports.
bottom_line: A real benefit if the belief is true, but hard to measure because political attention has no standard unit.

text: If violent video games do not make players more violent, teenagers who enjoy them are spared being treated as suspects by schools and adults because of what they play.
bottom_line: A modest but real benefit for millions of young players, with no good count of how often game choice is now held against them.

text: If violent video games do not make players more violent, game studios avoid lawsuits and laws that blame their products for violence they did not cause.
bottom_line: A benefit mainly to the industry, already partly secured by the 2011 Supreme Court decision in Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association.

text: If violent video games do raise physical aggression slightly and parents act on this belief, children will on average become a little more physically aggressive than they would have been.
bottom_line: Small per child, using the covariate-adjusted estimate from the 2018 PNAS meta-analysis, but it would apply across millions of children.

text: If violent video games do reduce empathy as some reviews report, pediatricians who stop advising families about violent game content will lose a tool for protecting children's social development.
bottom_line: A minor cost, because pediatric advice on screen time would continue for other reasons.

text: The pooled effect of violent video game play on later physical aggression, in preregistered longitudinal studies that control for earlier aggression, is a fair measure of whether violent video games make players more violent.

The difference in physical aggression between people randomly assigned to play violent and nonviolent video games for at least a month is a fair measure of whether violent video games cause more violent behavior.

The rate of violent offenses by young people in the weeks after a best-selling violent video game is released, compared with matched weeks without such a release, is a fair measure of whether violent games add violence to the real world.
Well-run studies of violent video games find no effect on players' aggression or violence large enough to matter.
Playing violent video games does not cause a person to act more violently than that same person would have acted without playing them.
Becoming more violent means doing more acts that hurt or threaten real people, not just scoring higher on lab tests of aggressive thoughts or mild aggression.
Lawmakers and officials would stop naming violent video games as a cause after mass shootings and turn their attention to other explanations.
Parents would treat violent video games as a question of age-appropriate content and time limits rather than as a threat to their children's safety.
Courts and schools would stop treating a young person's taste in violent video games as a warning sign when judging whether that person is dangerous.
Violent video games have no effect of any kind on the aggressive thoughts, feelings or behavior of the people who play them.
Violent video games reduce real-world violence, because they give aggressive people a harmless outlet and keep them off the street.
Violent video games do not make the people who play them commit serious violence, even if they may slightly raise mild aggression for a short time.
Any effect of violent video games on how violent their players become is too small to justify laws beyond the existing age ratings.
The United States will be in a recession at some point before the end of 2027.
bottom_line: The hard data through September 2026 show an economy still growing (2.2 percent in the second quarter, tracking near 3.7 percent in the third) while hiring has nearly stopped, energy prices are up sharply after a record oil shock, and the Fed is raising rates. The real fight is whether that oil shock plus tighter money can overpower AI investment and a country that now exports more oil than it imports; forecasters put the odds of trouble at roughly one in five, betting markets higher, and both have a poor record a year out.
hook: The 2026 war around the Strait of Hormuz cut world oil supply by about 10 million barrels a day, which the World Bank called the largest oil supply shock on record, and in September 2026 the Federal Reserve raised interest rates in the same month U.S. employers added just 29,000 jobs.
question: Will the United States fall into a recession, as dated by the NBER, at some point before the end of 2027?
ask: The page most needs a recession probability model with a published track record, scored against the NBER rule for October 2026 through December 2027, so the odds rest on something checkable rather than on opinion.

text: The 2026 war around the Strait of Hormuz caused the largest oil supply shock on record, and big oil price spikes have come before nearly every U.S. recession since World War II.
bottom_line: This is the strongest reason to agree. The shock is real and historic. But the United States now exports more oil than it imports, so the old link between oil spikes and recessions may be weaker than it was in 1973 or 1979.

text: The Federal Reserve raising interest rates in September 2026, at a time when U.S. hiring had nearly stalled, makes it more likely that tighter money pushes a slowing economy into recession.
bottom_line: Moderate weight. A rate increase made because of an oil shock is the classic recipe for a policy mistake. Still, a 3.75 to 4 percent policy rate is not tight by historical standards, and the Fed can reverse course quickly.

text: Economists and forecasting surveys have almost never predicted a recession a year ahead, so the low recession odds forecasters gave in 2026 are weak evidence that a U.S. recession before the end of 2027 is unlikely.
bottom_line: Real but limited weight. This argument knocks down the case against more than it builds the case for: a poor forecasting record means the odds are uncertain, not that they are high.

text: The U.S. economic expansion that began in April 2020 will be more than seven years old by the end of 2027, longer than the postwar average expansion of about 64 months.
bottom_line: Low weight. Age alone says little: postwar expansions have run anywhere from 12 months to 128 months, and none ended simply because it was old.

text: The 2026 Middle East war caused the largest oil supply shock on record, with an initial cut to world oil supply of about 10 million barrels a day, and energy prices were projected to rise 24 percent in 2026.
bottom_line: Strong evidence that the shock is historic in size; it does not by itself say how much of it reaches U.S. output.

text: All but one of the 11 U.S. recessions after World War II were associated with an increase in the price of oil, the exception being the recession of 1960.
bottom_line: A well-known historical pattern, but oil rises often and "associated with" is not proof the oil caused each recession, and the U.S. was a big oil importer for most of those years.

text: U.S. employers added just 29,000 jobs in September 2026, July was revised to a loss of 10,000 jobs, and July and August together were revised down by 60,000.
bottom_line: Solid official data showing hiring near a standstill; the unemployment rate (4.2 percent) has not yet risen, so this is a warning sign rather than a recession signal.

text: Of 153 recessions in 63 countries from 1992 to 2014, only 5 had been predicted by the consensus of forecasters by April of the year before the recession began.
bottom_line: Strong evidence that low forecast odds are weak comfort; it argues for humility about any forecast, including forecasts of a recession.

text: The real-time Sahm rule indicator reaches 0.50 or higher for at least one month between October 2026 and December 2027.
The Bureau of Economic Analysis advance estimate shows U.S. real GDP falling in at least one quarter from the fourth quarter of 2026 through the third quarter of 2027.
U.S. nonfarm payroll employment, after revisions, falls for three months in a row before July 2027.
The Federal Reserve raises interest rates again in late 2026 or early 2027 while Brent crude stays above $110 a barrel for a full quarter.
The harm that a record oil price spike does to U.S. households and fuel-heavy businesses outweighs the gains it brings to U.S. oil producers.
The Federal Reserve under Kevin Warsh will keep interest rates high, or raise them again, for long enough to deepen a slowdown rather than cutting in time to prevent one.

Mark Zandi, chief economist of Moody's Analytics, said in March 2026 that U.S. recession risks were very high and that a recession was more than likely by the second half of 2026 unless the hostilities with Iran came to an end (Fortune, March 25, 2026).

David Rosenberg, president of Rosenberg Research, told Business Insider in March 2026 that the United States could have a very significant recession in 2027 because fiscal stimulus and the boom in AI spending would both fade, leaving business spending facing a vacuum.
Historical Oil Shocks, James D. Hamilton, 2011
where_found: National Bureau of Economic Research, Working Paper 16790
bridge: Hamilton's review of every major oil price disruption since 1859 finds that all but one of the eleven U.S. recessions after World War II were preceded by a rise in the price of oil, which is the historical pattern the 2026 oil shock fits.
bottom_line: Heavy weight on the history, lighter on the forecast, since most of the episodes Hamilton studies came when the United States imported far more oil than it does now.

text: How Well Do Economists Forecast Recessions?, Zidong An, Joao Tovar Jalles and Prakash Loungani, 2018
where_found: International Monetary Fund, Working Paper WP/18/39
bridge: The study finds that consensus forecasts across dozens of countries from 1992 to 2014 almost never called a recession by the spring of the year before it began, so low recession odds from forecasters in 2026 say little about late 2027.
bottom_line: Solid weight against trusting forecasters' calm, but it shows the odds are uncertain, not that a recession is likely.

text: Systematic Monetary Policy and the Effects of Oil Price Shocks, Ben S. Bernanke, Mark Gertler and Mark Watson, 1997
bridge: The paper argues that much of the drop in U.S. output after past oil shocks came from the Federal Reserve raising interest rates in response, which is the same combination of oil shock and rate increase the United States faced in September 2026.
bottom_line: Moderate weight. The finding has been debated, notably by Hamilton and Herrera, but it names the exact path by which the 2026 shock could turn into a recession.

text: The U.S. economy grew at a 2.2 percent annual rate in the second quarter of 2026 and was tracking near 3.7 percent in the third quarter, months after the oil shock began.
bottom_line: Heavy weight for the near term. An economy growing this fast in the fall of 2026 is far from a recession, but strong growth now says less about late 2027.

text: The United States produces more oil than it consumes, so a higher world oil price moves money from U.S. drivers to U.S. producers instead of sending it abroad.
bottom_line: Strong weight. This is the main structural difference from the 1970s oil shocks, though the gain goes to oil states and firms while the pain is spread across every household.

text: Heavy U.S. business investment in artificial intelligence and data centers is supporting growth regardless of what happens to energy prices.
bottom_line: Moderate weight. The Federal Reserve itself cited strong productivity and robust capital investment in September 2026, but an investment boom can also stop suddenly.

text: Professional forecasters put the chance of a falling-GDP quarter in late 2026 and early 2027 at about one in five, so a U.S. recession before 2028 is less likely than not.
bottom_line: Moderate weight. These are the best-informed estimates available, but forecasters have a poor record of seeing recessions coming a year ahead.

text: The real-time Sahm rule unemployment indicator read 0.00 in September 2026, far below the 0.50 level that has marked the start of every U.S. recession since 1970.
bottom_line: Strong weight for now, weak for later. The Sahm rule detects a recession that has started; it cannot see one that is a year away.

text: A sharp slowdown in U.S. growth is not the same as a recession, and Federal Reserve models of the 2026 oil shock show it cutting growth rather than causing an outright decline.
bottom_line: Moderate weight. The Chicago Fed scenarios shave roughly 0.8 to 1.7 points off 2026 growth, which leaves room for a slowdown that never turns negative, though models built on past shocks may understate a record one.

text: U.S. real GDP grew at a 2.2 percent annual rate in the second quarter of 2026 and 2.5 percent in the first, and real gross domestic income grew 2.6 percent in the second quarter.
bottom_line: Strong evidence that the economy was not near recession through mid-2026, and both the spending and income measures agree.

text: The Atlanta Fed's GDPNow model estimated third-quarter 2026 real GDP growth at about 3.7 percent at an annual rate as of October 1, 2026.
bottom_line: Useful but provisional; GDPNow moves a lot before the official estimate and says nothing about 2027.

text: Thirty-two professional forecasters put the chance of a decline in real GDP at 20.0 percent for the fourth quarter of 2026, 21.5 percent for the first quarter of 2027 and 22.0 percent for the second quarter of 2027, and expected unemployment of 4.2 to 4.3 percent through mid-2027.
bottom_line: The best consensus estimate available, but it was taken before the September Fed hike and weak September jobs report, and such surveys rarely see recessions a year out.

text: The real-time Sahm rule recession indicator was 0.00 percentage points in September 2026, after readings of -0.03 in July and -0.07 in August, well below the 0.50 trigger.
bottom_line: Strong evidence that no recession had started as of September 2026, and no evidence at all about late 2027.

text: The U.S. unemployment rate stays below 4.7 percent in every monthly report covering October 2026 through December 2027.
BEA advance estimates show positive U.S. real GDP growth in every quarter of 2027.
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz returns to normal and U.S. gasoline prices fall back near their 2025 level by the spring of 2027.
Monthly U.S. payroll gains recover to an average above 100,000 through mid-2027 while the unemployment rate holds near 4.2 percent.
Business spending on artificial intelligence and data centers will keep growing through 2027 instead of peaking and falling back in 2026.
World oil prices will stay below their 2026 peak through 2027, so the squeeze on U.S. household budgets eases rather than deepens.
The Federal Reserve will reverse its September 2026 rate increase quickly if U.S. job losses begin, as it has done in past slowdowns.

Goldman Sachs economists led by Jan Hatzius cut their estimate of the chance of a U.S. recession within the next 12 months from 25 percent to 15 percent in June 2026, citing lower oil prices after the U.S.-Iran agreement and a sturdier job market.

Torsten Slok, chief economist of Apollo Global Management, wrote in his June 30, 2026 mid-year outlook that despite the Middle East conflict and higher oil prices the U.S. economy continued to be quite resilient and was actually doing quite well.

The American Bankers Association's Economic Advisory Committee, chaired by U.S. Bank chief economist Beth Ann Bovino, forecast on September 23, 2026 that U.S. real GDP would grow 2.2 percent in 2027 with unemployment steady near 4.2 percent.
Direct Stimulus Payments to Individuals, Claudia Sahm, 2019
where_found: The Hamilton Project, Brookings Institution, in the volume Recession Ready
bridge: Sahm's chapter introduces the rule that a recession has begun once the three-month average unemployment rate rises half a point above its low of the prior year, the measure that read 0.00 in September 2026.
bottom_line: Strong weight that no recession had started by the fall of 2026, but the rule was built to spot a recession early, not to forecast one a year out.

text: Hourly workers in trucking, airlines and other fuel-heavy industries need early warning of layoffs so they can build savings and look for steadier work.
measured_by: Layoff rates in transportation from the BLS Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, and the share of these workers with three months of savings.
if_true: Layoffs rise in 2027 and workers who saved early ride it out far better than those who did not.
if_false: Layoffs stay low and early saving costs these workers little beyond some spending put off.
bottom_line: A strong and concrete interest, since fuel-heavy industries are hit first by an oil shock.

text: Families paying far more for gasoline than a year ago need the Federal Reserve to stop raising interest rates before a slowdown turns into job losses.
measured_by: The federal funds rate path and the unemployment rate through 2027.
if_true: Further Fed increases would deepen a downturn that costs these families jobs on top of higher fuel bills.
if_false: The Fed can keep rates where they are to bring inflation down without costing these families their jobs.
bottom_line: A real interest, though the same families also lose when inflation stays high.

text: Retirees and savers holding long-term Treasury bonds need warning of a downturn, since bond prices usually rise when a recession pulls interest rates down.
measured_by: The 10-year Treasury yield and returns on long-term Treasury funds through 2027.
if_true: Yields fall in a recession and bond holders gain.
if_false: Yields stay high or rise with oil-driven inflation and long bonds lose value.
bottom_line: A narrower financial interest; it shows who gains from the belief being right, not why it is right.

text: Small-business owners need their customers to keep spending, and a widely expected recession can make customers cut back on their own.
measured_by: Retail sales and small-business sales and hiring plans in the NFIB Small Business Economic Trends survey.
if_true: Sales and hiring plans fall as the recession arrives.
if_false: Sales keep growing and owners who cut back early lose business to those who did not.
bottom_line: A strong interest, since small firms have the thinnest cushion in a downturn.

text: Workers saving for retirement in stock index funds need investors to avoid panic selling on recession forecasts that do not come true.
measured_by: Returns on broad U.S. stock index funds from October 2026 through December 2027.
if_true: Stocks likely fall as earnings shrink in a recession.
if_false: Stocks are free to rise with continued growth and those who stayed invested keep the gains.
bottom_line: A large group with a real stake, though their interest is in accurate forecasts, not in any one answer.

text: U.S. households that build about three months of emergency savings before a 2027 recession are much less likely to miss rent, mortgage or car payments if a worker is laid off.
bottom_line: The three months is a common planning target, not a measured effect; the benefit is real for any family that acts on it, recession or not.

text: If the Federal Reserve stops raising rates when recession warning signs appear, fewer U.S. workers lose their jobs in a 2027 downturn.
bottom_line: A rough estimate of a plausible benefit; the size depends on how early the Fed acts and on whether inflation lets it.

text: Savers who move money into long-term U.S. Treasury bonds before a recession usually gain as interest rates fall during the downturn.
bottom_line: Real for those who time it right, but no estimate is given because the gain depends on how far rates fall, and an oil-driven inflation could push them the other way.

text: A U.S. recession before the end of 2027 would push the unemployment rate well above its September 2026 level of 4.2 percent.
bottom_line: The two-point rise is a rough estimate of a mild recession, not a forecast; with 7.1 million already unemployed, each point means well over a million more people out of work.

text: If U.S. businesses and households cut spending because they expect a recession, the pullback itself can slow growth even when no recession was coming.
bottom_line: A real risk of acting on the belief, but no reliable estimate of its size exists.

text: Investors who sell stocks on a recession forecast that does not come true miss the gains of a continued expansion.
bottom_line: A well-known cost of acting on forecasts, left unestimated because returns over the period are unknown.

text: A National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) announcement placing a U.S. business cycle peak in November 2027 or earlier is a fair measure of whether the United States was in a recession at some point before the end of 2027.
The three-month average change in U.S. nonfarm payroll employment is a fair measure of whether the labor market has started shrinking.
The real-time Sahm rule indicator reaching 0.50 is a fair measure of whether a U.S. recession has begun.
A broad decline in U.S. output, jobs and incomes lasting more than a few months will begin at some point between October 2026 and December 2027.
The 2026 oil price shock and the Federal Reserve's September 2026 rate increase are strong enough to outweigh the support U.S. growth is getting from AI and data center investment.
U.S. employers who expect a recession before the end of 2027 would slow or freeze hiring in late 2026 and 2027, which would push the unemployment rate up even before output falls.
U.S. households expecting a recession by 2027 would raise their savings and put off big purchases like cars and homes, which would itself slow consumer spending.
A U.S. recession beginning before the end of 2027 would widen federal budget deficits for several years through lower tax receipts and higher spending on unemployment benefits.
U.S. workers who lose their jobs in a recession beginning by 2027 would likely earn less for years afterward, as research on workers laid off in past recessions has found.
The United States will enter a recession before the end of June 2027 that pushes the unemployment rate above 6 percent.
The 2026 oil shock will cause a U.S. recession as deep as the 2007 to 2009 Great Recession.
U.S. real GDP growth will fall below 1 percent for calendar year 2027, whether or not a recession is declared.
The Federal Reserve will cut its policy rate below 3 percent before the end of 2027.
bottom_line: As of early October 2026 the Fed has just raised its range to 3.75 to 4.00 percent, no Fed official projects a rate below 3.1 percent for the end of 2027, and futures markets give a cut that deep almost no chance, so the belief needs at least five quarter-point cuts that nobody in charge is planning. The real fight is over whether the Iran war oil shock fades and the weakening job market cracks into a recession; the Fed has cut that fast before in a recession (2001, 2008, 2020), but the evidence that a recession is coming is still thin.
hook: On September 16, 2026, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since 2023, the same day President Trump posted that U.S. interest rates "should be 1%, or less" (Federal Reserve press release and Yahoo Finance, September 16, 2026).
question: Will the Federal Reserve cut the top of its federal funds target range below 3 percent at any point before the end of 2027?
ask: The page most needs a dated, sourced estimate of the chance that a U.S. recession starts before mid-2027, from a model or survey that publishes its past track record.

text: Once a U.S. recession begins, the Federal Reserve has generally cut its policy rate by far more than 1.25 percentage points within a year, as it did in 2001, 2008 and 2020.
bottom_line: Strong weight on the condition of a recession, since the Fed's own records show the pattern, but it says nothing about whether a recession will actually come before the end of 2027.

text: The U.S. job market is weakening faster than the Federal Reserve's September 2026 projections assume, with only 29,000 jobs added in September 2026 and July's figure revised to a loss of 10,000.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because two soft months and a downward revision are an early warning sign, but one jobs report is noisy and the unemployment rate (4.2 percent) is still low.

text: Inflation outside food and energy is much closer to the Federal Reserve's 2 percent goal than headline inflation, with core consumer prices up 2.4 percent in the year to August 2026, so the September 2026 rate hike is responding to an oil shock that could reverse.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, since the core CPI figure is real, but the Fed's preferred core PCE measure runs hotter and Fed officials still project core PCE of 2.5 percent at the end of 2027.

text: Ten scheduled Federal Reserve meetings fall between October 2026 and December 2027, which is enough time for the five quarter-point cuts needed to bring the top of the range from 4.00 percent to 2.75 percent.
bottom_line: Low weight, since it only shows the deep cut is possible on the calendar, not that the Fed has any reason to make it.

text: Sustained public pressure from President Trump, who said on September 16, 2026 that U.S. interest rates should be 1 percent or less, makes it more likely that the Federal Reserve cuts quickly once the economy gives it any reason to.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight, because the Fed's 12-0 vote to raise rates over Trump's objection shows the committee is not bending to him now, though pressure may matter at the margin in a downturn.

text: During 2001 the Federal Reserve cut its federal funds target eleven times, from 6.50 percent to 1.75 percent, a total of 4.75 percentage points in under twelve months.
bottom_line: Strong as proof that the Fed can cut far more than 1.25 points within a year once a recession hits, but it bears on this belief only if a recession arrives.

text: In March 2020 the Federal Reserve cut its target range by 1.50 percentage points in two moves twelve days apart, from 1.50 to 1.75 percent down to 0 to 0.25 percent.
bottom_line: Strong evidence that a sudden shock can move the Fed through a whole year's planned path in weeks, though the 2020 shock was unusual.

text: U.S. payrolls rose by only 29,000 in September 2026, July was revised to a loss of 10,000, and the unemployment rate rose to 4.2 percent.
bottom_line: Moderate weight as a sign of a weakening job market, but monthly payroll numbers are heavily revised and unemployment is still low by historical standards.

text: Consumer prices excluding food and energy rose 2.4 percent in the 12 months ending August 2026, while energy prices rose 16.3 percent and gasoline 27.4 percent.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because it shows the inflation problem is concentrated in energy and could fade if oil falls, but the Fed targets PCE inflation, which runs higher on core.

text: The Federal Reserve will lower its target range at least once from the 3.75 to 4.00 percent level set in September 2026.
The U.S. unemployment rate will reach 4.8 percent or higher in at least one monthly report.

where_found: Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, Spring 2009
bridge: Hamilton found that the 2007-08 oil price spike was an important contributor to the U.S. downturn that became the Great Recession, which supports the idea that the 2026 Iran-war oil shock could push the economy into a slump that forces the Federal Reserve to cut deeply.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a careful study by a leading oil-shock economist, but it describes one past episode, and the 2026 economy uses less oil per dollar of output than the 2008 economy did.

text: The Federal Reserve raised its target range to 3.75 to 4.00 percent on September 16, 2026 by a unanimous 12-0 vote, so getting below 3 percent by the end of 2027 requires a full reversal of at least 1.25 percentage points from a committee that is currently tightening.
bottom_line: Strong weight, because the starting point and direction of policy are a matter of record and every further hike makes the required reversal larger.

text: None of the 19 Federal Reserve officials who submitted projections in September 2026 expects the federal funds rate to end 2027 below 3.1 percent, and the median expects 4.1 percent.
bottom_line: Strong weight as a statement of current intentions, though Fed projections have often missed by more than a point when the economy turned suddenly.

text: Federal funds futures traded on October 3, 2026 assign close to zero chance that the target range will be below 3.75 percent at the Federal Reserve's December 2027 meeting.
bottom_line: Strong weight, because traders with money at stake are pricing hikes, not cuts, but markets also missed the speed of the 2001 and 2020 cutting cycles.

text: Federal Reserve officials project U.S. growth of 2.4 percent in 2027 with unemployment at 4.1 percent, an economy that would not call for rates below neutral.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because the forecast reflects the committee's view of strong productivity and investment, but forecasts made in good times rarely predict the recession that follows.

text: A federal funds rate below 3 percent would sit below the Federal Reserve officials' own median estimate of the long-run neutral rate (3.2 percent in September 2026), which means deliberately stimulating the economy, something the Fed generally does only in a downturn.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, since it shows the belief effectively requires a recession or a sharp drop in inflation, which is exactly what is in dispute.

text: In the September 2026 projections, the median Federal Reserve official expected a federal funds rate of 4.1 percent at the end of 2027, and the lowest of all projections was 3.1 percent.
bottom_line: Strong as a record of what the people who set the rate intend today, weaker as a forecast because the projections are revised every quarter and moved up half a point between June and September 2026 alone.

text: Prices for federal funds futures on October 3, 2026 implied a 0.8 percent chance that the target range would be 3.75 to 4.00 percent after the December 8, 2027 meeting and no listed chance of any lower range, with the most likely outcome 4.50 to 4.75 percent.
bottom_line: Strong as a snapshot of market odds, but the snapshot changes daily and futures prices carry a risk premium that can overstate expected rates.

text: The Federal Open Market Committee voted 12-0 on September 16, 2026 to raise the target range by a quarter point to 3.75 to 4.00 percent, its first increase since 2023, saying inflation remains elevated.
bottom_line: Strong, because it fixes the starting point and shows the committee moving in the opposite direction from the belief, with no dissent.

text: Federal Reserve officials projected in September 2026 that core PCE inflation will still be 2.5 percent at the end of 2027, above the 2 percent goal, with unemployment at 4.1 percent.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because a projected above-target inflation rate and low unemployment leave no room in the Fed's own outlook for deep cuts, though the outlook is only a forecast.

bridge: The projections released with the September 2026 rate hike show the median Fed official expecting one more hike in 2026 and a federal funds rate around 4.1 percent at the end of 2027, far above the 3 percent line.
bottom_line: Strong weight as the committee's own stated plan, though such projections are revised quickly when the economy turns and are not promises.

text: BofA now sees no Fed rate cuts until 2028, Sam Boughedda, 2026
bridge: Bank of America economist Aditya Bhave forecast hikes in the second half of 2026 and no Fed cuts until 2028, saying the Fed's inflation problem had gotten unambiguously worse.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the forecast correctly called a September 2026 hike, but it was made before the soft September jobs report and bank forecasts have changed often in 2026.

text: Homebuyers and homeowners hoping to refinance need lower mortgage rates to afford a monthly house payment.
measured_by: The weekly average 30-year fixed mortgage rate in Freddie Mac's Primary Mortgage Market Survey.
if_true: The average mortgage rate falls, likely by well under a full point, as the Fed cuts.
if_false: Mortgage rates stay near their late-2026 level or rise if the Fed keeps hiking.
bottom_line: A large and real interest, though mortgage rates depend on long-term bond yields as much as on the Fed.

text: Households carrying credit card balances need lower interest charges so their payments go to the balance instead of interest.
measured_by: The average interest rate on credit card accounts assessed interest, from the Federal Reserve's G.19 Consumer Credit release.
if_true: Average card rates fall by roughly the size of the Fed's cuts.
if_false: Card rates stay high or rise with any further Fed hikes.
bottom_line: A direct and nearly mechanical interest, modest per household but spread across millions of families.

text: Construction workers and factory workers need steady demand for homes, cars and equipment, which cheaper borrowing supports.
measured_by: Construction and manufacturing employment in the Bureau of Labor Statistics Employment Situation release.
if_true: Rate cuts cushion hiring in these industries, though a recession behind the cuts could still cost jobs.
if_false: High rates keep pressure on housing starts and equipment orders.
bottom_line: A real interest, but it is served by a healthy economy more than by the deep cuts that usually come only with a downturn.

text: Retirees living on savings need interest income from bank deposits, CDs and money market funds to cover their living costs.
measured_by: Average money market fund yields and one-year CD rates.
if_true: Yields fall by at least about 1.25 percentage points from late-2026 levels.
if_false: Yields stay near 4 percent or rise.
bottom_line: A direct interest, though retirees also lose if inflation stays high, which cuts against them either way.

text: Low-income families who spend most of their pay on food, gas and rent need inflation brought back to 2 percent.
measured_by: The 12-month change in the Consumer Price Index for all items from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
if_true: Inflation may stay above 2 percent longer if the Fed cuts before the oil shock fades.
if_false: The Fed holds rates high until inflation returns toward 2 percent.
bottom_line: A strong interest because inflation takes the biggest bite from tight budgets, though a recession would hurt the same families through lost work.

text: Workers in industries that lay off first in a recession, such as finance, retail and trucking, need the economy to avoid the downturn that usually comes before deep rate cuts.
measured_by: The national unemployment rate and industry payroll counts in the Bureau of Labor Statistics Employment Situation release.
if_true: Unemployment most likely rises, since a recession is the usual reason the Fed cuts this deep.
if_false: Unemployment stays near 4.2 percent with no recession.
bottom_line: An important interest that sits against the belief because of what would cause it, not because of the cuts themselves.

text: Because most credit card rates are tied to the prime rate, which moves one for one with the Federal Reserve's rate, cutting the federal funds rate from a 4.00 percent upper bound to 2.75 percent would lower variable credit card rates by about 1.25 percentage points.
bottom_line: Close to mechanical arithmetic, though at card rates near 20 percent a 1.25-point cut is a modest saving for most families.

text: Lower borrowing costs after Federal Reserve rate cuts would support demand for homes, cars and business equipment, protecting jobs in construction and manufacturing.
bottom_line: Plausible direction, no reliable size, because if the cuts come in response to a recession they cushion job losses rather than add jobs.

text: Cutting the federal funds rate from a 4.00 percent upper bound to 2.75 percent or lower would reduce yields on money market funds and savings accounts by at least about 1.25 percentage points.
bottom_line: Close to mechanical, since money market yields track the Fed's rate closely, and it falls hardest on people who live on interest.

text: Whether the Sahm rule recession indicator (the three-month average unemployment rate rising at least 0.5 points above its low of the previous 12 months) is triggered is a fair measure of whether the kind of downturn that has historically produced deep Fed cuts has begun.

The Federal Reserve will respond to a weaker U.S. economy with at least 1.25 percentage points of cuts, plus enough to undo any further 2026 hikes, within the roughly 15 months left before the end of 2027.
Long-run U.S. inflation expectations will stay steady enough that the Federal Reserve can cut below 3 percent without setting off a new rise in prices.
If the Federal Reserve cuts its policy rate below 3 percent by the end of 2027, yields on money market funds and high-yield savings accounts will fall below 3 percent within months.

If the Federal Reserve cuts its policy rate below 3 percent by the end of 2027, rates on credit cards, home equity lines and other loans tied to the prime rate will fall by roughly the same amount as the cuts.
Cutting the federal funds rate below 3 percent quickly in a 2027 downturn would shorten the downturn and keep U.S. unemployment lower over the following decade than a slower cutting path would.
A Federal Reserve that cuts its policy rate below 3 percent while inflation is still above 2 percent would raise the risk that U.S. inflation averages above 2.5 percent over the following decade.
The Federal Reserve will cut its policy rate to 1 percent or less before the end of 2027.
The Federal Reserve will cut its policy rate below 3 percent before the end of June 2027.
The Federal Reserve will cut its policy rate at least once before the end of 2027.

bottom_line: The case for U.S. inflation under 2.5 percent by late 2027 is decent: core CPI is 2.4 percent, professional forecasters expect about 2.3 percent by the end of 2027, and the spring 2026 price jumps drop out of the comparison next spring. The case for every month of 2027 is thin, because the January and February 2027 readings need the price index to fall about half a percent from August 2026, which in practice means the Strait of Hormuz reopening and gasoline falling back near $3 a gallon within months.
hook: U.S. gasoline averaged $4.33 a gallon in September 2026, fifty cents above the previous September record, according to AAA, yet this belief bets that by January the yearly inflation rate will already be back under 2.5 percent.
question: Will every monthly U.S. consumer price index reading in 2027 show prices up less than 2.5 percent from a year earlier?
ask: This page most needs a sourced estimate of how fast U.S. gasoline prices would fall if the Strait of Hormuz fully reopened, because the January and February 2027 readings hinge on it.

text: U.S. consumer price inflation was already running at 2.4 percent in January and February 2026, before the Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz, so the underlying trend sits below 2.5 percent once the oil shock fades.
bottom_line: Strong starting point, because it shows where prices were heading without the war, but it only helps the belief if energy prices actually fall back.

text: Core CPI, which leaves out food and energy, rose only 2.4 percent in the year to August 2026, so nearly all of the U.S. inflation above 2.5 percent is coming from energy prices that can reverse.
bottom_line: Carries real weight, since core inflation moves slowly and is the best guide to where headline inflation settles, though it says nothing about how fast gasoline will drop.

text: U.S. headline inflation driven by an oil supply shock has generally fallen fast once oil prices fell, as in 2008 when the twelve-month CPI rate dropped from 5.6 percent in July to 0.1 percent in December.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the history shows the drop can be quick, but it needs an oil price collapse, and in 2008 that came with a deep recession.

text: The large monthly CPI jumps of March, April and May 2026 will fall out of the twelve-month comparison in spring 2027, which mechanically pulls the U.S. twelve-month inflation rate down for most of 2027.
bottom_line: Solid for the months from April 2027 on, but it does nothing for January and February 2027, which are compared with the low, pre-war prices of early 2026.

text: The Federal Reserve raised its policy rate to a range of 3.75 to 4.00 percent in September 2026 and Chair Kevin Warsh said its main focus is price stability, which should hold down demand-driven U.S. price increases through 2027.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: tight money restrains spending with a lag of a year or more, but interest rates cannot reopen a shipping lane or lower world oil prices.

text: Court rulings in 2026 against President Trump's IEEPA tariffs and against the 10 percent Section 122 replacement tariff make it less likely that new tariff costs keep pushing U.S. goods prices up in 2027.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight, because the Section 122 ruling is on appeal and other tariff laws remain available to the administration.

text: The U.S. CPI-U rose 2.4 percent over the twelve months ending January 2026 and 2.4 percent over the twelve months ending February 2026, before the Iran war oil shock reached consumer prices.
bottom_line: Official figures that show the pre-war rate was already under the 2.5 percent bar.

text: In August 2026 the U.S. CPI for all items less food and energy rose 2.4 percent over twelve months, while the energy index rose 16.3 percent and gasoline rose 27.4 percent.
bottom_line: Shows the overshoot is concentrated in energy, which is the part of the index that can fall fastest.

text: As oil prices collapsed in 2008, U.S. CPI twelve-month inflation fell from 5.6 percent in July to 0.1 percent in December, and in the 2014 to 2015 oil slump it fell from 2.1 percent in May 2014 to minus 0.2 percent in April 2015.
bottom_line: Shows headline inflation can drop several points within months, though both episodes had oil prices falling by half or more.

text: The median forecast in the Philadelphia Fed's third-quarter 2026 survey is 2.3 percent CPI inflation for 2027 measured fourth quarter over fourth quarter, after 3.6 percent for 2026.
bottom_line: Supports the belief for late 2027, but the same survey's quarterly path implies early-2027 twelve-month readings well above 2.5 percent.

A durable U.S.-Iran agreement that fully reopens the Strait of Hormuz before December 2026, followed by Brent crude falling below $75 a barrel, would strengthen the belief that U.S. CPI inflation stays under 2.5 percent all of 2027.
The Strait of Hormuz reopens, or world oil supply otherwise recovers, soon enough for U.S. gasoline prices to fall back close to their early-2026 level by about January 2027.
The higher U.S. energy prices of 2026 will not spread widely into wages, airfares, shipping and food prices before they reverse.
No new shock in 2027, such as new tariffs, a hurricane hitting refineries or a fresh Middle East flare-up, pushes any single monthly U.S. CPI reading back to 2.5 percent or above.

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said in a September 3, 2026 speech that he did not see elevated energy prices and tariffs as a significant source of ongoing U.S. inflation pressure, and that his earlier worry that higher energy prices would bleed into many other prices had not come to pass so far.

where_found: Hutchins Center on Fiscal and Monetary Policy at Brookings, Working Paper 86 (also NBER Working Paper 31417)
bridge: The study finds that most of the 2021 to 2022 U.S. inflation surge came from price shocks such as energy prices and shortages, each with a strong but largely short-lived effect, while labor market pressure was smaller and more lasting.
bottom_line: Solid general support for the idea that energy-driven inflation fades, though in that episode the twelve-month CPI rate took more than two years after its June 2022 peak to get back under 2.5 percent.

text: For the January 2027 U.S. CPI reading to come in under 2.5 percent, the unadjusted CPI-U index must fall from 334.98 in August 2026 to below about 333.4, a drop of about half a percent that has happened over an August-to-January span only four times since 1990, each during an oil price collapse.
bottom_line: The heaviest point against the belief, because it is plain arithmetic from published index levels and turns the question into whether oil collapses within four months.

text: U.S. shelter prices were understated from November 2025 through March 2026 because of the government shutdown data gap, so twelve-month shelter inflation for November 2026 through March 2027 will be measured against an artificially low starting point.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: shelter is about a third of the CPI, and even a small upward tilt in the early-2027 readings matters when the bar is 2.5 percent.

text: In the 36 August-to-January spans from 1990 to 2025, the unadjusted U.S. CPI-U index fell by 0.48 percent or more only four times (2006, 2008, 2014 and 2015), and the January 2027 reading needs at least that large a fall from the August 2026 level of 334.98.
bottom_line: The strongest single finding on the page, because anyone can redo the arithmetic from the published index.

text: Only 8 of the 42 calendar years from 1984 through 2025 had every monthly U.S. CPI twelve-month reading under 2.5 percent, and none of those years followed an August reading above 2.72 percent, compared with 3.4 percent in August 2026.
bottom_line: A sturdy base rate against the belief, though a sharp oil reversal is exactly the kind of event a base rate does not see coming.

text: As of October 2, 2026, the Cleveland Fed's nowcast put U.S. CPI twelve-month inflation at 3.60 percent for September 2026 and 3.58 percent for October 2026.
bottom_line: Shows inflation heading into the end of 2026 near its highs, not falling toward 2.5 percent.

text: The Energy Information Administration forecasts U.S. retail gasoline to average $3.35 a gallon and Brent crude $74 a barrel in 2027, while its own monthly series put gasoline at $2.94 a gallon in January 2026.
bottom_line: Even the government's forecast of falling oil prices leaves early-2027 gasoline above early-2026 levels, which pushes the first readings of 2027 up.

Tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz will still be far below pre-war levels on December 31, 2026.

Core U.S. CPI rising above 3 percent over twelve months in late 2026, as higher fuel costs pass into airfares, shipping and food, would weaken the belief that all 2027 readings stay under 2.5 percent.

bridge: The study finds that shocks to headline inflation, including energy price shocks, passed through into U.S. core inflation, and names the failure to expect that pass-through as one reason forecasters underestimated how long inflation would last.
bottom_line: Moderate to strong weight, because it describes the exact mechanism that would keep 2027 readings above 2.5 percent even after oil falls, though the labor market in 2022 was far tighter than in 2026.

text: Hourly workers need their pay to rise faster than the prices they pay
measured_by: Twelve-month change in BLS real average hourly earnings
if_true: Turns clearly positive during 2027 as price growth slows below wage growth.
if_false: Stays near zero or negative while prices keep pace with or outrun pay.
bottom_line: The largest group touched by the question, and the one with the least ability to shield itself from rising prices.

text: First-time home buyers need mortgage rates to come down
measured_by: Freddie Mac weekly average 30-year fixed mortgage rate
if_true: Drifts lower through 2027 as the Federal Reserve gains room to cut.
if_false: Stays high or rises as the Fed holds or raises its policy rate.
bottom_line: Real but indirect, since mortgage rates depend on long-term bond yields as much as on inflation.

text: Retirees on fixed pensions need prices to stop climbing quickly
measured_by: Twelve-month change in CPI-U compared with the yearly increase in a typical private pension, which is often zero
if_true: The gap between price growth and fixed pension income narrows to under 2.5 percent a year.
if_false: Fixed pension income keeps losing more than 2.5 percent of its buying power a year.
bottom_line: Small in number compared with workers but hit hardest, since a pension with no cost-of-living raise loses buying power every month inflation runs.

text: Oil and gas workers in Texas, New Mexico and North Dakota need crude prices high enough to keep drilling rigs running
measured_by: Baker Hughes weekly count of active U.S. oil rigs
if_true: Falls as crude drops toward the $74 a barrel the Energy Information Administration forecasts for 2027.
if_false: Holds steady or rises while crude stays near $100 a barrel.
bottom_line: A concentrated interest whose jobs depend on the same high oil prices that keep inflation above 2.5 percent.

text: Savers living on interest from CDs and money market funds need interest rates to stay high
measured_by: Average yield on U.S. retail money market funds
if_true: Falls in 2027 as lower inflation lets the Federal Reserve cut rates.
if_false: Stays near the 3.75 to 4.00 percent policy range or rises.
bottom_line: Genuine, though savers also gain from slower price growth, so their net stake against the belief is small.

text: U.S. inflation under 2.5 percent all of 2027 would let the Federal Reserve lower its policy rate from the 3.75 to 4.00 percent range, pulling down borrowing costs for home buyers.
bottom_line: Plausible but uncertain, since the Fed's own September 2026 median shows no cuts in 2027 and mortgage rates follow long-term yields, not only the policy rate.

text: U.S. households would spend less per gallon of gasoline in 2027 if prices fall from AAA's September 2026 average of $4.33 a gallon toward the Energy Information Administration's 2027 forecast of $3.35.
bottom_line: Large and widely felt if it happens, because falling gasoline is the most likely path by which the belief comes true at all.

text: Savers would earn less interest in 2027 if lower U.S. inflation lets the Federal Reserve cut its policy rate from the 3.75 to 4.00 percent range.
bottom_line: Modest, since savers would also face slower price increases, so their loss in buying power is smaller than the yield cut.

bottom_line: Moderate weight: Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley both forecast 2027 earnings well above 2026, but strategist earnings forecasts are often revised and the price-earnings link is loose over just one year.

text: The third year of a U.S. presidential term, which 2027 will be, has historically been the strongest year of the four-year cycle for the S&P 500.
bottom_line: Modest weight: the record since 1950 is striking, but nineteen cases is a small sample and no one has shown why the calendar of elections should move stock prices.

text: High stock valuations have historically told investors little about the next single year's return, so the S&P 500's elevated price-to-earnings ratio does not by itself predict a down 2027.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: Vanguard's research found valuations meaningful only at long horizons, and the S&P 500 gained about 21 percent in 1999 while valuations climbed to their record.

text: Corporate spending on AI data centers is expected to keep growing in 2027, which supports revenue at the chipmakers and suppliers that make up a large share of the S&P 500.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: Goldman Sachs expects capital spending to keep rising next year, but the same analysis warns that its boost to earnings growth will fade.

text: The U.S. economy was growing solidly enough in September 2026 that the Federal Reserve chose to raise interest rates rather than cut them, which suggests corporate sales are not about to collapse.
bottom_line: Modest weight: the Fed's statement describes solid growth and a steady job market, but a rate hike also raises the cost of money for companies and investors.

text: Of the 98 calendar years from 1928 through 2025, the S&P 500 had a positive total return, including dividends, in 72, or about 73 percent.
bottom_line: Solid record, but it counts dividends, so the share of years in which the price level alone rose is somewhat lower.

text: In every one of the 19 pre-election years from 1951 through 2023, the S&P 500 had a positive total return including dividends (computed from the Damodaran annual return table; 2015 was up 1.38 percent with dividends and slightly down on price alone).
bottom_line: A striking streak, but it is a small sample with no agreed cause, and 2015 shows a price-only miss.

text: Price-to-earnings ratios have had a meaningful relationship with future stock returns only at long horizons, and even then explained only about 40 percent of the variation in ten-year inflation-adjusted returns.
bottom_line: Strong reason not to read a one-year forecast off valuation, though it does not say high valuations are harmless.

bridge: The Stock Trader's Almanac 2027 lays out the four-year presidential election cycle, in which the third year of a term, as 2027 is, has historically been the strongest for stocks.
bottom_line: Modest weight: the calendar patterns are carefully recorded, but they rest on small samples and no proven cause.

text: Stocks for the Long Run, Sixth Edition (Jeremy J. Siegel with Jeremy Schwartz, 2022)
bridge: Stocks for the Long Run documents two centuries of U.S. stock returns and shows that stocks have risen in most years and over nearly every long stretch, which is the base rate a forecast for 2027 starts from.
bottom_line: Strong on the long-run record, weak on any one year, which Siegel himself treats as close to unpredictable.

text: The S&P 500's cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio near 41 in September 2026 was the second-highest reading on record, and the only higher reading, in late 1999, was followed by three straight years of losses.
bottom_line: Serious but imprecise: extreme valuations have preceded big declines, yet valuations explain long-run returns far better than the next single year.

text: S&P 500 earnings growth is expected to slow sharply in 2027 from the 30 percent pace of early 2026, and years of slowing but still above-trend earnings growth have typically brought weaker stock returns.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: Bank of America's finding is relevant, but weaker returns are not the same as a down year.

text: The Federal Reserve raised its policy rate in September 2026 and its officials project no rate cuts in 2027, which removes a common support for rising stock prices.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: tighter money has preceded past market peaks, but the Fed is hiking into a growing economy and stocks have risen during many hiking cycles.

text: The S&P 500 depends heavily on a few AI-linked companies, so a slowdown in AI spending or a drop in chip prices would pull the whole index down.

text: A U.S. recession in 2027 would very likely push the S&P 500 down for the year, because corporate profits usually fall when the economy shrinks.
bottom_line: The weight depends on the odds of a 2027 recession, which is argued on its own page on this site.

text: The Shiller cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio for the S&P 500 stood at 41.12 in September 2026, a level exceeded only at the November 1999 dot-com peak of 44.19.
bottom_line: An accurate measure of how expensive stocks are, but weak as a guide to any single calendar year.

text: In the ten calendar years from 1928 through 2025 that followed three straight years of S&P 500 total returns above 10 percent, the index rose in only five (computed from the Damodaran annual return table).
bottom_line: Suggestive but thin: ten cases is too few to separate a pattern from chance.

bottom_line: Relevant to 2027 because consensus expects growth to slow to the mid-teens, though weaker returns can still be positive.

bottom_line: A plain fact that money is getting tighter, though how much it weighs on stocks depends on how far the hikes go.
