bottom_line: Serious weight on valuations, though Shiller's own evidence is strongest over ten-year horizons rather than a single calendar year.

text: Valuation Ratios and the Long-Run Stock Market Outlook (John Y. Campbell and Robert J. Shiller, 1998)
bridge: Campbell and Shiller found that high price-to-earnings and low dividend-yield readings have historically been followed by below-average stock returns, with prices rather than earnings doing most of the adjusting.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the finding has held up as a long-run tendency, but it famously warned too early in the late 1990s, when stocks kept rising for two more years.

text: Stocks are in a late-stage bubble and poised to crash 21% next year, while Treasury yields above 5% will signal a new era of tight money, analysts say (Fortune, September 13, 2026)
bridge: The Fortune article reports Capital Economics' forecast that the S&P 500 will end 2026 at 8,250 and fall to 6,500 by the end of 2027, citing valuations near dot-com peaks, extreme concentration and hyperscaler free cash flow turning negative.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it is a specific, checkable forecast with stated reasons, but it is one firm's call, and year-ahead strategist targets have a poor record.

text: Workers saving for retirement in 401(k) plans need their stock index funds to grow.

if_false: Returns fall short, widening funding gaps that taxpayers or workers must fill.
bottom_line: Important because shortfalls land on taxpayers and public employees, not only on the funds.

text: Retirees drawing down stock portfolios need to avoid selling shares after a market drop.

if_true: Withdrawals come from a rising balance.

bottom_line: A small loss in an early retirement year can do outsized harm, which makes this group the most exposed to a down 2027.

bottom_line: Matters most to people near or in retirement, whose losses early in withdrawals do the most lasting harm.

bottom_line: Strong but not decisive: Fed projections have missed turning points before, yet none of the nineteen people with the most data saw 5 percent coming.

bottom_line: Strong weight as a starting point: about one chance in four from history alone, with nearly all of it riding on a recession.

text: Broken Money: Why Our Financial System Is Failing Us and How We Can Make It Better, Lyn Alden, 2023
bridge: Alden traces how government debt and currency debasement push savers toward scarce assets and makes the case that bitcoin can serve as one.
bottom_line: Moderate weight on the debt-and-scarcity reason, though the book does not forecast a price or a date.

text: The Price of Tomorrow: Why Deflation Is the Key to an Abundant Future, Jeff Booth, 2020
bridge: Booth argues that technology pushes prices down while central banks print money to fight it, and that bitcoin offers a way out of that pattern.
bottom_line: Low weight for a 2027 price target: it is a long-range argument about money, not a near-term forecast.

text: In neither of its last two cycles did bitcoin set a record far above its previous peak within about two years of that peak; after the November 2021 top it took 28 months just to edge past the old high, while reaching $200,000 by the end of 2027 would require beating the October 2025 record by about 58 percent within 27 months.
bottom_line: Heavy weight: it is the most direct historical comparison, though two cycles are a small sample and the market has changed since.

text: The Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September 2026 and signaled more increases, and higher interest rates generally reduce the money flowing into speculative assets such as bitcoin.
bottom_line: Heavy weight for 2027: tighter money is a clear headwind, though policy could reverse if the economy weakens.

text: Bitcoin's four-year halving pattern has put past price peaks about a year after each halving, and the next halving is expected in spring 2028, which places the next expected peak after the end of 2027.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the pattern has held three times, but it may be weakening now that fund flows matter more than miner supply.

text: Bitcoin treasury companies, which bought heavily in 2024 and 2025, largely stopped adding coins after their share prices fell, removing one of the main buyers behind the last rally.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: Standard Chartered cut its forecasts for this reason, though buying could resume if share prices recover.

text: Even Bernstein, one of the most bullish research firms on bitcoin, puts bitcoin at about $150,000 by mid-2027 in its base case and reaches $200,000 only in its more optimistic scenario.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: when bullish forecasters treat $200,000 by 2027 as an upside case, the belief is a bet on the optimistic tail.

text: The US Senate's failure to advance the CLARITY Act crypto market structure bill in September 2026 leaves US crypto rules unsettled, which generally slows the entry of large, cautious institutions.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight: rules matter for slow money, but bitcoin already has approved funds and is less affected than other tokens.

text: Bitcoin did not top its November 10, 2021 record of $68,982.20 until March 5, 2024, about 28 months later, and then only by about 0.3 percent, reaching $69,210.
bottom_line: Heavy weight: the last cycle's recovery pace, applied to the October 2025 peak, falls far short of $200,000 by the end of 2027.

text: On September 16, 2026 the Federal Reserve raised its target rate by a quarter point to 3.75 to 4 percent, its first increase since 2023, and 16 of 18 officials projected another increase later in 2026.
bottom_line: Heavy weight for the near term, because rising rates have historically coincided with weak bitcoin prices, but a policy path can change within months.

text: As of late September 2026, Kalshi's contract on bitcoin reaching $200,000 before January 1, 2027 traded at 2 to 3 cents, an implied chance of about 2 to 3 percent.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: real-money traders see the nearer deadline as very unlikely, though this contract ends a year before the belief's deadline.

text: With bitcoin's 30-day realized volatility at 44.89 and the CME CF Bitcoin Volatility Index at 39.12 at the end of August 2026, a simple random-walk calculation gives roughly a 5 to 9 percent chance of bitcoin touching $200,000 from $85,000 within 15 months.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a transparent baseline, but bitcoin's real moves come in bursts that a simple random walk understates.

text: Bitcoin stays below its October 2025 record of about $126,000 on the CME CF Bitcoin Reference Rate, New York Variant, through the first half of 2027.
The Federal Reserve's target range for the federal funds rate is at or above 3.75 to 4 percent at the end of 2027.
Bitcoin falls below its 2026 low of about $60,000 on the CME CF Bitcoin Reference Rate at any point in 2027.
Strategy or another large bitcoin treasury company sells a significant part of its bitcoin holdings to meet debt or dividend payments.
Bitcoin's price still follows a four-year cycle tied to its halvings, so its next peak is more likely to come after the 2028 halving than before the end of 2027.
Bitcoin pays no interest or dividends, so its price depends on new buyers arriving, and new buyers become scarcer when interest rates rise.
The spot bitcoin funds and bitcoin treasury companies that drove the 2024 and 2025 rally were a one-time wave of buyers that has largely already bought.

Ulrich Bindseil and Jürgen Schaaf of the European Central Bank wrote in a February 2024 post on The ECB Blog that bitcoin's fair value is still zero and that the approval of spot bitcoin funds did not make it a sound investment.

Peter Schiff, chief economist at Euro Pacific Asset Management, has argued in public for years that bitcoin has no intrinsic value and that its price will eventually collapse rather than keep setting new records.
ETF approval for bitcoin – the naked emperor's new clothes, Ulrich Bindseil and Jürgen Schaaf, 2024
where_found: The ECB Blog, European Central Bank
bridge: Two European Central Bank officials argue that approval of spot bitcoin funds did not change bitcoin's lack of underlying value and that its fair value is still zero.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight on the price: the authors' earlier 2022 warning came before a large rise, so their case is about value, not timing.

text: Easy Money: Cryptocurrency, Casino Capitalism, and the Golden Age of Fraud, Ben McKenzie with Jacob Silverman, 2023
bridge: McKenzie and Silverman argue that crypto prices rest on a constant inflow of new money from retail buyers, which makes them prone to sharp collapses.
bottom_line: Low weight on bitcoin specifically, since the book focuses on exchanges and tokens, but it states the skeptics' core case plainly.

text: Bitcoin miners need a bitcoin price high enough to cover their power and equipment costs after the 2024 halving cut the block reward to 3.125 bitcoin.
measured_by: Miner revenue per unit of computing power (hashprice) compared with miners' reported cost to mine one bitcoin.
if_true: Hashprice rises well above mining costs and miners expand.
if_false: Hashprice stays near or below costs and weaker miners shut down or sell out.
bottom_line: A strong, concrete interest: miner survival depends directly on price after the 2024 halving.

text: Shareholders of bitcoin treasury companies such as Strategy need bitcoin to rise faster than their companies issue new shares.
measured_by: Bitcoin held per share, and the company's share price compared with the value of its bitcoin.
if_true: Bitcoin per share value rises and the companies can raise money on good terms again.
if_false: Share prices lag, dilution continues, and pressure to sell bitcoin grows.
bottom_line: Important because these companies hold about 4 percent of all bitcoin and their health affects the whole market.

text: Long-term bitcoin holders need the price to reward years of holding through deep drops.
measured_by: Return on bitcoin held for four years or more compared with stocks or bonds over the same period.
if_true: Four-year returns stay well above stocks and bonds.
if_false: Holders who bought in 2024 or 2025 sit on small gains or losses by the end of 2027.
bottom_line: A broad interest, but it argues for wanting the price to rise, not for the price actually rising.

text: Household electricity customers in regions with large bitcoin mines need power prices that are not pushed up by mining demand.
measured_by: Residential electricity rates and grid demand in counties and states that host large bitcoin mines.
if_true: Mining expands and adds demand to local grids.
if_false: Mining stays flat or shrinks and its pressure on local power prices eases.
bottom_line: A real but local interest; its size depends on how each grid prices and manages large loads.

text: If bitcoin reaches $200,000, the 840,447 bitcoin held by Strategy would be worth about $97 billion more than at the late-September 2026 price of about $85,000.
bottom_line: Large and directly computed from reported holdings, though the gain is on paper until shares or coins are sold.

text: At $200,000 a coin, the roughly 450 new bitcoin mined each day would pay miners about $33 billion a year in block rewards, about $19 billion more than at $85,000.
bottom_line: Large and simple arithmetic, but higher prices also draw more competing machines, which eats into each miner's share.

text: Shareholders of US spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which held about $108 billion in late September 2026, would gain roughly $147 billion if bitcoin rose to $200,000 with the same number of coins held.
bottom_line: A rough estimate from fund assets and price; real gains depend on when each shareholder bought.

text: Retail investors who buy near a bitcoin top have historically faced drops of more than 50 percent, as when bitcoin fell from its October 2025 record of $126,198 to about $60,000 in early 2026.
bottom_line: Well documented and repeated across cycles; a run to $200,000 would likely be followed by another deep fall.

text: People who borrow to buy bitcoin in expectation of $200,000 can be wiped out by forced selling on the way, as happened when a wave of liquidations pulled bitcoin below $105,000 after October 10, 2025.
bottom_line: Real and recurring, but the size depends on how much borrowing builds up, which is not estimated here.

text: A bitcoin price of $200,000 would make more mining machines profitable, raising electricity demand in regions with large bitcoin mines.
bottom_line: The direction is clear from mining economics, but no sourced estimate of the size is on this page yet.

text: A daily value above $200,000 on the CME CF Bitcoin Reference Rate, New York Variant (BRRNY), on any day from October 4, 2026 through December 31, 2027, is a fair measure of whether this belief came true.
The total net assets of US spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds are a fair measure of whether new institutional money is arriving fast enough to carry bitcoin to $200,000.
The federal funds target rate set by the Federal Reserve is a fair measure of whether money conditions favor a large bitcoin rally in 2027.
Enough new money will flow into bitcoin before the end of 2027 to lift its price about 135 percent, from about $85,000 to above $200,000.
No regulatory crackdown, major exchange failure or technical flaw will cut demand for bitcoin badly enough to stop a rally before the end of 2027.
If bitcoin climbs above $200,000 in 2027, bitcoin treasury companies such as Strategy would likely be able to sell new shares on good terms again and resume buying bitcoin.
If bitcoin passes $200,000 before the 2028 halving, more pension funds, endowments and governments would treat bitcoin as a standard reserve holding over the following decade.
Bitcoin will trade above 300,000 dollars at some point before the end of 2027.
Bitcoin will close above 200,000 dollars on December 31, 2027, not just at some point before it.
Bitcoin will set a new record above its October 2025 high of about 126,000 dollars before the end of 2027.
Bitcoin will trade above 200,000 dollars at some point before the end of 2030.
Most cryptocurrencies other than Bitcoin and Ether will be worth less in 2030 than they are today.
bottom_line: The evidence that most crypto tokens fail is overwhelming if you count every token ever launched, and strong even for coins that once ranked in the top 100. The real fight is over the established altcoins bought near the October 2026 slump: crypto history holds only a few full boom-and-bust cycles, and the answer swings on whether stablecoins count and whether "most" means most coins or most dollars.
hook: CoinGecko counted 11,564,909 crypto tokens that stopped trading in 2025 alone, more than in the four years before it combined.
question: Will most cryptocurrencies other than Bitcoin and Ether be worth less in 2030 than they were in October 2026?
ask: The page most needs a dataset showing how the top 100 altcoins bought at the 2018 and 2022 market lows were priced four years later, which would show whether buying altcoins at a low has paid.

text: Anyone can now create a new crypto token in minutes for almost nothing, so the number of tokens keeps multiplying while the money available to buy them does not, which spreads buyers ever thinner across coins.
bottom_line: Strong for small tokens, since CoinGecko counted 11.6 million tokens that stopped trading in 2025 alone, but weaker for established coins whose buyers do not drift to each new launch.

text: Most cryptocurrencies other than Bitcoin and Ether keep releasing new tokens to founders, early investors and networks through scheduled unlocks, so the price of each token tends to fall even when total demand holds steady.
bottom_line: Fairly heavy, because Keyrock's study of more than 16,000 unlock events found 90% put downward pressure on price, though a growing network can absorb new supply.

text: Large institutional money arriving through exchange-traded funds and company treasuries has gone mostly to Bitcoin and Ether, leaving most other cryptocurrencies with thin trading and few deep-pocketed buyers.
bottom_line: Moderate, because JPMorgan analysts said in May 2026 that altcoins have lagged Bitcoin since 2023 on weak liquidity and repeated hacks, but altcoin ETFs began trading in late 2025 and could change that flow.

text: The failure of the CLARITY Act in the U.S. Senate on September 15, 2026 leaves the legal status of most tokens other than Bitcoin and Ether unsettled, which keeps cautious American investors and banks away from them.
bottom_line: Modest, since regulators are building rules without Congress and a later bill could pass well before 2030.

text: CoinGecko found that 53.2% of crypto tokens listed on its GeckoTerminal tracker between July 2021 and December 2025 were no longer actively traded, including 11,564,909 tokens that died in 2025 alone.
bottom_line: Strong evidence that most tokens by count fail, but most of these were short-lived meme tokens that few people ever held.

text: Of the 100 largest cryptocurrencies in July 2021, only 41 were still in the top 100 five years later, 13 were delisted or dead, and the 46 that fell out but kept trading lost a median of about 93% of their market value.
bottom_line: The most direct evidence for the claim, though it measures from a cycle peak in 2021 rather than from a slump like October 2026.

text: CryptoRank found that 71.9% of the 1,539 cryptocurrencies that ever reached the top 100 by market value were effectively defunct, defined as under $10,000 in daily trading for 90 straight days plus delisting from major exchanges.
bottom_line: Strong evidence that even large coins rarely last, though its projections of future failures are model estimates rather than observations.

text: Keyrock's analysis of more than 16,000 token unlock events across 40 tokens found that 90% produced downward price pressure, with unlocks to project teams linked to declines of around 25%.
bottom_line: Good evidence for one mechanism behind falling prices, from a trading firm rather than a peer-reviewed journal.

text: At least half of the coins in the CoinGecko top 100 on October 4, 2026, not counting Bitcoin, Ether and stablecoins, will have dropped out of the top 100 or been delisted.
The share of total crypto market value held by coins other than Bitcoin, Ether and stablecoins will be lower than on October 4, 2026.
A study shows that most of the top-100 altcoins bought at the December 2018 or December 2022 market lows were still worth less four years later.
U.S. courts or regulators rule that most large altcoins are unregistered securities, and major U.S. exchanges delist them.
A cryptocurrency's long-run price depends mainly on lasting demand to use or hold it, not on the excitement of its launch or of a bull market.
The pattern of the 2018 and 2022 crypto crashes, after which most cryptocurrencies other than Bitcoin and Ether never regained their earlier prices, will hold through 2030.
Judging the claim coin by coin, rather than by total dollars invested, is a fair way to decide whether most cryptocurrencies other than Bitcoin and Ether lost value.

JPMorgan analysts led by Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou wrote in May 2026 that cryptocurrencies other than Bitcoin had underperformed Bitcoin since 2023 because of tighter liquidity, weaker market depth and limited DeFi growth, and said ether and other altcoins would not catch up to Bitcoin without a major boom in network activity.
Number Go Up: Inside Crypto's Wild Rise and Staggering Fall, Zeke Faux, 2023
where_found: Currency (Crown Publishing Group, Penguin Random House)
bridge: Bloomberg reporter Zeke Faux shows how many crypto tokens rose on hype and recruitment of new buyers rather than use, then collapsed when the buyers stopped coming, as in the 2022 crash and the FTX bankruptcy.
bottom_line: Useful reporting on why many tokens lose value, but it tells stories rather than counting how often altcoins recover, so it supports the mechanism more than the 2030 forecast.

text: Crypto prices in October 2026 are already deep in a slump, with Bitcoin about 34% below its October 2025 record and Solana and XRP down roughly 40% and 47% for the year by August, so most altcoins are being measured from a low starting price.
bottom_line: Strong, because the claim compares 2030 to a depressed date, and past crypto lows have been followed by large rebounds, though altcoins have also kept falling after earlier lows.

text: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission approved generic listing standards for crypto funds in September 2025, so the largest altcoins such as Solana and XRP now have the same exchange-traded fund channel that brought steady institutional buying to Bitcoin after January 2024.
bottom_line: Moderate, since the funds exist and are trading, but early 2026 saw net outflows from crypto funds and only a handful of altcoins qualify.

text: A growing number of crypto projects, such as the trading platform Hyperliquid, use their fee revenue to buy back their own tokens, so tokens tied to real businesses can rise in value as usage grows, much like stocks.
bottom_line: Modest for the claim as a whole, because only a small minority of tokens have meaningful revenue, but it shows the losers are not a law of nature.

text: Stablecoin use reached a record value of about $318.6 billion in April 2026, and the blockchains those dollars move across collect fees, so the busiest networks other than Bitcoin and Ethereum can see their tokens gain value by 2030.
bottom_line: Moderate, since rising stablecoin use is well documented, but much of it runs on Ethereum and Tron and the fees often do not reach token holders.

text: By mid-August 2026, Solana was down 39.6% and XRP down 46.8% for the year, steeper falls than Bitcoin's 28.86%, which leaves major altcoins especially far below their recent prices.
bottom_line: Moderate, since a deep drawdown raises the room for recovery but does not show recovery will come.

text: The total value of stablecoins reached a record of about $318.6 billion on April 11, 2026, with USDT at $184.3 billion and USDC at $78.8 billion, assets designed to keep a steady dollar value.
bottom_line: Matters only if stablecoins count toward the claim, in which case a large block of top coins will not fall in dollar terms.

text: More than half of the non-stablecoin coins in the CoinGecko top 100 on October 4, 2026, other than Bitcoin and Ether, will close above their October 4, 2026 price.
Total fees paid by users of blockchains and apps other than Bitcoin and Ethereum will be higher in calendar 2030 than in calendar 2026.
A study shows that most of the top-100 altcoins bought at the December 2018 or December 2022 market lows were worth more four years later.
Data show new token launches falling sharply while fees collected by the largest altcoin networks rise year after year through 2028.
Crypto prices in October 2026 sit near the low point of a market cycle, so an ordinary recovery by 2030 would lift most established cryptocurrencies above their October 2026 prices.
Growing use of crypto for payments, stablecoins and tokenized assets will spread value across many blockchains rather than concentrating it in Bitcoin and Ethereum.

The fair set for judging cryptocurrencies other than Bitcoin and Ether is the established coins people actually hold, such as the top few hundred by market value, not millions of abandoned meme tokens.

Geoff Kendrick, head of digital assets research at Standard Chartered, cut his end-2026 forecast for XRP from $8 to $2.80 in February 2026 but kept a forecast of $28 per XRP by 2030, far above XRP's price in 2026.
Read Write Own: Building the Next Era of the Internet, Chris Dixon, 2024
bridge: Andreessen Horowitz investor Chris Dixon argues that blockchain networks with their own tokens will become the base layer of the internet, which would give many tokens beyond Bitcoin and Ether lasting value.
bottom_line: The clearest case for why many tokens could gain value, but Dixon's firm holds large token positions, so the book is advocacy from an interested party.

text: Cryptoassets: The Innovative Investor's Guide to Bitcoin and Beyond, Chris Burniske and Jack Tatar, 2017
bridge: The book lays out a way to value crypto tokens by the use of their networks, arguing that tokens beyond Bitcoin can be a lasting asset class rather than pure speculation.
bottom_line: Gives a fair framework for telling durable tokens from doomed ones, though many tokens it treated as promising in 2017 have since lost most of their value.

text: State of Crypto 2025: The year crypto went mainstream, Daren Matsuoka, Robert Hackett, Jeremy Zhang, Stephanie Zinn and Eddy Lazzarin, 2025
bridge: The report found Solana generating about $3 billion a year in application revenue and Hyperliquid over $1 billion in annualized revenue, evidence that some networks other than Bitcoin and Ethereum have real, paying use.
bottom_line: Good evidence that a few networks have real businesses, but it comes from a crypto investor and covers a handful of leaders, not most tokens.

text: Small retail investors need warnings about crypto tokens that are likely to lose most of their value
measured_by: Average loss on altcoin holdings among U.S. retail crypto buyers between 2026 and 2030, from exchange and survey data.
if_true: Investors who heed the warning show smaller losses than those who held altcoins.
if_false: Investors who heeded the warning show smaller gains than those who held altcoins.
bottom_line: The largest group affected, and the one least able to absorb a 90% loss.

text: Hedge fund traders who bet against altcoins need altcoin prices to fall
measured_by: Returns on short positions in altcoin futures and perpetual contracts from 2026 to 2030.
if_true: Short positions on most altcoins pay off.
if_false: Short positions on most altcoins lose money.
bottom_line: A narrow interest, but it shows people with money at stake on the agree side too.

text: Crypto developers and founders need token prices to hold so they can pay for their work
measured_by: Venture and token-sale funding raised by crypto projects outside Bitcoin and Ethereum each year.
if_true: Funding shrinks as token prices fall.
if_false: Funding holds or grows with token prices.
bottom_line: A strong interest, and the group with the most inside knowledge and the most bias.

text: People who already hold altcoins need their holdings to recover before they sell
measured_by: The 2030 price of their coins compared with what they paid.
if_true: Most holders end 2030 with less than they have in October 2026.
if_false: Most holders end 2030 with more than they have in October 2026.
bottom_line: Millions of people are in this group, and many bought at prices far above today's.

text: Crypto exchange employees and shareholders need active trading in many tokens
measured_by: Exchange trading volume in tokens other than Bitcoin, Ether and stablecoins.
if_true: Altcoin trading volume falls as prices fall.
if_false: Altcoin trading volume rises with prices.
bottom_line: Exchanges earn fees on listings and trades, so they benefit from many tokens whatever happens to holders.

text: Small retail investors who believe most altcoins will lose value and avoid them will lose less money between 2026 and 2030.
bottom_line: Real if the belief is true, but no reliable figure exists for how much retail money sits in altcoins.

text: Less money flowing into new tokens means fewer people fall for pump-and-dump schemes and token launches built to cash out early insiders.
bottom_line: Plausible and important, but hard to measure since fraud losses are not tracked by token type.

text: Useful projects such as payment networks and tokenized-asset platforms find it harder to raise money when investors write off tokens as a class.
bottom_line: Moderate, since good projects can still raise money with equity, but tokens are how many open networks pay developers.

text: Crypto exchanges and their workers lose trading revenue when fewer people trade tokens other than Bitcoin and Ether.
bottom_line: Real but modest for the wider economy, since exchanges can shift to other products.

text: The share of the CoinGecko top 100 on October 4, 2026, excluding Bitcoin, Ether, stablecoins and wrapped or staked copies of Bitcoin and Ether, whose average daily closing price in calendar 2030 is below their October 4, 2026 price is a fair measure of whether most cryptocurrencies other than Bitcoin and Ether lost value.
The share of total crypto market value held by coins other than Bitcoin, Ether and stablecoins is a fair measure of whether money is moving away from altcoins.
Total fees paid by users of blockchains and apps other than Bitcoin and Ethereum is a fair measure of whether real use of altcoins is growing.
Most cryptocurrencies other than Bitcoin and Ether have historically lost dollar value over periods of four years or more.
The forces that pushed most altcoins down after the 2018 and 2021 peaks, such as new token supply, fading attention and money concentrating in Bitcoin, will keep working between 2026 and 2030.
A token's dollar price on a public market at the end of 2030, compared with its price in October 2026, is the right measure of whether it is worth less.
Retail investors who move money out of small cryptocurrencies other than Bitcoin and Ether in 2026 and 2027 avoid losses as thinly traded tokens keep falling and are dropped by exchanges.
Crypto exchanges delist more cryptocurrencies with little trading during 2027, shrinking the number of altcoins that U.S. buyers can easily purchase.
By the mid-2030s the crypto market narrows to a handful of large networks plus dollar stablecoins, much as the list of internet stocks narrowed after the 2000 crash.
Investors fund fewer new crypto token launches over the next decade and crypto startups raise money by selling company shares instead of tokens.
Most cryptocurrencies other than Bitcoin and Ether will be worth nothing by 2030.
Every cryptocurrency other than Bitcoin will lose most of its dollar value between 2026 and 2030.
Most of the 100 largest cryptocurrencies other than Bitcoin and Ether will lose value measured against Bitcoin between October 2026 and the end of 2030.
Most newly launched crypto tokens will stop trading within five years of their launch.
By the end of 2030, AI systems will do most of the work now done by entry-level software programmers.
bottom_line: The evidence that AI is already reshaping junior programming is solid: employment of U.S. software developers aged 22 to 25 fell about 20 percent from late 2022, and Google says AI writes 75 percent of its new code. Whether AI does most entry-level programming work by the end of 2030 rests on two thinner things, that capability trends keep climbing and that writing code is most of the job, while economy-wide studies still find no broad AI disruption and the official forecast is for software jobs to grow.
hook: By July 2025, employment of U.S. software developers aged 22 to 25 had fallen nearly 20 percent from its late-2022 peak while older developers kept their jobs (Stanford Digital Economy Lab, ADP payroll data).
question: By the end of 2030, will AI systems be doing most of the work that entry-level software programmers do today?
ask: Real measurements, from any company that tracks them, of what share of the tasks normally given to first-year programmers AI agents now finish without human edits.

text: The length of software tasks that AI agents can finish on their own has doubled roughly every seven months for six years, a pace that would put multi-day programming tasks within reach of AI agents well before 2030.
bottom_line: Strong weight as a measured trend, but the belief stands or falls on whether the trend keeps going, and METR itself says most of its uncertainty is about exactly that.

text: Most of the work given to entry-level programmers is small, well-specified, self-contained tasks, which is the kind of programming work today's AI coding agents handle best.
bottom_line: Moderate to strong weight, because junior tickets really are the most bounded work in software, though juniors also spend time on meetings, debugging and learning the codebase.

text: Large software companies already report that AI writes most of their new code, with Google saying in April 2026 that 75 percent of its new code was AI-generated and approved by engineers.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, since it shows the direction clearly, but it is a self-reported count of code lines, and writing lines is not the same as doing the whole job.

text: Employment of U.S. software developers aged 22 to 25 has fallen about 20 percent from its late-2022 peak while employment of older developers grew, which is the pattern AI taking over junior tasks would produce.
bottom_line: Strong weight as the most direct evidence so far, held back because the authors themselves say other causes, like interest rates, may share the blame.

text: Software programming is the office job where AI output is easiest to check automatically, because compilers and tests tell an AI agent whether its code works, so programming should be automated before most other desk work.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because automatic checking is a real advantage for AI in coding, but tests only catch the problems someone thought to test for.

text: The length of software tasks that frontier AI agents can complete with 50 percent reliability has doubled about every seven months over the past six years.
bottom_line: Strong weight as a careful measurement, though 50 percent reliability is far below what an employer expects of a paid junior programmer.

text: 79 percent of conversations on Claude Code, an AI coding agent, were classified as automation (the AI doing the task directly) rather than augmentation, compared with 49 percent of coding conversations on the regular Claude.ai chat site.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because it shows agent tools shift work toward full handoff, but it comes from the tool's maker and counts conversations, not jobs.

text: Employment of U.S. software developers aged 22 to 25 will be at least 35 percent below its late-2022 peak.

At least three of the five largest U.S. technology companies by market value will publicly report that AI writes 90 percent or more of their new code while cutting new-graduate engineering hiring below 2022 levels.
A study comparing similar companies finds that firms that adopted AI coding agents cut junior developer hiring by more than half relative to firms that did not adopt them.
A controlled test at several companies finds AI agents completing at least 80 percent of the real tickets assigned to first-year engineers with no human edits before the code is merged.
The growth in the length of programming tasks AI agents can finish on their own will continue at roughly its 2019 to 2025 pace through the end of 2030.
Companies will put AI coding agents into everyday use about as fast as the agents become capable, without years of delay from testing, regulation or old systems.

The job of an entry-level programmer can be broken into separate tasks that can each be handed to software, rather than being a bundle of learning and coordination that only works when done by one person.

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei told Axios in May 2025 that AI could eliminate half of all entry-level white-collar jobs within one to five years and push U.S. unemployment to 10 to 20 percent.

Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg said on The Joe Rogan Experience in January 2025 that Meta and other companies would probably have AI in 2025 that could effectively work as a mid-level software engineer.
Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence, Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen, 2025 (revised August 2026)
bridge: Payroll records covering millions of U.S. workers show employment of 22-to-25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed jobs, software developers among them, running well below that of less-exposed peers, mostly through less hiring rather than layoffs.
bottom_line: High weight as the largest direct measurement of young workers in AI-exposed jobs, though the authors call it descriptive rather than proof of cause.

text: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks, Thomas Kwa, Ben West and others (METR), 2025
bridge: The study measures how long a software task, timed by how long it takes skilled people, AI agents can finish half the time, and finds that length has doubled about every seven months since 2019.
bottom_line: Medium to high weight, since the trend is carefully measured, but carrying it forward to 2030 is a forecast, not a finding.

text: Most of an entry-level programmer's working day is spent understanding what people want, tracking down bugs, reading other people's code and coordinating with teammates, not typing new code, and AI does that other work far less reliably.
bottom_line: Strong weight, because counting AI-written lines measures only the part of the job AI is best at.

text: Cheaper software production has historically raised demand for programmers rather than cut it, because lower costs make worthwhile many projects that were too expensive to build before.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, since compilers, open-source libraries and cloud services all followed this pattern, though no law guarantees AI will too.

text: The drop in hiring of young software developers since 2022 is largely explained by higher interest rates and companies correcting for pandemic over-hiring, both of which began before AI coding tools were widely used.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because the timing does overlap, but Stanford's researchers found the young-worker decline held even after controlling for company-level shocks.

text: Software companies need junior programmers to train into the senior engineers they will need later, so most firms will keep hiring beginners even when AI could do many of their current tasks.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, since leaders like AWS chief Matt Garman say this openly, but each firm can be tempted to let other firms do the training.

text: AI-generated code still needs careful human review for security and correctness, so AI coding tools mostly move a junior programmer's hours from writing code to checking it rather than eliminating them.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, backed by surveys where more developers distrust AI accuracy than trust it, though review burdens may fall as models improve.

text: Banks, hospitals, governments and other large organizations adopt new tools slowly because of old code, regulation and legal liability, so AI will not take over most junior programming work across the whole economy by 2030 even if the technology is ready.
bottom_line: Moderate to strong weight, because past technologies took a decade or more to spread, and four years is short for the slowest adopters.

text: In a randomized trial, 16 experienced open-source developers took 19 percent longer to finish real tasks when allowed to use early-2025 AI tools, even though they believed the tools had sped them up by 20 percent.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight now, since the sample was small, it studied experts rather than juniors, and METR's February 2026 follow-up pointed to speedups instead while calling its new data unreliable.

text: The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects employment of software developers to grow 15.8 percent from 2024 to 2034, adding about 267,700 jobs, the largest gain among computer occupations.
bottom_line: Moderate weight as the official consensus forecast, though BLS projections track past trends and are slow to catch sudden technology shifts.

text: Indeed job postings for software development rose from a low of 61.1 in May 2025 to 74.4 in August 2026, on an index where February 1, 2020 equals 100.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because demand recovered while AI coding tools spread fast, though postings are still about a quarter below 2020 and are not broken out for entry-level roles.

text: Indeed's software development postings index will climb back above 90, where February 1, 2020 equals 100.
The unemployment rate for recent U.S. computer science graduates will fall back below the average unemployment rate for all recent college graduates.
Employment of U.S. software developers aged 22 to 25 returns to its 2022 level by 2028 even as AI coding tool use keeps rising.
Firms that adopted AI coding tools early turn out to have hired more junior developers per year since 2023 than similar firms that adopted late.
Making software cheaper to build will create enough new software projects to keep employers hiring junior programmers, as happened after compilers, open-source libraries and cloud computing.
The hardest parts of an entry-level programmer's job, such as figuring out what people actually want and learning an unfamiliar codebase, are the parts AI improves at most slowly.
Banks, hospitals, governments and other large employers will take most of a decade to trust AI agents with production code, whatever the agents can do in a lab.

Amazon Web Services chief executive Matt Garman said in an August 2025 interview with Matthew Berman that replacing junior employees with AI was the dumbest thing he had ever heard, because companies would have no one trained to lead in ten years.

where_found: Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University
bridge: The essay argues that adoption of AI, unlike its invention, is held back by testing, organizational change and regulation, so its effects on work will unfold over decades rather than a few years.
bottom_line: Medium weight as a well-argued case from the history of past technologies, though it predicts pace in general rather than measuring programming specifically.

bridge: The survey of working developers finds that more of them distrust the accuracy of AI coding tools than trust it, which means AI output still needs human checking.
bottom_line: Low to medium weight, since it records developer opinion rather than measured output, and opinion can lag fast-improving tools.

text: Startup founders need to ship working products with fewer paid engineers.
measured_by: Engineering headcount needed to launch a product, as reported in startup surveys and funding data.
if_true: Headcount per launched product falls sharply and small teams ship what once took dozens of engineers.
if_false: Founders still have to raise money to hire junior engineers before shipping.
bottom_line: A real and growing interest, already visible in startups' heavier use of agent tools.

text: Small-business owners need custom software they can afford without hiring a development team.
measured_by: Share of small businesses that build or commission their own software tools, and the price they pay.
if_true: More small businesses get custom tools at lower prices.
if_false: Custom software stays priced for companies that can afford programmers.
bottom_line: Broad interest that gains most if AI can do junior-level work reliably and cheaply.

text: Computer science graduates need entry-level programming jobs where they can learn the trade.
measured_by: Unemployment rate for recent computer science and computer engineering graduates in the New York Fed's recent-graduate data.
if_true: Their unemployment rate stays well above the average for recent graduates.
if_false: Their unemployment rate falls back toward or below the recent-graduate average.
bottom_line: Directly harmed if the belief comes true, and already showing above-average unemployment.

text: Hospitals, banks and other organizations that run critical software need human programmers who understand the code and can answer for it.
measured_by: Security incidents and outages traced to code no human fully understood.
if_true: Fewer people understand the code these organizations depend on, raising the risk of failures.
if_false: Human programmers stay in the loop and accountability stays clear.
bottom_line: High-stakes interest, since a failure in critical software lands on patients and customers, not just on the firm.

text: Senior software engineers need a steady supply of trained juniors to hand work to and eventually take over their systems.
measured_by: Number of engineers promoted from junior to mid-level roles each year at large firms.
if_true: The supply of mid-level engineers shrinks a few years after junior hiring falls.
if_false: The usual path from junior to senior keeps working.
bottom_line: Moderate interest whose costs show up years after junior hiring stops.

text: Handing routine programming tasks to AI would raise the amount of software work each team completes by about a quarter, based on field experiments with nearly 4,900 developers.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, since the 26 percent figure comes from randomized field trials at Microsoft, Accenture and a Fortune 100 firm, but those trials studied AI assistance rather than full replacement.

bottom_line: Plausible and important, but no source yet measures the price change, so it is left unestimated.

text: Students who heed an early, accurate warning about shrinking entry-level programming jobs would move into fields still hiring beginners before taking on years of tuition debt.
bottom_line: Real value if the belief is true, and real harm if it is false and steers students away from a field that keeps growing.

text: Companies that stop hiring juniors will face a shortage of experienced engineers a decade later, because senior engineers are made from junior ones.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, widely predicted by industry leaders but not yet measured anywhere.

text: More AI-written code reviewed by fewer people will let more security holes and hidden bugs reach the software people rely on.

Bob Chew, the Forward Party candidate, is the best choice for the Colorado office he is seeking in 2026.
bottom_line: The record is solid on what Chew offers: he has the only published debt plan of the three candidates, his money is almost all his own, and the 2026 Trustees Report confirms the 2032 Social Security deadline he campaigns on, though his own numbers overstate how bad it is. It is thin on how he would actually vote, since he has never held elected office and has not picked among his 13 Social Security options, so the real fight is whether a debt-first candidate free of both parties is worth more than an incumbent who ranked 27th of the 98 senators it ranked on the Lugar Center's Bipartisan Index in 2023 and has built six years of seniority.
hook: Bob Chew has put $1.1 million of his own money and a $150,000 loan into his Senate campaign, while every other donor combined gave about $20,000 (Colorado Politics, July 14, 2026).
question: Is Bob Chew, the Forward Party nominee, a better choice for Colorado's U.S. Senate seat in 2026 than John Hickenlooper or Mark Baisley?
ask: This page most needs a nonpartisan poll of the Colorado Senate race that includes Bob Chew by name, since no such poll could be found as of October 17, 2026.

text: Bob Chew has made the national debt and Social Security solvency the center of his 2026 U.S. Senate campaign in Colorado, while the published priorities of Democrat John Hickenlooper (prices, health care, water, opposing Trump) and Republican Mark Baisley (smaller government, property tax) include no debt reduction plan.
bottom_line: This deserves real weight if a voter ranks the debt as the top federal problem, since Chew is the only one of the three with a published debt plan (bobchew2026.com; Colorado Politics, October 2, 2026), but it only decides the race for voters who share that ranking.

text: Bob Chew's campaign is almost entirely self-funded, with $1.1 million donated and $150,000 lent by the candidate against about $20,000 from other donors through June 30, 2026, so no party committee or large donor holds a claim on his votes.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the figures are in his FEC reports as reported by Colorado Politics (July 14, 2026), but self-funding proves only that he is free of donors, not that he would vote well.

text: Bob Chew co-founded an engineering firm in 1996, grew it to roughly 750 employees and $150 million in annual revenue, moved it to employee ownership in 2008, and ran it as CEO for about 25 years, which is the kind of long budget-balancing experience most senators lack.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the business record is documented (IVN, June 17, 2026; smarter.vote), but running a company and legislating are different jobs, and Hickenlooper ran a city and a state.

text: Bob Chew's positions cross party lines (universal background checks and assault weapon limits alongside spending restraint and nuclear power, opposing both Trump's tariffs and Trump's Iran war), which matches the mixed views of Colorado's unaffiliated majority better than either party platform does.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: his positions are on record (smarter.vote; bobchew2026.com), and unaffiliated voters are 50.8 percent of active registrants (Colorado Secretary of State via Colorado Politics, October 2, 2026), but whether those voters actually hold his mix of views is not shown.

text: Bob Chew publishes 13 options for fixing Social Security, including raising the retirement age and the payroll tax, which is more honest than campaigns that promise no changes to benefits while the retirement trust fund heads toward depletion in 2032.
bottom_line: Modest weight: naming hard choices is a real difference from his opponents, but listing options without choosing one is also a way of avoiding the hard choice.

text: Through June 30, 2026, Bob Chew's Senate campaign reported about $1.27 million in receipts, of which $1.1 million was his own donation, $150,000 his own loan, and about $20,000 came from other individuals, including $1,000 each from Andrew Yang and Christine Todd Whitman.
bottom_line: A public filing, so the independence-from-donors claim rests on checkable numbers, though independence from donors is only one part of being the best choice.

text: As of September 1, 2026, Colorado had 2,034,154 active unaffiliated voters out of 4,006,449 active voters (50.8 percent), against 987,582 Democrats and 887,577 Republicans.
bottom_line: Official counts; they show a large pool of voters outside both parties but say nothing about whether those voters want a third candidate.

text: The 2026 Social Security Trustees Report, released June 9, 2026, projects the retirement (OASI) trust fund to be depleted in the fourth quarter of 2032, after which incoming taxes would cover about 78 percent of scheduled benefits.
bottom_line: The CBO's February 2026 projection agreed on the 2032 date (with a steeper cut), so the deadline Chew campaigns on is well supported even though his own numbers overstate it.

text: Bob Chew will win a larger share of the vote than any minor-party or independent candidate for U.S. Senate in Colorado since 1950, beating the roughly 3.5 percent Libertarian result of 2016.
At least one independent, non-campaign poll of the Colorado Senate race will show Bob Chew at 10 percent or more.
A nonpartisan poll of likely Colorado voters shows Bob Chew in double digits and drawing roughly equally from voters who otherwise lean Democratic and Republican.
An independent budget group scores Bob Chew's published debt plan as reducing ten-year deficits by more than any plan put forward by Hickenlooper or Baisley.
A candidate with no voting record can be judged fairly by his business record and his published positions.
The national debt is the most important problem the next Colorado senator will face, and neither major party will address it without outside pressure.
A senator who belongs to neither caucus can still be useful, either by brokering fiscal deals between the parties or by forcing the debt onto the agenda, even if he passes no bill of his own.

Lindsey Drath, chief executive of the Forward Party, announced the party's endorsement of Bob Chew for U.S. Senate in Colorado on June 18, 2026, saying of Chew and three other endorsed Senate candidates that they "are not running to fit into the system as it exists today" (Forward Party, June 18, 2026).

Andrew Yang and Christie Todd Whitman, the Forward Party's national co-chairs, each gave $1,000 to Bob Chew's Senate campaign, according to the campaign's second-quarter FEC filing as reported by Colorado Politics on July 14, 2026.
Breaking the Two-Party Doom Loop: The Case for Multiparty Democracy in America, Lee Drutman, 2020
bridge: Drutman argues that competition between only two parties has turned them into enemies rather than opponents and that American government works better when voters have more than two real options, which is the case Bob Chew makes for sending a senator from neither party to Washington.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the book is a careful argument for more parties in general, but it is about electoral rules, not about whether any one candidate deserves a particular seat.

text: The Politics Industry: How Political Innovation Can Break Partisan Gridlock and Save Our Democracy, Katherine M. Gehl and Michael E. Porter, 2020
bridge: Gehl and Porter describe the two parties as a duopoly that competes for donors and primary voters rather than for results, and they argue that candidates outside the duopoly are one way to force it to compete, which is the premise behind Chew's self-funded run.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it explains why a voter might prize a candidate who owes nothing to either party, but it offers no evidence about Chew himself.

text: Bob Chew has never held any elected office, so voters have no voting record on which to judge how he would actually vote under pressure.
bottom_line: Strong weight: this is undisputed (smarter.vote lists no voting record; Colorado Politics calls him a first-time candidate), and an untested candidate is a real risk for a six-year term.

text: Bob Chew's campaign site says Social Security and Medicare are 'going bankrupt in the next few years' with a 25 to 30 percent cut coming, but the 2026 Trustees Report projects the retirement trust fund lasting until late 2032 and then paying about 78 percent of benefits, so his central message overstates the problem he claims to be honest about.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the gap between his numbers (bobchew2026.com) and the trustees' (2026 Social Security Trustees Report, June 9, 2026) is real but not huge, and the trustees do confirm a serious shortfall.

text: Bob Chew lists 13 Social Security options without choosing any and proposes to study health care systems rather than pick a plan, so voters cannot know what he would vote for on the two biggest budget items.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: his own issues page shows this (bobchew2026.com), and it matters because he asks voters to trust his judgment on exactly these items.

text: A Colorado senator with no party caucus would receive no committee assignments of his own choosing and would carry less weight on Colorado River water deals and public lands than a member of either party's caucus.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: Senate committee seats are allocated through the two caucuses, and Hickenlooper's campaign claims he helped secure over $12 billion in federal western water funding (Colorado Politics, October 2, 2026), though that figure is a campaign claim.

text: Bob Chew was a registered Republican until August 2025 and, according to Hickenlooper's campaign, donated heavily to Republican senators including Susan Collins of Maine, so his independence from the two parties is a little over a year old.
bottom_line: Modest weight: the registration date is confirmed by Colorado Politics (July 14, 2026), but the donation claim comes from an opponent's campaign, and Chew says he gave to moderates of both parties.

text: John Hickenlooper ranked 27th of the 98 senators it ranked on the Lugar Center and McCourt School Bipartisan Index for 2023 with a score of 0.41157, up from 45th for the full 117th Congress (2021 to 2022).
bottom_line: A published measure built from cosponsorship records, so it is checkable; it shows the incumbent is above the Senate median on cross-party work, which weakens the case that Colorado needs an outsider for that.

text: Bob Chew will finish below 5 percent of the vote and Hickenlooper will win by a margin at least as large as his 9.3-point win over Cory Gardner in 2020.
FEC filings or news reporting show that Bob Chew's campaign spending or advertising was coordinated with or paid for by a party committee or a partisan outside group.
A six-year Senate term should go to a candidate whose votes under pressure can be checked against a public record.
A senator delivers for Colorado mainly through committee seats, seniority and caucus relationships, which a member of neither party would lack.

Mark Baisley, the Republican nominee for the same seat, said minor-party candidates like Bob Chew "seem to only serve as the spoiler, frustrating the will of the majority by splitting their votes," and invited Chew to seek the Republican nomination instead (Colorado Politics, August 12, 2026).

Jess Cohen, spokesman for John Hickenlooper's campaign, called Bob Chew a "Republican mega-donor" who is "too extreme for Colorado" and pointed to his proposals to change Social Security and Medicare benefits (Colorado Politics, September 30, 2026).
3rd-party U.S. Senate candidate Bob Chew boosts Colorado ads by $1.5M, Ernest Luning, Colorado Politics, September 30, 2026
bridge: The article records that Colorado has never elected an independent or third-party candidate to the U.S. Senate, that election analysts rate the seat a safe Democratic hold, and that Hickenlooper's campaign calls Chew a former Republican mega-donor who proposes cutting Social Security and Medicare.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the history and the race rating are checkable facts, while the campaign's characterization of Chew is an opponent's claim.

text: Can third-party candidates gain traction in Colorado? Maybe not, but it's not stopping them from trying, Caitlyn Kim, CPR News via The Colorado Sun, August 26, 2026
where_found: The Colorado Sun (Colorado Capitol News Alliance)
bridge: The report shows third-party vote totals exceeding the winning margin in Colorado's 8th Congressional District in both 2022 (over 9,200 Libertarian votes against a roughly 1,600-vote gap) and 2024, and quotes former Green county commissioner Art Goodtimes on the money and organization advantages minor-party candidates lack.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it documents both the spoiler risk and the structural odds against Chew, though a safe Democratic Senate seat is not a toss-up House district.

text: Workers who will retire after 2032 need Social Security financed before its retirement trust fund runs out.
measured_by: The trust fund depletion year and the percentage of scheduled benefits payable after depletion in the annual Trustees Report.
if_true: Congress acts before 2032 and the Trustees Report stops projecting a 22 percent automatic cut.
if_false: The depletion year stays at 2032 or moves earlier and the projected cut remains.
bottom_line: This interest does not depend on Chew personally, since any senator could push a fix, but Chew is the only candidate in this race who has made it a stated deadline.

text: Colorado taxpayers under 40 need federal borrowing slowed before interest payments crowd out everything else.
measured_by: Net interest paid by the federal government as a share of federal revenue, reported by the Congressional Budget Office.
if_true: Net interest as a share of revenue stabilizes or falls over the next decade.
if_false: Net interest keeps rising as a share of revenue, as CBO's baseline currently projects.
bottom_line: One senator cannot move this measure alone, so the interest is served only if Chew's election is part of a larger shift in Congress.

text: Colorado River farmers and city water utilities need a senator with the seniority to bring federal water money home.
measured_by: Federal dollars appropriated for Colorado River basin conservation and infrastructure in each Congress.
if_true: Colorado's junior senator starts over with no seniority and water dollars become harder to secure.
if_false: Hickenlooper keeps his seat and his Colorado River Caucus role and water appropriations continue at or near current levels.
bottom_line: Seniority matters for appropriations, but the $12 billion figure Hickenlooper cites is a campaign claim that credits him with money many senators worked on.

text: Colorado Republican voters need every center-right vote consolidated behind one candidate to make the race competitive.
measured_by: The gap in percentage points between Baisley's vote share and Hickenlooper's in the certified result, compared with the 9.3-point gap of 2020.
if_true: Chew draws center-right votes and the Republican gap grows beyond 2020's.
if_false: Chew draws few votes or draws evenly from both sides and the gap tracks the state's partisan lean.
bottom_line: The spoiler concern is the main Republican objection, but Baisley's $138,210 raised against Hickenlooper's $11.5 million suggests the race was not competitive before Chew entered.

text: Colorado Democrats need Hickenlooper's seat held to count toward a Senate majority that can check the Trump administration.
measured_by: Whether Colorado's seat is counted in the Democratic caucus total after the 2026 election.
if_true: The seat leaves the Democratic caucus count unless Chew agrees to caucus with Democrats.
if_false: The seat stays Democratic and counts toward the caucus total.
bottom_line: This is the strongest interest against Chew for roughly a quarter of Colorado's registered voters, and Chew has not said which caucus, if any, he would join.

text: Electing Bob Chew would place one senator in the chamber whose vote on budgets and confirmations is controlled by neither party's leadership.
bottom_line: Certain if he is elected, but one vote of 100 changes Senate rules only if other independents join him, which his Forward Party allies in Idaho, Montana and South Dakota would also have to win.

text: Electing Bob Chew would put a debt reduction bill with a Colorado sponsor before the Senate in 2027, since he has pledged to introduce one in his first year.
bottom_line: Introducing a bill is cheap and within one senator's power; passing it is not, so the realistic benefit is agenda-setting rather than deficit reduction.

text: Electing Bob Chew would cost Colorado the six years of Senate seniority and committee standing that John Hickenlooper has built since 2021.
bottom_line: Certain if the incumbent loses; how much seniority is worth in federal dollars is disputed, and Hickenlooper's $12 billion water funding claim is his campaign's own figure.

text: A senator with no party caucus would receive committee assignments only by the two caucuses' leave, leaving Colorado with weaker seats on the committees that handle water, public lands and appropriations.
bottom_line: Independents such as Angus King and Bernie Sanders have solved this by caucusing with a party, which Chew has not promised to do, so the cost is real unless he strikes such a deal.

text: A ten-year deficit score of each Senate candidate's published fiscal plan by a nonpartisan budget group is a fair measure of which candidate is most serious about the national debt.
The sitting senator's rank on the Lugar Center Bipartisan Index for the 2025 to 2026 Congress is a fair measure of whether Colorado already has the cross-party senator that Bob Chew promises to be.
Neither John Hickenlooper nor Mark Baisley has published a plan to reduce the national debt, while Bob Chew has.
A senator outside both party caucuses would do more to force a fiscal compromise than a member of either caucus with the same views.
Voters should weigh a candidate's published positions and private-sector record at least as heavily as an incumbent's public voting record and seniority.

Within a year of the November 3, 2026 election, a double-digit vote share for Bob Chew would push the national debt into both parties' Colorado messaging, in the way Chew himself says Ross Perot's 19 percent in 1992 put balanced budgets on the agenda (CPR News, August 26, 2026).

If Bob Chew won and took office in January 2027, his committee assignments and his access to Colorado River and public lands negotiations would depend on terms he struck with one of the two caucuses, with no precedent in Colorado to show how that would go.

Over a decade, a Forward Party senator who held the Colorado seat through a 2032 reelection would show that a minor-party candidate can win statewide, drawing candidates and money to minor-party runs for the legislature and governor in Colorado.

Over a decade, a debt-reduction bill of the kind Bob Chew proposes, if enacted, would bend the CBO's current-law path, under which debt held by the public reaches 108 percent of GDP in 2030 and 129 percent in 2040, while a Chew term that passed nothing would leave Colorado with a senator outside both caucuses and the debt on the same path.
Bob Chew will win Colorado's U.S. Senate election on November 3, 2026.
Every Colorado voter who ranks the national debt as the country's top problem should vote for Bob Chew for U.S. Senate in 2026.
Bob Chew's 2026 Senate campaign is worth having because it forces the national debt into Colorado's Senate race, whether or not he wins.
Bob Chew is a better choice than Mark Baisley for Colorado voters who will not vote for John Hickenlooper in 2026.
A Forward Party candidate can win a seat in the Colorado legislature in 2026.
bottom_line: For 2026 the record is narrow: the Forward Party has one Colorado legislative candidate, Bill Hare in House District 4, where the Democrat won 78.94% in 2024 and 13 voters are registered Forward. The real fight is over what "can" means and whether the party's openings outweigh that record: 52% of Colorado voters are unaffiliated, and a Forward member now holds a Utah Senate seat by appointment, but the party's best Colorado legislative result, 28.46% in House District 36, came with no Republican on the ballot, and its two 2025 Virginia nominees drew 1.92% and 1.88% against both major parties.
hook: The Forward Party is on the 2026 ballot for one of Colorado's 86 legislative seats, a Denver district with 13 registered Forward voters, 23,174 Democrats and an incumbent who won 79% last time.
question: Can a Forward Party candidate actually win a seat in the Colorado House or Senate in November 2026, or is the party's only legislative race a placeholder?
ask: The page most needs Bill Hare's certified House District 4 vote share once the Secretary of State publishes 2026 results, to replace the 2024 Forward and Center Party figures as the measure of what the label draws.

text: A Forward Party member already sits in a state legislature, because Utah Gov. Spencer Cox appointed Forward Party member Emily Buss to Utah Senate District 11 in December 2025 after Dan Thatcher left the Republican Party and then resigned.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it shows the Forward label is compatible with holding a legislative seat, but the seat came by appointment in a different state, not by winning a Colorado election.

text: Colorado's electorate is unusually open to a non-major-party choice, since 52% of its registered voters were unaffiliated as of June 2026 against 25% Democratic and 23% Republican.
bottom_line: Some weight: unaffiliated registration is a necessary condition for a third-party win, but most unaffiliated Coloradans still vote for one of the two major parties in general elections.

text: The Forward Party has secured a Colorado legislative ballot line for 2026, with Bill Hare certified on the Secretary of State's official candidate list for House District 4, so a win is procedurally possible rather than hypothetical.
bottom_line: Modest weight: being on the ballot is the minimum condition for winning, and the belief is about winning, not qualifying.

text: Colorado's minor-party rules let the Forward Party place a nominee on the November ballot by assembly or petition without a primary when only one candidate is designated, so the party can target whichever district has the weakest two-party competition each cycle.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight: the rule lowers the cost of trying, but it says nothing about whether voters will respond.

text: In the 2024 Colorado House District 36 general election, Forward Party candidate Eric Mulder received 8,532 votes (28.46%) against Democratic incumbent Michael Carter's 21,452 (71.54%) in a two-way race.
bottom_line: The Forward Party's best Colorado legislative result to date, and a floor for what the label can draw against an unopposed-by-Republicans Democrat.

text: Utah Senate District 11 has been held since December 17, 2025 by Forward Party member Emily Buss, appointed by Gov. Spencer Cox after Forward's Dan Thatcher resigned, in a chamber of 22 Republicans, 6 Democrats and 1 Forward member.
bottom_line: Proves a Forward legislator can exist, while leaving open whether one can be elected.

text: Enough voters in at least one Colorado legislative district will judge a Forward Party candidate on the person and the platform rather than on the party label next to the name.
Dissatisfaction with both major parties in 2026 is strong enough in Colorado to overcome a district's usual partisan lean in a single election.
Saying a Forward Party candidate "can" win a Colorado legislative seat means a real chance worth testing, not that a win is likely.

Andrew Yang, who founded the Forward Party, told Fox 13 in Salt Lake City that the party aims to be "not the third party, but the second party to create meaningful competition" in Utah, a state where one party dominates the legislature.

Greg Lopez, a former Republican congressman running for Colorado governor as an unaffiliated candidate in 2026, told CPR News in August 2026 that "the major voting block today is the unaffiliated voter" and that Democrats and Republicans are now the minor parties in Colorado.
Michelle Quist, chair of the Forward Party of Utah, told KUER in December 2025 that voters are "interested in looking for the candidate and what the candidate believes in, rather than the party."
Forward: Notes on the Future of Our Democracy, Andrew Yang, 2021
bridge: The Forward Party's founder lays out the case that voters are ready to back candidates outside the two major parties and proposes ranked-choice voting and open primaries to make such candidates viable.
bottom_line: Low weight as evidence about a 2026 Colorado race, since it argues for what should happen rather than showing a Forward candidate winning a legislative general election anywhere.

text: The Forward Party of Utah has a new senator. Can they hold on in 2026?, Sean Higgins (KUER), 2025
bridge: The report shows the Forward Party holding a state Senate seat in Utah through Emily Buss and quotes University of Utah political scientist Matthew Burbank that incumbency, the hardest advantage for a third-party candidate to get, is one she will now have.
bottom_line: Moderate weight for the claim that a Forward member can hold a legislative seat, but the seat came by appointment in Utah, and the same article doubts the party can keep it in a Republican-leaning district.

text: Utah Forward Party's first-of-its-kind preference poll picks a winner to replace Sen. Thatcher, Katie McKellar, 2025
bridge: The article records that Emily Buss won an open approval-voting poll of District 11 voters with 625 approvals and was sent to Gov. Spencer Cox as the Forward Party's pick, with the Utah Republican chair saying his party would field a challenger in 2026.
bottom_line: Some weight as proof that the Forward Party can organize and fill a legislative seat, though it shows nothing about how the party performs against both major parties in a Colorado general election.

text: The Forward Party has exactly one candidate in Colorado's 86 legislative races in 2026, Bill Hare in House District 4, and that district gave Democrat Cecelia Espenoza 78.94% of the vote against a Republican in 2024.
bottom_line: This deserves the most weight on the page, because the belief can only come true in one race in 2026 and that race is among the least winnable for anyone other than the Democrat.

text: No candidate from outside the two major parties has won a Colorado legislative seat in modern times, and the closest recent try, Kathleen Curry's 2010 write-in campaign in House District 61, lost by about 300 votes after a court-ordered recount of undervotes.
bottom_line: High weight as a track record: Curry was a sitting legislator with name recognition and still fell short, and no Forward candidate in Colorado has anything like her standing.

text: The Forward Party's one Colorado legislative candidate faces both a Democratic incumbent and a Republican in House District 4, so unlike the 2024 Center Party race in District 52 there is no vacant major-party lane to fill.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the single scenario in which Colorado minor-party candidates have reached a third of the vote is absent from the only 2026 race that matters for this belief.

text: The Colorado Secretary of State's official 2026 General Election candidate list, updated September 15, 2026, shows one Forward Party candidate across all 65 House and 21 Senate races, Bill Hare in House District 4, against Democratic incumbent Cecelia Espenoza and Republican Ellwood Ervin.
bottom_line: The primary record of who is on the ballot, and it narrows the belief to a single race.

text: House District 4 had 23,174 active Democratic, 4,105 Republican, 29,583 unaffiliated and 13 Forward Party registrants out of 58,328 active voters as of October 1, 2026, and its Democratic nominee won 78.94% to 21.06% in November 2024.
bottom_line: Official registration and return figures that describe one of the safest Democratic seats in the state.

text: Statewide, 451 active voters were affiliated with the Forward Party as of October 1, 2026, compared with 32,741 Libertarians, 994,101 Democrats, 888,741 Republicans and 2,051,528 unaffiliated voters.
bottom_line: An official count showing the party has almost no registered base two years after gaining minor-party status.

text: Forward Party nominees in Virginia's November 4, 2025 House of Delegates election received 1.92% (Brandon Givens, District 11) and 1.88% (Kristin Farry, District 72, 853 votes) in three-way races.
bottom_line: The party's only recent own-label legislative returns outside Colorado, both under 2% when both major parties ran.

text: Democrat Cecelia Espenoza will win Colorado House District 4 in November 2026 with more than 65% of the vote, and the Forward Party candidate will finish third.
The Colorado Forward Party will have fewer than 1,000 active registered voters statewide on July 1, 2028, so its minor-party status will depend on a statewide candidate reaching 1% of the vote.
Party labels and straight-ticket habits decide most down-ballot Colorado legislative votes, especially in a district that gave the Democrat nearly four votes in five in 2024.
Past Colorado legislative results for minor-party and unaffiliated candidates are a reliable guide to how a Forward Party candidate will do in 2026.

Art Goodtimes, who was re-elected four times as a Green Party San Miguel County commissioner in Colorado, told CPR News in August 2026 that he is not sure he could win as a Green today because "it's hard to go against the major parties that have money and publicity and organizations," and that minor parties should be built from the local level up.
Third Parties in America: Citizen Response to Major Party Failure, Steven J. Rosenstone, Roy L. Behr and Edward H. Lazarus, 1996 (second edition; first edition 1984)
bridge: Using U.S. elections from 1840 to 1992, the authors show that third parties gain ground only when the major parties fail badly and that ballot access, the wasted-vote fear and thin media coverage hold them back the rest of the time.
bottom_line: High weight as the standard account of why American third parties rarely win, though its data are presidential and it predates the rise of unaffiliated registration in states like Colorado.

text: Residents of Colorado House District 4 in northwest and west Denver need a representative inside the Democratic majority that controls both chambers, so that bills and constituent requests from the district move through committees run by that caucus.
measured_by: The number of bills prime-sponsored by the House District 4 representative that become law in the 2027 regular session, from the General Assembly's bill records.
if_true: A Forward legislator outside both caucuses would likely sponsor fewer bills that pass, since committee assignments and chairs in the Colorado House are set by party leadership.
if_false: The district keeps a member of the majority caucus with access to committee chairs and party leaders.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: caucus membership generally helps a legislator pass bills, though a lone independent can still pass bipartisan bills and the size of the effect for one seat is not measured.

text: In a Colorado district decided by a few hundred votes, a Forward candidate drawing 3% to 5% could decide the seat between the two major parties, as Kathleen Curry's 2010 write-in run made House District 61 a three-way contest decided by about 300 votes.
bottom_line: A real risk under plurality rules, but no 2026 Forward legislative candidate is in a competitive district, so the cost is zero this cycle unless the party expands.

text: A Forward Party nominee being certified the winner of any Colorado House or Senate seat in the November 3, 2026 general election, in the Colorado Secretary of State's official certified results published in December 2026, is a fair measure of whether a Forward Party candidate can win a Colorado legislative seat in 2026.

The number of active Colorado voters registered with the Forward Party in the Secretary of State's monthly statistics is a fair measure of whether the party is building the base a district win requires.
At least one Forward Party nominee appears on the November 3, 2026 general-election ballot for a seat in the Colorado House or Senate.

Enough voters in at least one Colorado legislative district can be persuaded to choose a Forward Party nominee over both major-party nominees to give the Forward nominee the most votes on November 3, 2026.
Under Colorado's plurality rule, which voters kept when they rejected Proposition 131 in 2024, a Forward Party nominee wins a legislative seat by finishing first, without needing a majority.
A Forward Party win in a Colorado legislative race in 2026 would lead the Colorado Forward Party to field more legislative candidates in 2028 than the single one it fielded in 2026.

A Forward Party member elected to the Colorado legislature in 2026 would have to decide whether to caucus with Democrats, Republicans or neither before the 2027 session, which would shape that member's committee assignments and influence.
Over the next decade, a proven Forward Party legislative win would make it more common for Colorado candidates to run on a minor-party line instead of entering a Democratic or Republican primary.

A Forward Party seat in the Colorado legislature would strengthen future campaigns for ranked-choice or fusion voting in Colorado by undercutting the argument that a third candidate can only be a spoiler.
