A Forward Party candidate will win a seat in the Colorado legislature in 2026.
Forward Party candidates will win several seats in the Colorado legislature by 2028.
A Forward Party candidate can win more than 10% of the vote in a Colorado legislative race in 2026.
A candidate from outside the Democratic and Republican parties can win a Colorado legislative seat within the next decade.
Electing Forward Party candidates would make Colorado's legislature work better than electing another Democrat or Republican would.
bottom_line: Colorado's own vote counts are the firmest evidence here: the Colorado Sun found 88.8 percent of the laws enacted in 2024 passed with votes from both parties, down from 95.9 percent in 2019 as the Democratic majority grew. The evidence on what a third-party member would actually change is thin, because the closest cases, Alaska's cross-party coalitions and Minnesota's tied House, involved no third party, so the fight is really over whether the few remaining party-line laws and the majority's own internal splits are a problem big enough to need a new party.
hook: Colorado's Forward Party counted 451 registered members in 2026 and fields one candidate for the state House, in a legislature where 88.8 percent of the 519 laws passed in 2024 already drew votes from both parties.
question: Would putting Forward Party members in Colorado's legislature make it pass more laws across party lines, settle its budget on time and vote less often by party than electing another Democrat or Republican would?
ask: The page most needs the Colorado Sun's 2025 and 2026 bipartisan-vote counts, so the trend since the 2024 election can be read before any Forward member is seated.

text: A legislator who belongs to neither major party can vote for a bill on its merits without facing a party caucus that punishes crossing the aisle.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the freedom is real, but a single member only matters on votes where the two parties are otherwise tied or split.

text: Colorado's legislature grew less bipartisan as the Democratic majority grew larger, so breaking up one-party dominance should restore some of the lost cross-party lawmaking.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the Colorado Sun's vote counts show bipartisanship fell from 95.9 percent in 2019 to 88.2 percent in 2023 as the majority expanded, but the fall is small and the cause is disputed.

text: Alaska's cross-party governing coalitions spread effective lawmaking across both parties and independents instead of leaving it to one majority.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the Center for Effective Lawmaking's 2026 Alaska report supports it, but Alaska's coalitions are built from Republicans, Democrats and independents, not from a third party.

text: When a majority party splits internally, as Colorado Democrats did on data centers, immigration enforcement and farmworker overtime in 2026, a small bloc outside both parties can broker the compromise that gets a bill to the floor.
bottom_line: Modest weight: the 2026 splits are documented by KUNC, but Republicans already played the broker role on the farmworker overtime bill without any third party.

text: The Colorado Sun's count of final floor votes shows the share of enacted laws with support from both parties fell from 95.9 percent in 2019 to 88.2 percent in 2023 and 88.8 percent in 2024, the years after Democrats gained a 46 to 19 House supermajority.
bottom_line: Shows that a bigger one-party majority coincided with less cross-party lawmaking, which is the problem a Forward bloc claims to fix, though the drop is seven points, not a collapse.

text: Open Primaries reported in 2015 that although about 71 percent of Nebraska's legislators were registered Republicans, cross-party coalitions in the nonpartisan unicameral took up and passed measures such as repeal of the death penalty and immigration reform that Nebraska's party-primary congressional delegation never would.
bottom_line: Advocacy research from a group that favors the reform, so it carries less weight than the Masket and Shor study that reached the opposite reading of the same legislature.

text: A study of U.S. state legislatures finding that chambers with a pivotal third-party or independent bloc passed their budgets on time more often and enacted a higher share of bipartisan laws than comparable chambers without one would strengthen the belief.
A record showing a Forward Party legislator in any state brokering a bill that both parties had blocked, with the bill becoming law, would strengthen the belief.
Most party-line voting in Colorado's legislature comes from caucus pressure on members rather than from real differences in what their districts want.
A legislator elected on the Forward Party label would stay independent in office instead of voting as a reliable member of one major party.
A small number of members outside both caucuses can change how a legislature works even in sessions where the majority does not need their votes.

Bob Chew, the Forward Party's 2026 nominee for U.S. Senate in Colorado, said at his campaign launch that "the only way things change in this country is if we start electing people who are free from the control of party bosses, party mega-donors, and lobbyists" (Colorado Politics, July 14, 2026).

Andrew Yang, co-founder of the Forward Party, said at a 2022 speaking event in New York that "in a polarized country, you get one senator, you can end up controlling the whole thing," arguing that a few members outside both major parties could hold decisive power in a legislature (Straight Arrow News, August 16, 2022).
The Politics Industry: How Political Innovation Can Break Partisan Gridlock and Save Our Democracy, by Katherine M. Gehl and Michael E. Porter (2020)
bridge: Gehl and Porter argue that the two major parties act as a duopoly that competes for partisan base voters, not for results, so legislators face little pressure to solve problems across party lines.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the analysis of party incentives is careful and widely cited, but the book's remedy is changing primaries and voting rules, not electing third-party members, so it supports the diagnosis more than Forward's route.

text: Forward: Notes on the Future of Our Democracy, by Andrew Yang (2021)
bridge: Yang, who went on to co-found the Forward Party, lays out the case that legislators freed from party discipline and the primary system would govern more pragmatically.
bottom_line: Modest weight: it is the founding statement of the party's own reasoning, written by an advocate, and offers argument rather than evidence from any legislature.

text: Breaking the Two-Party Doom Loop: The Case for Multiparty Democracy in America, by Lee Drutman (2020)
bridge: Drutman argues that a strict two-party system turns every vote into a team contest and that more parties would allow shifting cross-party coalitions in legislatures.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a serious political science case that more than two parties improves lawmaking, but Drutman ties the benefit to proportional representation, which Colorado does not use, rather than to scattered third-party winners.

text: Colorado's legislature already passes nearly nine of every ten laws with votes from both parties, so there is little party-line gridlock for a Forward Party member to fix.
bottom_line: Strong weight: the Colorado Sun counted 88.8 percent of the 519 laws enacted in 2024 as bipartisan and only 17 passed on a pure party-line vote.

text: A legislature with one or two third-party members who hold the balance of power hands outsized influence to a handful of people whom most Coloradans never voted for.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a pivotal member's power is a real feature of narrow majorities, though Colorado's current 43 to 22 House and 23 to 12 Senate margins leave no pivot to hold.

text: A third-party candidate in a Colorado legislative race mostly splits the vote of the major party closest to them, which can elect the candidate that a majority of the district opposed.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: Colorado's 2022 and 2024 8th Congressional District results show minor-party votes larger than the winning margin, and the same arithmetic applies to state races.

text: Third-party legislators tend to join a major party caucus or leave office, as Vermont Progressives did in 2022 and Utah's Forward senator did in 2025, so the independence they promise does not last.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the pattern is documented, but two states and a handful of members are a small sample.

text: Power-sharing legislatures are slower, as Minnesota's tied House showed in 2025 when it passed only a handful of bills in three months and needed a June special session to finish the budget.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: Minnesota's slowdown is well documented, but it came from a 67 to 67 tie between the two major parties rather than from a third party.

text: Minnesota's House, tied 67 to 67 in 2025 under a power-sharing agreement that required bipartisan support for a bill to reach the floor, had passed only about four bills three months into the session, compared with 26 by mid-April 2023 under one-party control, and the state budget was finished in a June special session.
bottom_line: Shows a chamber with no majority can stall, but a two-party tie is not the same as a third-party pivot, and the budget did eventually pass in a one-day special session.

text: Any Forward Party member seated in a state legislature in 2026 will either caucus formally with a major party or pass no prime-sponsored bills by the end of the 2027 sessions.
Vote records showing that Forward Party legislators vote with one major party at least 90 percent of the time, matching a typical member of that party, would weaken the belief.
A Colorado session in which a seated Forward member coincides with no change, or a fall, in the Colorado Sun's bipartisan share and no change in the count of party-line laws would weaken the belief.
Party labels give voters a cheap and reliable signal of how a legislator will vote, so a candidate without a major party label leaves voters less able to hold the legislature accountable.
Colorado's legislature already works reasonably well, passing most laws with votes from both parties and finishing the budget on time.
Partisanship in a legislature mostly reflects real disagreement among voters, so a new party label would be absorbed into the existing divide rather than ending it.

Mark Baisley, the Republican state senator running for U.S. Senate in Colorado in 2026, said that "minor party candidates seem to only serve as the spoiler, frustrating the will of the majority" and described "a process of elimination that works very well with a two-party system" (Colorado Politics, August 12, 2026).
Centrist third parties like No Labels are not the solution for Americans unhappy with the two-party system, by Victor Y. Wu (2024)
where_found: LSE United States Politics and Policy blog (USAPP), London School of Economics
bridge: Wu reports survey work with Joseph Bafumi finding that Democrats and Republicans who want a third party are as polarized as those who do not, and names the Forward Party as a centrist group unlikely to win and likely to act as a spoiler.
bottom_line: Modest weight: a short blog post drawing on one survey, focused on national elections rather than state legislatures.

text: Colorado small-business owners need rules that survive a change of legislative majority.
measured_by: number of major business regulations repealed or substantially reversed within four years of enactment
if_true: Fewer reversals, because laws need cross-party votes to pass in the first place.
if_false: No change, because Colorado's one-party majorities already produce few reversals.
bottom_line: A genuine interest, but hard to measure in a state with twenty years of mostly one-party control.

text: Colorado Democratic voters need the majority they elected to be able to pass the program it campaigned on.
measured_by: share of the majority party's announced session priorities that become law
if_true: The share falls, because a pivotal Forward member can block or rewrite priority bills.
if_false: The share is unchanged, because the Forward member has no pivotal vote or votes with the majority.
bottom_line: A majority that cannot govern cannot be judged on its record, which is the core democratic case against pivotal small blocs.

text: Colorado voters in competitive districts need to know before voting which coalition their legislator will join.
measured_by: share of Forward candidates who state before the election which party caucus they would join or whether they would stay independent
if_true: Forward candidates publish their caucus plans and voters can judge them.
if_false: Forward candidates leave the question open and decide after the votes are counted.
bottom_line: Alaska's coalitions form after election night, and that uncertainty is a real cost to voters who want to know what their vote buys.

text: A legislature that needs a Forward member's vote would pass fewer laws that a future majority of the other party reverses, giving Colorado businesses more stable rules.
bottom_line: Reasonable in theory, but Colorado has had one-party control for so long that there is no recent reversal baseline to measure against.

text: A chamber that must assemble a cross-party coalition for every floor vote would pass fewer bills early in the session and push more work to the final weeks or a special session, as Minnesota's tied House did in 2025.
bottom_line: Minnesota went from 26 bills by mid-April 2023 to about four in 2025, but that was a two-party tie, so the estimate for a one-member pivot is rough.

text: The share of laws enacted in a Colorado session with at least one yes vote from each major party on final passage, counted the way the Colorado Sun has since 2019, is a fair measure of whether the legislature works across party lines.

The number of bills with a Forward Party legislator as prime sponsor that become law in a session, compared with the median member of the same chamber, is a fair measure of whether a third-party member can get things done rather than only cast protest votes.
A Forward Party legislator in Colorado would vote differently from the Democrat or Republican who would otherwise hold the same seat on a meaningful share of contested bills.
Colorado's legislature has problems, such as party-line votes on major bills or long-run fiscal questions left unaddressed, that a member outside both caucuses could reduce.
Better legislative work can be judged by measures both sides accept, such as bills passed across party lines, budgets finished on time and fewer party-line votes.
A Forward Party legislator seated in Colorado would vote with Democrats on some contested bills and with Republicans on others, rather than siding with one caucus nearly every time.

Colorado's majority party would negotiate with a seated Forward Party legislator on bills where the majority's own members are split, such as the 2026 fights over data centers and immigration enforcement.
Colorado's Democratic and Republican parties would recruit more legislative candidates who appeal to unaffiliated voters, to avoid losing seats to Forward Party challengers.
A Colorado legislature in which no party holds a majority and Forward Party members hold the balance of power would govern the state better than any one-party majority.
Electing Forward Party candidates throughout Colorado government would end partisan gridlock in the state.
Electing one Forward Party legislator in a closely divided Colorado chamber would increase the number of bills passed with votes from both parties.
Having at least a few Colorado legislators who belong to neither major party would give unaffiliated Colorado voters better representation in the statehouse.
Voting for a third-party candidate in a Colorado state race wastes the vote.
bottom_line: On who wins, the case for the belief is solid: Colorado counts state races by plurality in a single round, and voters rejected ranked-choice counting 53.5 percent to 46.5 percent in 2024, so a third-party vote almost never helps elect anyone. The evidence that such a vote does other work is real but modest (1 percent statewide keeps a minor party on the ballot, and the Libertarian's 9,280 votes in the 8th District in 2022 led Colorado Republicans to agree to a Libertarian pledge in 2023), so the real fight is over whether a ballot exists only to pick a winner or also to record what voters want.
hook: Colorado's House District 16 was decided in 2024 by three votes, 20,641 to 20,638, in a race where the winning Republican had signed a Libertarian pledge to keep a third candidate off the ballot.
question: When a Coloradan marks the ballot for Bob Chew or another third-party candidate in a race that candidate will not win, does the vote accomplish anything?
ask: The page most needs a post-election survey or ballot-level study of Colorado's 2026 third-party voters showing whom they would have chosen, or whether they would have voted at all, without their candidate.

text: No third-party or independent candidate has won a Colorado state legislative seat at the ballot box in the modern era, so a third-party vote in those races has never helped elect anyone.
bottom_line: This deserves heavy weight on the narrow question of who wins: Wikipedia's compiled list of Colorado third-party legislative performances shows no winner, and the first independent legislator, Kathleen Curry, got there in 2009 by leaving the Democratic Party and then lost as a write-in in 2010 with 33 percent.

text: Colorado counts state and federal races by plurality in a single round, so a vote for a candidate who finishes third has no bearing on which of the two front-runners takes the office.
bottom_line: This is the mechanical core of the belief and is simply correct about the counting rule; the dispute is over whether choosing the winner is all a vote is for.

text: A third-party vote drawn mostly from one side can hand the office to the candidate those voters like least, as Republicans say happened in Colorado's 8th Congressional District in 2022 when the Libertarian's 9,280 votes dwarfed Yadira Caraveo's 1,632-vote margin over Barbara Kirkmeyer.
bottom_line: Strong as a warning about close races, weaker as a general rule, because it assumes the third-party voters would otherwise have voted for the nearer major candidate rather than staying home.

text: Colorado voters rejected ranked-choice general elections in 2024 by 53.5 percent to 46.5 percent on Proposition 131, so the counting rule under which a third-party vote could transfer to a second choice is not coming to state races soon.
bottom_line: Deserves real weight because it removes the most common rebuttal to the belief for at least the next several cycles.

text: Colorado's two million unaffiliated voters can already vote in either major party's primary, so a voter who wants to change what the major parties offer has a channel that decides nominations rather than one that elects no one.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it answers the protest-vote argument on its own terms, but it only works for voters who find either major party acceptable.

text: Colorado's Proposition 131, which would have brought ranked-choice general elections to state and congressional races, failed 1,385,060 votes (46.47 percent) to 1,595,256 (53.53 percent) in November 2024.
bottom_line: Official and final; it shows the rule that would make the belief false for state races was put to voters and rejected.

text: No Forward, Libertarian, Unity, Green, Center or Approval Voting candidate will win any Colorado state legislative or statewide partisan office in November 2026.
Bob Chew will finish third in the 2026 Colorado U.S. Senate race with under 5 percent, and John Hickenlooper's margin over Mark Baisley will exceed the combined vote of every minor-party candidate.
Certified 2026 results show every Colorado third-party legislative candidate below 5 percent and no legislative race in which the combined third-party vote exceeded the winner's margin.

A post-election survey or ballot-order study of 2026 Colorado third-party voters finds that most would have voted for one of the two major candidates, rather than staying home, had their candidate not run.
The main purpose of a vote in a Colorado general election is to help decide which candidate takes the office.
Most people who vote for a third-party candidate in Colorado would otherwise have voted for one of the two major-party candidates rather than staying home.
Colorado's major parties rarely change their positions or nominees in response to third-party vote totals, so a protest vote buys little in later elections.

Mark Baisley, the Republican nominee for Colorado's U.S. Senate seat in 2026, told Colorado Politics in August 2026 that "minor party candidates seem to only serve as the spoiler," frustrating the will of the majority by splitting their votes.

Jon Caldara, president of the Independence Institute, wrote in a November 2022 Colorado Politics column that the Libertarian candidate in Colorado's 8th Congressional District "cost Kirkmeyer her seat" and urged voters not to throw their votes away on protest candidates.
Making Votes Count: Strategic Coordination in the World's Electoral Systems, Gary W. Cox, 1997
bridge: Cox shows that in single-winner plurality districts voters who expect a candidate to finish out of the running tend to desert that candidate for one of the two front-runners, so support concentrates on two candidates, which is the counting logic behind calling a Colorado third-party vote wasted.
bottom_line: Heavy weight on the mechanism: it is the standard comparative study of strategic voting, though it explains why voters abandon third parties rather than proving that those who stay have wasted their votes.

text: The Two-Party System and Duverger's Law: An Essay on the History of Political Science, William H. Riker, 1982
bridge: Riker traces how plurality elections push voters away from candidates they see as likely losers to avoid wasting their votes, and argues that this tendency is one of the closest things political science has to a law.
bottom_line: Moderate to heavy weight: a foundational account of why plurality systems like Colorado's punish third-party votes, written about national systems rather than Colorado races specifically.

text: Spoilers | CALDARA, Jon Caldara, 2022
bridge: Caldara reviews Colorado's 2022 results, concludes that the Libertarian vote in the 8th Congressional District cost Barbara Kirkmeyer the seat, and urges voters not to throw their votes away on protest candidates, while also judging spoilers a non-factor in some 35 other races.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a named Colorado commentator working from the certified 2022 results, though it is an opinion column and its own count shows the spoiler effect deciding only a few races.

text: In a race every forecaster rates Safe Democratic, like Colorado's 2026 U.S. Senate contest between John Hickenlooper, Mark Baisley and Bob Chew, a vote for the Republican is as powerless over the winner as a vote for the Forward candidate, so calling only the third-party vote wasted singles it out for a property most votes share.
bottom_line: Deserves heavy weight: in lopsided races, which are most Colorado races, the belief has to rest on something other than who wins, and that is where it is weakest.

text: A statewide third-party vote in Colorado buys future ballot access, because state law keeps a minor party's status when one of its statewide candidates reaches 1 percent of the vote in either of the last two general elections.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the effect is real and written into Title 1 of the Colorado Revised Statutes, but a party can also keep its status with 1,000 affiliated voters, so the vote is not the only route.

text: Third-party vote shares change what major parties do, as when Colorado Republicans agreed in 2023 to sign a Libertarian pledge in exchange for Libertarians standing down in close races after the Libertarian drew 4 percent in the 8th District in 2022.
bottom_line: Strong as a documented Colorado case: a 9,280-vote showing produced a written pledge that at least one winning candidate, Rebecca Keltie, signed in 2024.

text: Colorado keeps a minor party's recognized status if one of its statewide candidates received at least 1 percent of the votes cast in any statewide race in either of the last two general elections, or if at least 1,000 registered electors were affiliated with it before July 1 of either of those elections.
bottom_line: A legal effect of the vote that has nothing to do with who wins; it is small, but it is not nothing.

text: A Colorado major party will publicly adopt a pledge, platform plank or candidate stand-down agreement aimed at a minor party's voters, as Republicans did with Libertarians in 2023, in response to a 2026 third-party vote share.

Bob Chew will receive at least 1 percent of the statewide vote, preserving the Colorado Forward Party's minor-party status through the 2030 election under Title 1, Article 4 of the Colorado Revised Statutes.
A Forward Party or other minor-party candidate, such as Bill Hare in House District 4, wins a Colorado legislative seat in November 2026.

A Colorado major party documents a platform change or candidate pledge adopted in response to a 2026 minor-party vote share, as the 2024 Liberty Pledge followed the 2022 Libertarian showing in the 8th District.
A vote is put to use when it records the voter's honest preference, whether or not that candidate wins.
Third-party vote totals in Colorado shape what major parties, donors and future candidates do in later elections.
In a Colorado race whose winner is not in doubt, no single vote changes the outcome, so a vote for a major-party candidate is no less wasted than a vote for a third-party candidate.

Eric Mulder, the Libertarian nominee for Colorado governor in 2026, told the Colorado Sun in August 2026 that voters who dislike the two major-party options have other choices, and that a major-party candidate who loses a vote to him "needs to take a hard look in the mirror."
Third Parties in America: Citizen Response to Major Party Failure, Steven J. Rosenstone, Roy L. Behr and Edward H. Lazarus, 1984
bridge: The authors argue that third-party voting rises when the major parties fail to address what voters care about and that major parties respond by taking up the issues third parties raise, so a third-party vote can change policy without electing anyone.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a standard scholarly account of third-party influence in the United States, built mostly on national and presidential cases rather than state races.

text: Donors who give to Colorado campaigns need their money to go where it can change a result.
measured_by: Share of total Colorado campaign spending in a cycle that goes to candidates who finish third or lower
if_true: That share shrinks toward zero.
if_false: That share stays in the low single digits, dominated by self-funders like Bob Chew.
bottom_line: Minor weight: most minor-party spending in Colorado is the candidates' own, so other donors lose little either way.

text: If Colorado voters who prefer one of the two front-runners stopped casting third-party votes, fewer Colorado legislative races would be decided by a margin smaller than the third-party vote, which happened in four races in 2022 (House Districts 16, 25 and 50 and Senate District 11) and in one in 2024 (Senate District 12).
bottom_line: Real but small: the counts come from the certified results tabulated on Wikipedia's 2022 and 2024 Colorado House and Senate election pages (for example, House District 25 in 2022, where Tammy Story beat Colin Larson by 719 votes while Libertarian Todd Dennison drew 1,060), but whether any of those results would have flipped depends on where the third-party voters would otherwise have gone.

text: If Colorado voters abandoned third-party candidates as wasted votes, minor parties would stop fielding candidates and most Colorado House districts would offer only two names, as 58 of 65 districts already did in 2024, when only 7 House races had a third candidate, down from 22 in 2022.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the counts come from the certified results tabulated on Wikipedia's 2022 and 2024 Colorado House election pages, and the people affected are real (Cronin and Loevy's June 2026 Colorado Politics column puts total registration at 4,072,990, of whom 3,974,036 are Democrats, Republicans or unaffiliated, leaving roughly 99,000 others), but the 2022 to 2024 drop came mostly from the Libertarian stand-down deal, not from voters deserting.

text: If Colorado Libertarians stopped casting Libertarian votes, the party would lose the bargaining power that in 2023 got the Colorado Republican Party to agree to a Liberty Pledge, under which Republican candidates such as Rebecca Keltie committed to positions like opposing a state income tax and mandatory vaccine programs in exchange for Libertarians not running against them.
bottom_line: Strong as a documented case: Colorado Politics and CPR reported the 2023 deal and its pledge terms, Libertarian state House candidates fell from 20 in 2022 to 3 in 2024 on Wikipedia's certified-results tables, and Keltie won House District 16 by three votes; the weight is tempered because the Colorado Times Recorder reports the Libertarian board nullified the pledge in February 2026, so it may not recur.

text: The number of third-party or independent candidates who win a Colorado state legislative or statewide partisan office between 2026 and 2034 is a fair measure of whether such a vote can elect anyone.
Bob Chew's certified share of the 2026 Colorado U.S. Senate vote is a fair measure of whether a well-funded Forward candidate can gather enough votes to matter in a Colorado race.

The number of times a Colorado major party adopts a pledge, platform plank or stand-down agreement aimed at a minor party's voters within one cycle after that party drew more than 3 percent in a race is a fair measure of whether third-party votes change what the major parties do.
Third-party candidates in Colorado state races almost never finish first, so a vote for one almost never helps elect anyone.
Colorado state races are counted by plurality in a single round, so a vote for a candidate who finishes third is never transferred to another candidate.
A vote that does not change which candidate wins is wasted, whatever it signals to parties or future candidates.
If Colorado voters treat third-party votes as wasted, third-party candidates' combined share of the vote in Colorado's 2026 and 2028 state races falls below their 2022 share.
If Colorado voters treat third-party votes as wasted, fewer Colorado legislative races in 2026 and 2028 have a combined third-party vote larger than the winner's margin.

If Colorado voters keep avoiding third-party candidates for a decade, minor parties that keep their ballot status through the 1 percent statewide vote rule lose it and must rely on registering 1,000 members instead.
If Colorado voters keep avoiding third-party candidates for a decade, every seat in the Colorado General Assembly is still held by a Democrat or a Republican in 2036.
Voting for a third-party candidate in any American election is wasted, and voters should never do it.
A vote for a third-party candidate in a close Colorado race is in effect a vote for the major-party candidate the voter likes least.
Voting for a third-party candidate in a close Colorado state race risks helping elect the major-party candidate the voter likes least.
Under Colorado's plurality counting, a third-party vote almost never changes who wins a state race, though it can still serve other purposes such as keeping a party on the ballot.
The United States should keep sending military aid to Ukraine until Russia withdraws from the territory it has taken since February 2022.
bottom_line: The evidence is strong that American weapons, especially air defense, still matter to Ukraine and that Russia is paying an enormous price for very small gains; it is thin on whether any realistic level of US aid can push Russia out of the roughly 19 percent of Ukraine it holds. The real fight is over the goal (full withdrawal or a defensible ceasefire) and over who pays, since Congress has passed no major Ukraine funding since April 2024 and most US weapons now reach Ukraine because European allies buy them.
hook: Russia has taken an estimated 1.2 million casualties in Ukraine, far more than in any war it has fought since World War II, yet in April 2026 it still held about 19 percent of the country (CSIS, January 2026; Reuters, April 2026).
question: Should the United States keep arming Ukraine until Russia leaves the land it has seized since February 2022, or accept something less?
ask: The page most needs a month-by-month comparison of Russian territorial gains against the timing of American weapons deliveries and pauses since 2022.

text: Tying US military aid to a Russian withdrawal, instead of to a calendar or a budget cycle, takes away the Kremlin's reason to drag out the war and wait for American support to fade.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the logic is sound, but it depends on Moscow believing the commitment will last, and Congress has passed no major Ukraine funding since April 2024.

text: Russia's ground advance in Ukraine has slowed to a few dozen meters a day at the cost of enormous casualties, so continued US military aid helps hold a front that Russia cannot break without losses it cannot sustain forever.
bottom_line: Heavy weight for holding the line, lighter weight for the full belief: attrition favoring Ukraine is supported by CSIS and ISW estimates, but holding a line is not the same as forcing a withdrawal.

text: A settlement that lets Russia keep land it seized by force since 2022 would teach governments outside Europe, including China with respect to Taiwan, that conquest pays if the conqueror outlasts Western patience.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the precedent concern is widely shared among security analysts, but how much any one war's outcome shapes another government's choices is hard to measure.

text: Russia suffered an estimated 1.2 million casualties in Ukraine between February 2022 and December 2025, including up to 325,000 troops killed, while its most prominent offensives advanced an average of 15 to 70 meters a day.
bottom_line: Strong for the claim that Russia is paying heavily for small gains; UK Defence Intelligence's February 2026 figure of about 1,245,000 Russian casualties is close, though no casualty count can be independently verified.

text: If continued US military aid can force a Russian withdrawal, Ukraine will hold more territory on December 31, 2027 than it did on October 17, 2026.
If sustained Western pressure is wearing Russia down, Moscow will drop its demand for the remaining Ukrainian-held part of Donetsk as a condition of any ceasefire.

A careful month-by-month study finds that Russian advances sped up during the periods when US weapons deliveries stalled (late 2023 to April 2024, and the 2025 pauses) and slowed after deliveries resumed.
Credible reporting shows Russian units forced to pull back from occupied Ukrainian land because of manpower or equipment shortages caused by attrition.
Russia will not keep to a ceasefire that leaves it holding occupied Ukrainian land, so any pause in the fighting would be used to rearm and attack again.
With enough US weapons over enough time, Ukraine can make holding occupied territory too costly for Russia to continue, even if Ukraine cannot take all of it back by force.
The United States has a lasting interest in showing that borders changed by force will not be accepted, strong enough to justify an aid commitment with no fixed end date.

Joe Biden, as president, repeatedly pledged that the United States would support Ukraine against Russia's invasion "for as long as it takes," including in his speech in Vilnius at the July 2023 NATO summit.

Senator Mitch McConnell, then the Senate Republican leader, pushed for and voted for the April 2024 package that provided about $60.8 billion for Ukraine, and argued that helping Ukraine defeat Russia served American interests.
The Russo-Ukrainian War: The Return of History, Serhii Plokhy (2023)
bridge: The Harvard historian traces Russia's war from the 2014 seizure of Crimea through the 2022 invasion and argues that Moscow's aim is to undo Ukraine as an independent nation, not to settle a border dispute.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: strong on Russian aims and history, which bear on whether a ceasefire would hold, but it does not weigh the costs of continued aid against the alternatives.

text: Each additional year of fighting costs tens of thousands of Ukrainian soldiers' lives, so a negotiated ceasefire along current lines may save more Ukrainian lives than holding out for a Russian withdrawal that may never come.
bottom_line: Heavy weight on the human cost, which CSIS estimates at up to 140,000 Ukrainian military deaths through 2025, but it assumes a ceasefire would hold and that occupation itself costs fewer lives.

text: Making US military aid conditional only on full Russian withdrawal throws away the United States' ability to push both Kyiv and Moscow toward a negotiated deal, which is how wars of attrition generally end.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: most long wars do end in negotiation, but supporters answer that steady aid is what gives Ukraine a stronger hand at the table.

text: An open-ended US military commitment to Ukraine should rest on clear congressional and public support, and Americans are closely divided on whether to help Ukraine regain territory at the cost of a longer war.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: Gallup found a 52 to 45 split in August 2025 with a deep partisan divide, and the House passed new aid in June 2026 only by discharge petition over the administration's objection.

text: Continued US supply of long-range weapons to Ukraine raises the risk of a direct clash between NATO and Russia, a nuclear-armed power.
bottom_line: Light to moderate weight: escalation fears have repeatedly failed to come true as new weapons were sent, but the downside if they did would be catastrophic, so the risk cannot be set to zero.

text: Russia controlled about 116,793 square kilometers of Ukraine, or 19.35 percent of the country, in April 2026, more than four years after the full-scale invasion and after more than $68 billion in US military aid commitments.
bottom_line: Strong evidence that US aid has not so far produced a Russian withdrawal, though it says nothing about how much more Russia would hold without the aid.

text: Congress has made no significant new funding available for Ukraine since April 2024; as of June 30, 2026 only $4.96 billion of authorized drawdown authority remained, and the FY2026 defense law authorized just $400 million a year for the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative.
bottom_line: Strong evidence that the elected branches have not sustained aid at earlier levels, which weighs on whether an open-ended commitment is realistic, not on whether it is wise.

text: Ukraine suffered an estimated 500,000 to 600,000 military casualties between February 2022 and December 2025, including up to 140,000 deaths.
bottom_line: Weighty because it measures what holding out for withdrawal costs Ukrainians, though estimates are uncertain and Kyiv's own published figures are far lower.

text: Russia spent an estimated $190 billion on its military in 2025, 7.5 percent of its GDP and a 5.9 percent real increase over 2024, which is nearly three times the total US military aid committed to Ukraine from February 2022 through June 2026.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it shows Russia can keep paying for the war, though spending growth slowed sharply from 38 percent in 2024 and the comparison ignores European aid.

text: If a full Russian withdrawal is out of reach, Russia will still control at least 15 percent of Ukraine's internationally recognized territory at the end of 2028, whatever the level of US aid.

If the withdrawal condition is unrealistic, a ceasefire or armistice will be signed that leaves Russia holding most of the land it has taken since February 2022, and large-scale fighting will stop for at least six months.
Independent estimates show Russia replacing all its battlefield losses through volunteers and bonuses for several years running without new mobilization.
European producers are shown to be able to replace US Patriot interceptors and long-range strike weapons for Ukraine within two years, making the US supply line unnecessary.
Russia has the population, industry and willingness to absorb losses to outlast Ukraine in a war of attrition, so more US weapons lengthen the war without changing how it ends.
A ceasefire along the current front lines, backed by European security guarantees, could hold long enough to save lives and let Ukraine rebuild.
American military resources and public patience are limited, and the United States has more pressing priorities, such as deterring China in the Pacific, that should come before Ukraine.

J.D. Vance, then a senator from Ohio, voted against the $95 billion foreign aid package that passed the Senate 79 to 18 on April 23, 2024, which included about $60.8 billion for Ukraine, after long opposing continued US aid to Ukraine.
An Unwinnable War: Washington Needs an Endgame in Ukraine, Samuel Charap (Foreign Affairs, July/August 2023)
bridge: Charap argues that neither side can win decisively, that a full peace treaty is out of reach, and that the United States should work toward an armistice that stops the fighting without settling the territorial dispute.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the forecast that the 2023 counteroffensive would not be decisive proved right, but critics answer that an armistice without guarantees would let Russia rearm and attack again.

text: Ukrainians living in cities hit by Russian missiles and drones need a steady supply of air-defense interceptors.
measured_by: Civilian deaths from missile and drone strikes as counted by the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, and the share of incoming missiles intercepted.
if_true: Interception rates stay high and civilian deaths from air strikes fall or hold steady.
if_false: Interceptor shortages let more strikes through and civilian deaths rise.
bottom_line: The most immediate and best-documented interest on this side, since Ukraine's Patriot supply depends on US stocks.

text: Ukrainians living under Russian occupation since 2022 need a realistic path back to Ukrainian rule.
measured_by: The population and area returned to Ukrainian control, and documented reports of deportations, detentions and forced passportization in occupied areas.
if_true: Occupied areas shrink over time and fewer people live under Russian rule.
if_false: The occupation hardens and its residents are absorbed into Russia.
bottom_line: A heavy interest, but meeting it depends on battlefield gains that have been small since 2022.

text: Lithuanians, Latvians, Estonians and Poles need Russia's army too worn down to threaten NATO's eastern border.
measured_by: Russian ground-force strength and equipment stocks near NATO borders, as estimated by NATO and independent trackers.
if_true: Russian forces near the Baltic and Polish borders stay depleted for years.
if_false: Russia rebuilds a larger, combat-tested army able to pressure NATO's eastern members.
bottom_line: Widely voiced in those countries, though how much a longer war weakens rather than hardens Russia is debated.

text: US service members need munition stockpiles full enough for a war in the Pacific or the Middle East.
measured_by: Inventories of Patriot interceptors, 155mm shells and other key munitions against Pentagon war-plan requirements.
if_true: Stockpiles are drawn down further unless production keeps pace.
if_false: Munitions stay home and stockpiles recover faster.
bottom_line: Real, especially after US operations against Iran, but partly answered by allied payments through PURL that fund replenishment.

text: Ukrainian soldiers at the front and their families need the fighting to end as soon as it safely can.
measured_by: Ukrainian military deaths and injuries per year, as estimated by CSIS and other independent researchers.
if_true: The war runs longer and military deaths keep accumulating.
if_false: A ceasefire ends most front-line deaths, if it holds.
bottom_line: A grave interest; many Ukrainian soldiers themselves reject a settlement that cedes land, so this interest cuts both ways.

text: Continued US military aid keeps Ukraine supplied with air-defense interceptors that shoot down Russian missiles and drones aimed at its cities.
bottom_line: Large and direct, but no source we read puts a defensible number on lives saved, so the estimate is left blank.

text: Continued US military aid keeps Russia's army losing men and equipment at a rate that limits its ability to threaten NATO members.
bottom_line: The figure is the CSIS estimate of 1.2 million casualties spread over 46 months; whether attrition makes Russia less dangerous or more hostile afterward is disputed.

text: Continued US military aid keeps open the possibility that Ukrainians now under Russian occupation return to Ukrainian rule.
bottom_line: The stakes are high, but since 2022 net returns have been small, so no honest point estimate is possible.

text: Keeping US military aid at its 2022 to 2026 pace costs American taxpayers about $15.7 billion a year.
bottom_line: Derived from the CRS figure of $68.2 billion committed over about 52 months; AEI estimates most of that is spent in the United States, which offsets but does not erase the cost.

text: Sending Patriot interceptors and precision munitions to Ukraine draws down US stockpiles that American forces may need elsewhere.
bottom_line: Real but disputed: the Pentagon paused shipments in 2025 and the Guardian reported stocks at about a quarter of plan, while the Pentagon denied any shortfall.

text: Holding out for a full Russian withdrawal instead of a ceasefire prolongs fighting that kills Ukrainian soldiers every month.
bottom_line: The figure is the upper CSIS estimate of 140,000 deaths spread over 46 months; whether a ceasefire would actually stop the killing is the open question.

text: The net change in Ukrainian-held territory over a calendar year, as mapped by DeepState and the Institute for the Study of War, is a fair measure of whether continued US military aid is moving Russia toward withdrawal.
Russia's monthly military losses compared with its monthly recruitment are a fair measure of whether sustained US military aid can force Russia to give up occupied land.
US stockpiles of Patriot interceptors and 155mm shells measured against the Pentagon's war-plan requirements are a fair measure of whether arming Ukraine is weakening American readiness.
Continued US military aid can bring about a Russian withdrawal from the Ukrainian territory taken since February 2022, whether by battlefield defeat or by making occupation too costly to keep.
The benefits to the United States and Ukraine of holding out for a full Russian withdrawal are greater than the added lives, money and munitions a longer war would cost.
The United States can sustain military aid to Ukraine for as long as the war lasts without running short of weapons it needs for its own defense or for other allies.

If the United States keeps sending military aid to Ukraine, Ukraine's air defenses keep intercepting most incoming Russian missiles and drones within the next year, holding civilian deaths from air strikes at or below current levels.

If the United States ties continued military aid to a Russian withdrawal, Russia keeps up its offensive within the next year or two instead of accepting a ceasefire, and the front line moves only a few miles in either direction.

If the United States keeps sending military aid to Ukraine until Russia withdraws, US and European production of air-defense interceptors and artillery shells expands over the next decade to several times its 2022 level.

If the United States keeps sending military aid to Ukraine until Russia withdraws, the war either ends with Russia giving back much of the land it took since 2022 or settles into a long frozen conflict that still requires Western aid to hold the line a decade from now.
The United States should keep sending military aid to Ukraine until Russia withdraws from all Ukrainian territory, including Crimea and the parts of Donetsk and Luhansk it seized in 2014.

The United States should greatly increase its military aid to Ukraine, lifting all limits on the range and targets of American weapons, until Russia withdraws from the territory it has taken since February 2022.
The United States should keep sending military aid to Ukraine until a ceasefire is reached that Ukraine's elected government accepts.
The United States should keep supplying Ukraine with air-defense weapons to protect its cities, even if it stops sending offensive weapons.
Supporting Ukraine serves the United States' own security and economic interests, not only Ukraine's.
bottom_line: The evidence is strong that Russia's army has taken enormous losses, and a Defense Department Inspector General report found US artillery shell output still far short of its goal in 2026; it is thin on whether backing Ukraine helps deter China over Taiwan. The real fight is over priorities: whether Russia or China is the threat that should get America's limited weapons, and how much of the load Europe should carry.
hook: By the end of 2025, a CSIS estimate put Russia's losses in Ukraine at about 1.2 million soldiers killed or wounded, in a war where the United States sent weapons and money but no combat troops.
question: Does backing Ukraine serve America's own security and economic interests, or mainly Ukraine's?
ask: This page most needs sourced evidence on whether Western support for Ukraine has changed China's plans toward Taiwan, such as official Chinese statements, intelligence assessments or expert studies.

text: Russia's army, the main conventional military threat to the NATO allies the United States is pledged by treaty to defend, has been badly worn down in Ukraine without any American troops sent into combat.
bottom_line: Heavy weight: independent and US government estimates agree Russian losses are enormous, though Russia has kept recruiting and rebuilding, so the gain is real but not permanent.

text: A Russian victory in Ukraine would likely encourage Russia to test NATO's eastern members next, and a war with a NATO member would oblige the United States to fight directly at far greater cost.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: Russia's record in Georgia, Crimea and Ukraine makes the worry reasonable, but whether Russia would risk attacking NATO is a forecast, not a finding.

text: Leaders in China, Iran and North Korea generally judge American resolve partly by whether the United States stands by partners it has backed, so abandoning Ukraine would make deterring China over Taiwan harder.
bottom_line: Moderate to low weight until better evidence arrives: the logic is widely held among defense analysts, but direct evidence of how Beijing reads the Ukraine war is scarce.

text: The war in Ukraine has exposed weaknesses in American munitions production and taught the US military hard lessons about drones and electronic warfare that it would otherwise have learned only in its own war.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the lessons are real and are reshaping Pentagon programs, though the United States could have learned much of this by watching the war without paying for it.

text: Keeping Ukraine able to export grain through the Black Sea helps hold down world food prices, which reduces the kind of hunger and unrest in poor countries that tends to draw in American aid and attention.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight: Ukrainian exports did ease prices, but the benefit to American security is indirect and hard to measure.

text: Russia suffered about 1.2 million military casualties, including up to 325,000 deaths, from February 2022 through December 2025, by a CSIS estimate.
bottom_line: Fairly strong: the death range roughly matches the independent Mediazona and BBC count, but the wounded figures are harder to verify and the report does not fully explain its method.

text: The United States supplied 44 percent of Europe's liquefied natural gas imports in 2022 and 48 percent in 2023, up from 27 percent in 2021, as Europe turned away from Russian gas.
bottom_line: Solid figures, but the gain follows from Europe's break with Russia rather than from US aid itself, so it bears only indirectly on this belief.

text: Russia's active inventory of modern tanks and armored vehicles will remain below its February 2022 level through the end of 2027.
European and other allies will have spent a combined $15 billion or more buying American weapons for Ukraine through NATO's PURL program.
Official Chinese documents, statements or credible intelligence assessments show that Beijing delayed or scaled back plans against Taiwan after watching Western support for Ukraine.
Pentagon or Government Accountability Office reviews find that factories expanded for Ukraine orders now supply US forces faster or at lower unit cost than before 2022.
Russia's leaders would keep expanding by force if they won in Ukraine, so a Russian army worn down in Ukraine is one less likely to threaten NATO later.
Rival governments such as China's judge how far the United States will go for its partners partly by watching how it treats Ukraine.
The weapons and money sent to Ukraine can be replaced faster than the readiness and deterrence they buy would otherwise be lost.

Mitch McConnell, the Senate Republican leader, said in 2023 Senate floor remarks that helping Ukraine resist Russia was directly strengthening the US military, growing the US defense industrial base and supporting thousands of American jobs in at least 38 states.
President Joe Biden, in an Oval Office address on October 19, 2023, called his request for aid to Ukraine and Israel a smart investment that would pay dividends for American security for generations.

Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin said in April 2022, after visiting Kyiv, that the United States wanted to see Russia weakened to the degree that it could not do the kinds of things it had done in invading Ukraine.
"Most Aid to Ukraine Is Spent in the US. A Total Shutdown Would Be Irresponsible," Mark F. Cancian, 2023
bridge: A Center for Strategic and International Studies analyst breaks the Ukraine appropriations into categories and finds that less than half of the money goes overseas, with most of the rest spent in the American economy and on US forces.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it is careful accounting from a nonpartisan defense analyst, but showing where money is spent does not by itself show the spending buys security.

text: "The High Price of Losing Ukraine," Thomas Bergeron, Noel Mikkelsen, Mitchell Belcher, Kateryna Stepanenko and Frederick W. Kagan, 2023
where_found: Institute for the Study of War (December 14, 2023)
bridge: The report argues that a Russian victory would bring a larger Russian army to NATO's border and force the United States to spend far more on its own forces in Europe than aid to Ukraine costs.
bottom_line: Moderate to low weight: the cost comparison is a forecast built on assumptions about Russian behavior, from an institute that openly favors backing Ukraine.

text: Weapons sent to Ukraine, especially Patriot air-defense interceptors and artillery shells, drew American stockpiles below what Pentagon war plans require, leaving US forces less ready for a war with China.
bottom_line: Heavy weight: the Pentagon's own 2025 review found shortfalls, though the answer could be faster production rather than less support for Ukraine.

text: Europe's combined economy dwarfs Russia's, so European countries can pay for their own defense and Ukraine's, and American money spent there mostly lets wealthy allies spend less.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: Europe has the means and has been raising its share, but it still depends on American weapons systems it cannot yet replace.

text: Prolonging the war in Ukraine pushes Russia into a closer partnership with China, which is a worse outcome for the United States than a Russia left neutral by a negotiated settlement.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: China-Russia trade hit records during the war, but it is unclear that any settlement would pull Russia away from China.

text: The United States could have rebuilt its own defense industry by buying weapons for American forces directly, without shipping the products to a foreign war.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: true in principle, as Senator J.D. Vance argued in 2024, though Congress had not funded such a buildup before the war gave it a reason.

text: Without a realistic route to Ukraine retaking its occupied land, American aid mostly prolongs a costly stalemate and buys little lasting security for the United States.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the front has moved little since 2023, but a stalemate that keeps Russia's army tied down can itself be a security gain for the United States.

text: As of March 2026 the US Army was producing about 36,000 155-mm artillery shells a month, up from about 14,000 but far short of its goal of 100,000 a month by October 2025, and its $469 million Mesquite, Texas plant had produced no parts meeting specifications.
bottom_line: Strong evidence that the promised industrial revival is slower and more troubled than aid supporters claimed, though output did more than double.

text: Trade between China and Russia rose 26.3 percent to a record $240.1 billion in 2023 and reached a new high of $244.8 billion in 2024, according to Chinese customs data.
bottom_line: Solid figures showing the war drove Russia toward China, though trade fell in 2025 and the growth followed Western sanctions as much as Western aid.

text: The Pentagon will report that Patriot interceptor or 155-mm shell stockpiles remain below war-plan requirements, citing deliveries to Ukraine as a cause.
Russia's active army will be larger in personnel and armored vehicles than it was in February 2022.
A Pentagon or Government Accountability Office review finds that US forces went short of interceptors or shells in an actual crisis because stocks had been sent to Ukraine.
Credible evidence shows China sped up its preparations against Taiwan because American munitions stocks had been drawn down by the Ukraine war.
China is the main long-term threat to the United States, so weapons and money spent in Europe are mostly taken away from deterring China.
European countries would spend enough on their own defense and on Ukraine if the United States stepped back.
The risk that the war in Ukraine escalates into a direct clash with nuclear-armed Russia is serious enough to outweigh likely gains for the United States.

J.D. Vance, then a US senator from Ohio, argued in an April 2024 New York Times column that Ukraine needs more soldiers than it can field and the United States cannot make the weapons Ukraine would need, so continued American aid could not reach its stated goal.

Elbridge Colby argued in his 2021 book The Strategy of Denial that the United States should put denying China dominance in Asia ahead of commitments in Europe, and he was the Pentagon's policy chief when it held back some weapons promised to Ukraine in July 2025 over concerns about low US stockpiles.
"Avoiding a Long War: U.S. Policy and the Trajectory of the Russia-Ukraine Conflict," Samuel Charap and Miranda Priebe, 2023
bridge: The authors argue that the costs and escalation risks of a long war outweigh the gains to the United States from further Ukrainian territorial gains, so American interests are best served by steps that make a negotiated end more likely.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it is a careful study from a respected research group, though it argues against a long war rather than against supporting Ukraine at all.

text: The Strategy of Denial: American Defense in an Age of Great-Power Conflict, Elbridge A. Colby, 2021
bridge: Colby argues that China is the main threat to the United States and that American forces and weapons should be focused on denying China dominance in Asia, with Europe carrying more of its own defense.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it is the most developed case for putting Asia first, and its author later shaped Pentagon policy, but it predates the war and does not measure what Ukraine aid costs China deterrence.

text: "The Math on Ukraine Doesn't Add Up," J.D. Vance, 2024
bridge: Then-Senator Vance argued that Ukraine cannot field enough soldiers and the United States cannot make enough weapons to restore Ukraine's borders, so more aid mostly prolongs a war it cannot win.
bottom_line: Moderate to low weight: it states the manpower and production limits clearly, but it is a political column, not a study, and its forecast is disputed.

text: Workers at American munitions and defense plants need steady orders to keep production lines open.
measured_by: Employment and monthly output at US munitions plants, such as 155-mm shell production reported by the Army and its Inspector General.
if_true: Output and hiring rise and stay up as orders for Ukraine, allies and replacement stocks continue.
if_false: Orders end with the war and new lines close or sit idle.
bottom_line: A real but secondary interest, since the jobs depend on orders that could also come from direct US purchases.

text: American service members need a Russian military too weakened to threaten the NATO allies they are pledged to defend.
measured_by: Russia's active tanks, armored vehicles and trained troops in the International Institute for Strategic Studies' Military Balance, compared with 2022.
if_true: Russia's usable ground forces stay well below their 2022 level for years.
if_false: Russia rebuilds a larger, combat-tested army that could threaten NATO soon after the war.
bottom_line: The strongest security interest on this side, resting on well-documented Russian losses.

text: Poles, Lithuanians, Latvians and Estonians need a Russia that cannot invade a NATO neighbor.
measured_by: Russian troop levels and exercises near NATO's eastern border, and the number of Russian incursions into NATO airspace reported by NATO.
if_true: Russian forces near the border thin out and incursions stay rare.
if_false: Russia masses forces and probes NATO's borders more often after the war.
bottom_line: Weighs heavily for the allies themselves, and for the United States through its treaty obligations to them.

text: American taxpayers need federal money spent on priorities at home rather than on a foreign war.
measured_by: Dollars appropriated by Congress for Ukraine each year, compared with spending on domestic programs and the deficit.
if_true: Spending on Ukraine is modest and largely returns to the US economy, so domestic priorities lose little.
if_false: Large sums leave the country with no measurable return, crowding out spending at home.
bottom_line: A legitimate interest, weakened somewhat by evidence that most of the money was spent in the United States.

text: Ukraine-related spending puts about $120 billion into American factories, weapons replacement and US military accounts.
bottom_line: Well documented by the American Enterprise Institute, though it measures dollars spent at home, not lasting jobs or capacity.

text: Russia's army loses most of its prewar strength without any American troops in combat, lowering the threat to NATO allies.
bottom_line: The CSIS estimate is large and partly corroborated, but Russia keeps replacing losses, so the security gain shrinks if it rebuilds.

text: Allies buy American-made weapons for Ukraine through NATO's PURL program, paying US manufacturers instead of US taxpayers.
bottom_line: Ukraine's Defense Ministry put first-year contributions at $6.7 billion from 29 countries; the figure is growing but well short of Ukraine's stated needs.

text: Congress appropriated about $175 billion in Ukraine-related aid, money unavailable for other federal priorities or debt reduction.
bottom_line: A real cost, though about 70 percent of it was spent inside the United States, and new US appropriations largely stopped in 2025.

text: Continued US involvement keeps open a small but grave risk of direct or nuclear conflict with Russia.
bottom_line: The stakes are the highest of any item here, but the risk cannot be estimated with any confidence and Russian threats have not been carried out so far.

text: The share of US Ukraine-related appropriations spent in American factories or on replacing US military stocks is a fair measure of the economic return to the United States.
US stockpiles of Patriot interceptors and 155-mm shells, measured against Pentagon war-plan requirements, are a fair measure of whether backing Ukraine has cost American military readiness.

Russia's active inventory of tanks and armored vehicles, as estimated in the International Institute for Strategic Studies' annual Military Balance, is a fair measure of how far the war has reduced Russia's threat to NATO.
American support has substantially weakened Russia's ability to threaten NATO countries without costing American lives in combat.
The security and economic benefits of supporting Ukraine to the United States are larger than the costs, including drawn-down stockpiles and the money spent.
A country's own interests can justify foreign aid even when it carries no treaty obligation to the recipient.
If supporting Ukraine serves US interests and Congress keeps funding it, orders to American munitions plants for artillery shells and air-defense interceptors keep rising over the next two years.

If supporting Ukraine serves US interests and the support continues, Russia keeps most of its ground forces tied down in Ukraine rather than massing them near NATO's eastern members within the next year or two.
If supporting Ukraine serves US interests and the support is sustained, Russia makes no armed attack on a NATO member over the next decade.

If supporting Ukraine serves US interests and the support is sustained, the expanded US munitions production lines built during the war remain open over the next decade and leave American forces better stocked than before 2022.
Supporting Ukraine is the cheapest and most effective investment in American security the United States has made in decades.
Ending American support for Ukraine would directly endanger the safety of Americans at home.
Supporting Ukraine brings the United States some security and economic benefits, though they may not outweigh the costs.
Some forms of US support for Ukraine, such as intelligence sharing and selling weapons Europe pays for, serve American interests even if direct aid does not.
Ukraine should be admitted to NATO once the fighting stops.
bottom_line: The record is strong that Russia has attacked only neighbors outside NATO and that neutrality and the 1994 paper assurances did not protect Ukraine; the evidence is thin on whether a membership promise would keep Russia from agreeing to stop fighting, and on whether every member would actually fight for Ukraine. The real fight is over which risk is larger, an unprotected Ukraine that Russia can attack again or an alliance bound to defend a long front line against a nuclear power, and over whether guarantees short of membership, like the January 2026 Paris Declaration, can do the same job while NATO's members remain divided.
hook: Ukraine gave up an estimated 1,900 strategic nuclear warheads after Russia signed a 1994 promise to respect its borders, and twenty years later Russia annexed Crimea (Arms Control Association).
question: Once the fighting stops, should NATO admit Ukraine as a full member, with Article 5's promise that an attack on one is an attack on all?
ask: This page most needs evidence, with figures from studies of past wars, on whether security guarantees short of alliance membership have kept ceasefires from collapsing.

text: Russia has invaded two neighbors that were outside NATO, Georgia in 2008 and Ukraine in 2014 and 2022, and has never attacked a NATO member, so NATO membership is the one security arrangement Russia has so far treated as off limits.
bottom_line: Heavy weight: the pattern is real and consistent, though a short list of cases cannot prove that membership alone, rather than other factors, explains it.

text: Paper promises have already failed Ukraine once, because Russia signed the 1994 Budapest Memorandum pledging to respect Ukraine's borders in exchange for Ukraine giving up its Soviet nuclear arsenal and then seized Crimea in 2014.
bottom_line: Heavy weight: it is the clearest historical test of a guarantee short of alliance membership, and it failed, though the memorandum promised far less than the guarantees now on offer.

text: A ceasefire in Ukraine without NATO membership would likely become a pause in which Russia rebuilds its army and attacks again, as happened when the 2014 and 2015 Minsk ceasefires were followed by the full-scale invasion of February 2022.
bottom_line: Moderate to heavy weight: the Minsk precedent is strong, but whether a future Russia would choose renewed war depends on costs and leaders that no one can see in advance.

text: Ukraine's armed forces, which Ukraine's government puts at about 800,000 troops with more recent large-scale combat experience than any NATO member's, would add to NATO's defense of its eastern flank rather than only drain it.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the asset is real, but the troop figure comes from Kyiv, observers doubt the army's true strength, and Ukraine says it cannot pay for that army alone in peacetime.

text: Ukraine inherited an estimated 1,900 strategic nuclear warheads at independence in 1991 and had returned all of its nuclear warheads to Russia by 1996, after Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom signed the 1994 Budapest Memorandum pledging to respect its borders; Russia annexed Crimea in 2014.
bottom_line: Strong as a record of what happened, weaker as proof about the future, since the memorandum offered political assurances rather than a promise to fight.

text: Ukraine was legally non-aligned under a 2010 law barring it from seeking membership in military alliances when Russia seized Crimea in early 2014; Ukraine's parliament repealed that status on December 23, 2014, by 303 votes.
bottom_line: Strong against the claim that neutrality would keep Ukraine safe, though people who blame NATO expansion argue Russia was reacting to the West's longer-run courting of Kyiv, not to a law.

text: Russia will not use military force against Finland, Sweden or any other NATO member despite its warnings about NATO's 2023 and 2024 expansion.
If a ceasefire is signed without NATO membership for Ukraine, Russia will launch a new large-scale offensive against Ukraine within five years, as it did after the Minsk agreements.
Russian military documents or credible intelligence come to light showing Russia planned to rebuild its forces during any ceasefire in order to attack Ukraine again.
Russia agrees to a lasting settlement while Ukraine's NATO path remains open, showing the membership question was not the obstacle to peace.
Russia's leaders weigh the risk of fighting NATO and would be deterred by Article 5 from attacking Ukraine again.
NATO members, including the United States, would actually honor Article 5 if Russia attacked Ukraine after Ukraine joined NATO.
Russia's goal is to control Ukraine, not only to keep it out of NATO, so a neutral Ukraine would not buy a lasting peace.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky made an invitation to join NATO the first point of the victory plan he presented to Ukraine's parliament in October 2024.
Vilnius Summit Communiqué, North Atlantic Treaty Organization, 2023
where_found: NATO, issued by the heads of state and government meeting in Vilnius on July 11, 2023
bridge: Every NATO member signed a statement that Ukraine's future is in NATO and that the alliance will be in a position to invite Ukraine to join when allies agree and conditions are met.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it shows the alliance itself has endorsed eventual membership, but it sets no date and leaves every member's veto in place.

text: Admitting Ukraine to NATO would bind every member, including the United States, to treat a new Russian attack across a front line hundreds of miles long as an attack on itself, which raises the risk of direct war between nuclear powers.
bottom_line: Heavy weight: this is the central risk opponents name, though how large it is depends on whether membership deters Russia (lowering the risk) or tempts a test of the alliance (raising it).

text: Admitting Ukraine while Russia occupies part of its territory would leave NATO with a disputed border, where an incident along an unrecognized line could set off an argument over whether Article 5 applies.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the problem is real, but West Germany joined NATO in 1955 while divided, with Article 5 applied in practice only to the territory it controlled, which shows a workable model exists.

text: A NATO membership promise without a firm plan can invite Russian attack instead of preventing it, as when the 2008 Bucharest summit declared that Georgia and Ukraine would become members and Russia invaded Georgia four months later.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the timing is real, but it supports giving Ukraine actual membership or a firm guarantee more than it supports giving it nothing.

text: Defending Ukraine as a NATO member would cost the United States billions of dollars a year and pull forces from other commitments, including in the Pacific, at a time when American and European militaries are already stretched.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the cost is real (a 2021 CSIS study put it at about $11 billion a year to the United States), but it must be weighed against the cost of another war if Ukraine is left unprotected.

text: NATO's April 2008 Bucharest summit declared that Georgia and Ukraine would become members without offering a plan or date, and Russia went to war with Georgia four months later, in August 2008.
bottom_line: Moderate: the sequence is documented, but whether the promise caused the war or merely preceded it is disputed among historians.

text: A September 2021 CSIS study estimated that extending NATO's Article 5 guarantee to Ukraine would cost the United States about $11 billion a year, against half a billion dollars or less for Sweden.
bottom_line: Useful as an order of magnitude, but it predates the full-scale invasion and Ukraine's much larger army, so the real figure today could be higher or lower.

text: A ceasefire backed only by the security guarantees of the January 2026 Paris Declaration, without NATO membership, will hold without a major Russian offensive for at least five years.
Within a year of any formal NATO invitation to Ukraine, Russia will resume full-scale war against Ukraine or attack forces or territory of a NATO member.
Russia honors a ceasefire for ten years with Ukraine protected only by bilateral and coalition guarantees, showing NATO membership was not needed to deter a renewed attack.
Parliaments in several NATO countries refuse to ratify Ukraine's accession or say they would not send forces if Russia attacked again, showing an Article 5 pledge to Ukraine would be hollow.
Russia's objection to Ukraine joining NATO reflects a security fear that any lasting settlement of the war must take into account.
Guarantees short of NATO membership, such as Western weapons, training and bilateral defense pacts, can deter Russia from attacking Ukraine nearly as well as membership would.

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Ukraine's allies in Brussels on February 12, 2025, that the United States does not believe NATO membership for Ukraine is a realistic outcome of a negotiated settlement.
Why the Ukraine Crisis Is the West's Fault: The Liberal Delusions That Provoked Putin, John J. Mearsheimer, 2014
bridge: A University of Chicago political scientist argues that the push to bring Ukraine into NATO and the European Union was the main cause of Russia's seizure of Crimea, so admitting Ukraine would deepen the conflict rather than end it.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the most influential case against expansion, though critics note Russia invaded in 2022 when NATO membership was nowhere near on offer.

text: The Talks That Could Have Ended the War in Ukraine, Samuel Charap and Sergey Radchenko, 2024
bridge: Using draft texts from the spring 2022 talks in Belarus and Istanbul, the authors show that Ukraine and Russia came close to a deal built on Ukrainian neutrality with outside security guarantees, which suggests a non-NATO settlement was once negotiable.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: rests on real draft documents, but the drafts left the hardest questions open and the talks collapsed, so how close they came is disputed.

text: Ukrainians living near the front line need protection from a renewed Russian invasion.
measured_by: Civilian deaths and injuries recorded by the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine in the years after a ceasefire.
if_true: Civilian casualties fall close to zero and stay there because Russia is deterred from attacking again.
if_false: Casualties drop during a pause and then rise again when Russia resumes the war.
bottom_line: The most direct interest at stake, and the one both sides claim to serve by different means.

text: Poles, Lithuanians, Latvians, Estonians and Finns need Russia deterred from attacking another neighbor.
measured_by: Russian military incidents and attacks on NATO's eastern members, and how much those countries must spend on defense.
if_true: Incidents stay rare and a strong Ukraine inside NATO absorbs part of the burden of guarding the eastern flank.
if_false: A Russia that wins in Ukraine without facing an alliance tests the eastern members next.
bottom_line: A strong interest, though some in these countries also fear that admitting Ukraine draws them into a larger war.

text: Ukrainian business owners and their workers need a lasting peace that makes rebuilding worth investing in.
measured_by: Foreign direct investment into Ukraine and the rate of reconstruction of damaged homes and factories.
if_true: Investment rises once the risk of renewed war is credibly lowered.
if_false: Investors stay away while the risk of another invasion hangs over the country.
bottom_line: Real but secondary to safety, and it depends on many factors besides alliance membership.

text: American taxpayers need limits on open-ended defense commitments abroad.
measured_by: U.S. defense spending tied to European commitments, in dollars a year.
if_true: Spending rises to garrison and reinforce a new member with a long border with Russia.
if_false: Spending stays flat as Europe and bilateral guarantees carry Ukraine's defense.
bottom_line: A legitimate interest, weighed against the cost to Americans if a renewed war spreads.

text: American and European service members need to avoid being sent to fight a nuclear-armed Russia.
measured_by: Direct military clashes between NATO and Russian forces, and NATO casualties from them.
if_true: Clashes remain zero because membership deters Russia.
