bridge: Using insurance claims rather than company-chosen crash counts, the study found 88 percent fewer property damage claims and 92 percent fewer bodily injury claims for Waymo's driverless miles than for human drivers, which is the record state lawmakers are asked to weigh before letting robotaxis into a new metro.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because an outside insurer took part and claims data are hard to game, but Waymo coauthored it and 25 million miles is still a small sample for rare serious crashes.

text: Comparison of Waymo Rider-Only Crash Data to Human Benchmarks at 7.1 Million Miles, Kristofer D. Kusano et al., 2024
bridge: Drawing on federal crash reports over 7.14 million driverless miles in Phoenix, San Francisco and Los Angeles, the paper found Waymo vehicles reported far fewer injury crashes and police-reported crashes per mile than human benchmarks, the safety case behind each new city launch.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, since it is peer reviewed and uses public federal data, but every author works for Waymo and the safety record speaks to permission, not to how fast new metros can be opened.

text: Waymo goes driverless in Las Vegas, with Denver, San Diego, Tampa next, Fred Lambert, 2026
bridge: The article documents Waymo adding Las Vegas to ten existing driverless markets in July 2026, naming Denver, San Diego and Tampa as next, with a fleet of roughly 3,500 cars and a 16 billion dollar funding round behind the expansion.
bottom_line: Useful as a dated count of launched and announced metros, though it is trade press reporting company statements, not an independent audit.

text: A single bad crash can erase a company from the count, as it did when GM shut Cruise in December 2024 after more than ten billion dollars of losses following one pedestrian injury in San Francisco, so a count that assumes every operator keeps growing is counting events that history shows can reverse.
bottom_line: Deserves real weight, since the Cruise shutdown removed an operator that was once in several cities, though Waymo has so far survived its own federal investigations without pausing service.

text: General Motors ended Cruise's robotaxi business in December 2024 after more than 10 billion dollars in losses and less than 500 million dollars in revenue, citing the time and money still needed to scale, and laid off about half the remaining staff two months later.
bottom_line: This is the clearest case of an operator leaving the count, and it shows the belief rests on companies choosing to keep spending for two more years.

text: New York Governor Kathy Hochul proposed in January 2026 to allow robotaxis statewide except in cities over one million people, then withdrew the proposal in February 2026 after her office said legislative support was not there, leaving a law that still requires a hand on the wheel.
bottom_line: The largest metro in the country is legally closed and the one attempt to open it failed, which is strong evidence that the next ten metros will not all come from the biggest cities.

text: Washington D.C.'s council held its first hearing on a robotaxi authorization bill in July 2026, more than a year after Waymo began supervised testing there, with a proposed 200-vehicle cap and no public rides before 2028 under the pending text.
bottom_line: Direct evidence that a city Waymo publicly labeled a 2026 launch can slip two years on politics alone.

text: Waymo's count of paid driverless U.S. metros will rise by fewer than six between October 2026 and the end of 2027, as it exhausts states with permissive law and waits on winter validation.
A federal or state regulator will order at least one robotaxi operator to suspend paid driverless service in at least one metro for 90 days or more.
A regulator-ordered halt of Waymo's paid service in two or more metros lasting six months or longer would show the count can shrink as well as grow and would freeze the company's launch pipeline.
The easiest U.S. metro areas for robotaxis have already been served, so each additional metro will take longer to open than the last.
A serious robotaxi crash is likely enough over two more years of rapid growth that at least one operator will pause or shrink its service, as Cruise did after October 2023.
Vehicle supply and the cost of depots and remote-assistance staff, not maps or software, will limit how many new metro areas robotaxi companies can open by 2028.

Teamsters General President Sean O'Brien testified to Congress in July 2025 that allowing the unfettered and unregulated operation of autonomous vehicles is unequivocally a threat to safety on our roadways, and his union has backed state bills requiring a human operator in every autonomous vehicle.
Autonorama: The Illusory Promise of High-Tech Driving, Peter Norton, 2021
bridge: A University of Virginia historian of technology argues that driverless car promises repeat a century of overstated transportation forecasts going back to GM's 1939 Futurama exhibit, a pattern that cautions against reading announced city lists as launches.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight for this belief, since it predates paid driverless service in most cities and argues mainly about social value rather than the count of metros by 2028.

text: What Self-Driving Cars Tell Us About AI Risks, Mary "Missy" Cummings, 2023
bridge: A former safety adviser to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration argues that driving software cannot grasp context or unseen factors the way a person can and links automotive AI to at least 25 confirmed U.S. deaths, the kind of risk that can stall approvals in new cities.
bottom_line: Moderate weight as an informed expert view, though the death count mixes driver-assistance systems with true robotaxis and the piece was written before most 2025 and 2026 launches.

text: New York's Robotaxi Plan Pulled in Setback to Waymo Expansion, Bloomberg News, 2026
bridge: The report records Governor Kathy Hochul's office dropping, in February 2026, a budget proposal that would have let companies pilot commercial driverless service outside New York City, after a spokesperson said the support was not there.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because it shows a large state saying no in 2026, though New York's metros are not needed if enough Sun Belt metros launch.

text: Alphabet and Tesla shareholders need the tens of billions of dollars spent on self-driving to turn into revenue before the capital is written off the way GM wrote off Cruise.
measured_by: Paid robotaxi rides per week and metros served, as reported on earnings calls
if_true: Weekly paid rides pass one million and metros pass 25
if_false: Rides plateau near 500,000 a week and metros stall under 20
bottom_line: A concentrated financial interest that funds the expansion and also funds the lobbying, so a reader should weigh its claims accordingly.

text: Parents of children who walk to school in cities with robotaxi service need the vehicles to stop for school buses and crossing guards every time, not after a recall.
measured_by: Reported school-zone incidents involving driverless vehicles per metro per school year
if_true: Incidents spread to more metros even if the per-mile rate stays low
if_false: Incidents stay confined to the current markets
bottom_line: Austin's school district asked Waymo to pause during school hours and was refused, so this interest has already lost one round and will be back at every new council.

text: Pedestrians and cyclists in cities that have not yet approved robotaxis need their council to see a local safety study before vehicles with no human aboard share their streets.
measured_by: Share of newly opened metros where a local safety study was completed before the first paid driverless ride
if_true: Falls, since reaching 25 by 2028 leaves little time for studies in each city
if_false: Rises, as slower approval gives studies time to finish
bottom_line: This interest holds the procedural high ground in Washington D.C. and Boston and almost none in Texas or Florida, where state law preempts the council.

text: Reaching 25 metros by 2028 would confirm that a U.S. company can turn a self-driving research program into a multi-city business, which is the result Alphabet's and Tesla's investors have funded for more than a decade.
bottom_line: The benefit is large if the belief is true and lands entirely on a small group of owners, which is why the cost side matters as much.

text: A 25-metro footprint would give city transportation staff in most large U.S. cities their own local crash and ridership data instead of having to rely on Waymo's Phoenix and San Francisco figures.
bottom_line: A modest but durable benefit, since local data is what lets a council argue from its own streets rather than from another city's.

text: Each new robotaxi metro moves some share of ride-hail fares from human drivers to a fleet owner, so 25 metros by 2028 would shrink the earnings of Uber and Lyft drivers in most large U.S. cities during the same years their expenses rise.
bottom_line: The direction is clear and the size is not, because no public figure yet shows how many driver trips a Waymo launch displaces in a given metro.

text: The number of distinct U.S. metropolitan statistical areas where, on December 31, 2028, at least one company is carrying riders who pay a fare in a vehicle with no company employee aboard is a fair measure of whether the belief that driverless robotaxis will serve 25 metros by the end of 2028 came true.
State and local governments covering at least 25 U.S. metro areas will allow commercial driverless ride service with no safety driver by the end of 2028.
No crash or federal safety action will force the leading robotaxi operator to pause new launches for a year or longer before the end of 2028.
Within a year or two, ride-hail drivers in newly served metro areas would see robotaxis take a share of trips in the downtown and airport areas where service usually starts.
Over a decade, paid driverless rides would become an ordinary option in most large U.S. metro areas, giving people who cannot drive a way to travel without a human driver.
Over a decade, the number of people earning a living as ride-hail and taxi drivers in U.S. cities would shrink as robotaxi fleets take over more trips.
Fully driverless robotaxis will carry paying passengers in at least 50 U.S. metropolitan areas by the end of 2028.
Fully driverless robotaxis will provide more than 10 percent of all U.S. ride-hail trips by the end of 2030.
Fully driverless robotaxis will carry paying passengers in at least 15 U.S. metropolitan areas by the end of 2028.
At least two different companies will each run paid, fully driverless ride service in five or more U.S. metropolitan areas by the end of 2028.
AI will have destroyed more U.S. jobs than it created by the end of 2030.
bottom_line: The evidence is strong that AI is already cutting entry-level hiring in exposed occupations and strong that the national labor market has not yet shown a net loss; the fight is really about whether a concentrated hit on young workers in a few fields becomes an economy-wide net loss within four years, and the honest answer is that no measurement published by October 2026 can settle that yet.
hook: Employers blamed AI for 101,743 announced U.S. job cuts in the first six months of 2026, nearly twice the 54,836 they blamed on it in all of 2025, yet the U.S. unemployment rate was still 4.2 percent in September 2026.
question: Will artificial intelligence have eliminated more U.S. jobs than it created by the end of 2030?
ask: The page most needs a payroll-data study that compares net hiring between 2025 and 2028 at firms with the highest AI adoption and similar firms with the lowest, because that one dataset could count against the belief or for it.

text: Early-career workers in the occupations most exposed to AI have already lost ground relative to their peers, which is the pattern an economy shows when AI is replacing entry-level labor.
bottom_line: This deserves real weight because it rests on payroll records for millions of workers rather than on forecasts, but it covers one age band and about three years.

text: Job creation from a new technology generally arrives years after the job destruction, because new firms and new occupations take longer to form than a layoff takes to announce.
bottom_line: This is the strongest structural reason to expect a net loss by a date as near as 2030 even if AI creates more jobs than it destroys over a longer run.

text: Companies have an incentive to hold headcount flat and let attrition do the cutting, so the net loss can be large while the layoff count stays modest.
bottom_line: This deserves moderate weight because it explains how a net loss could hide from the layoff statistics, but it is also hard to confirm or refute, which is a weakness.

text: Early-career workers aged 22 to 25 in the occupations most exposed to AI saw a 13 percent relative decline in employment after generative AI spread, while older workers in the same occupations held steady or grew.
bottom_line: The best direct evidence of AI-linked job loss so far, built on payroll data from the largest U.S. payroll processor, but it measures a relative decline in one age group and the authors say they cannot prove AI is the cause.

text: Employers cited artificial intelligence as the reason for 101,743 announced U.S. job cuts in the first six months of 2026, about 23 percent of all announced cuts, compared with 54,836 AI-attributed cuts in all of 2025.
bottom_line: A real and rising count, but it records what employers say in press releases, and total announced cuts in 2026 were running 40 percent below 2025, so AI's share rose partly because other reasons fell.

text: In a September 2026 survey of 123 economists, 45 percent said AI's net effect on U.S. employment is a minor negative, 25 percent said a minor positive, and 21 percent said no net effect.
bottom_line: Expert opinion leans slightly toward the belief, but the modal answer is 'minor', and a survey of forecasts is not a measurement of jobs.

text: Employment of customer service representatives in the May 2028 OEWS estimates will be at least 5 percent below the May 2025 level.
Challenger, Gray & Christmas will record more than 200,000 AI-attributed job cuts in calendar year 2027.
A follow-up to the Stanford payroll study finds the relative employment decline in AI-exposed occupations has spread from workers aged 22 to 25 to workers aged 26 to 40.

The fall in entry-level hiring in AI-exposed occupations since 2022 is caused mainly by AI rather than by higher interest rates, the post-pandemic correction in technology hiring, or a general cooling of the labor market.
AI systems will keep getting better and cheaper through 2030 at something like the pace they improved between 2022 and 2026.
Most U.S. firms that adopt AI will use the savings to do the same work with fewer people rather than to produce more with the same number of people.

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei told Axios in May 2025 that AI could eliminate half of all entry-level white-collar jobs and push U.S. unemployment to 10 to 20 percent within one to five years.
Ford chief executive Jim Farley said at the Aspen Ideas Festival in June 2025 that AI will replace about half of all white-collar workers in the United States, though he gave no date.

Geoffrey Hinton, who shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for work underlying modern AI, said on the Diary of a CEO podcast in June 2025 that AI will replace everybody doing mundane intellectual labor and advised young people to train as plumbers.
Power and Progress: Our Thousand-Year Struggle Over Technology and Prosperity, Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson, 2023
bridge: The book argues from history that new technology does not automatically create more and better jobs, and that the gains go to workers only when firms choose to use machines to help people rather than replace them.
bottom_line: This is a serious argument against assuming that job creation will catch up on its own, but it is a historical case rather than a measurement of AI's effect on jobs through 2030.

text: AI generally raises the output of a worker rather than replacing the worker, and firms whose workers produce more tend to hire more, not fewer.
bottom_line: This argument is well supported for the first wave of AI tools, but it is weakest where AI handles a whole task end to end, which is where the entry-level losses are showing up.

text: The U.S. population is aging and the labor force is growing slowly, so employers facing a shortage of workers are more likely to use AI to fill gaps than to cut people.
bottom_line: Demographics put a floor under total employment, which matters for a claim about net loss, but the floor does not protect any particular occupation.

text: Counting jobs AI destroyed is easy and counting jobs it created is hard, so any tally will look worse than the truth because new jobs in new firms are not labeled as AI jobs.
bottom_line: This is a measurement objection rather than a claim about the world, but it is a serious one for any resolution rule that relies on labeling.

text: Thirty-three months after ChatGPT's release, the U.S. labor market showed no discernible disruption, and measures of occupational AI exposure showed no relationship to changes in employment or unemployment.
bottom_line: Strong evidence against an economy-wide effect as of late 2025, but it uses broad government survey data that can miss a shift concentrated in young workers, and the authors flag early-career workers as a possible exception.

text: The U.S. unemployment rate was 4.2 percent in September 2026, had stayed between 4.1 and 4.3 percent since March, and total nonfarm employment stood at about 159 million.
bottom_line: A steady headline rate is the single most important fact against a net loss already under way, but it says nothing about which jobs are being lost and which created.

text: Employment of software developers in the May 2028 OEWS estimates will be higher than in May 2025.
The unemployment rate for recent college graduates aged 22 to 27 will be below 6 percent in the fourth quarter of 2028.
The 2026 BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics show employment of customer service representatives and claims adjusters at or above the May 2024 level despite three years of AI adoption.
A payroll-data study finds that firms with the highest measured AI adoption added more net jobs between 2025 and 2028 than otherwise similar firms with the lowest adoption.
Demand for most goods and services rises when they get cheaper, so a worker made more productive by AI will generally lead an employer to hire more, not fewer.
The weak hiring of young college graduates since 2023 would have happened without AI because of interest rates, overhiring in 2021 and 2022, and a slowing economy.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang said at the VivaTech conference in Paris in June 2025 that he disagreed with almost everything Dario Amodei had said about AI eliminating entry-level office jobs, arguing that productivity gains have historically led companies to hire more people.
Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects, Anders Humlum and Emilie Vestergaard, 2025
where_found: National Bureau of Economic Research, Working Paper 33777
bridge: Linking adoption surveys to Danish government records for 25,000 workers in 11 exposed occupations, the study finds that AI chatbots had close to zero effect on earnings or recorded hours, with average time savings of about 3 percent.
bottom_line: This is careful evidence that early AI tools changed tasks without cutting work, but Denmark is not the United States and the tools studied are older than the ones firms use now.

text: New Frontiers: The Origins and Content of New Work, 1940-2018, David Autor, Caroline Chin, Anna Salomons and Bryan Seegmiller, 2024
bridge: The study finds that most U.S. employment in 2018 was in kinds of work that did not exist in 1940, showing how much of the job creation from new technology comes in forms nobody could have counted in advance.
bottom_line: This is strong evidence that new work arrives over decades, which cuts against the belief in the long run but says little about whether it arrives fast enough to offset losses by 2030.

text: Customer service representatives and claims processors need enough warning to retrain before their jobs disappear.
measured_by: Share of workers laid off from these occupations who are reemployed at similar pay within a year
if_true: The share falls as displaced workers compete for a shrinking pool of similar jobs.
if_false: The share holds near its pre-2023 level.
bottom_line: The BLS already projects these occupations to shrink, so this group is on the side of the belief whether or not the net national figure turns negative.

text: Recent college graduates need entry-level openings that still exist when they finish their degrees.
measured_by: Unemployment and underemployment rates for graduates aged 22 to 27 on the New York Fed's series
if_true: Both rates rise above their 2026 levels of 5.6 and 42 percent.
if_false: Both rates drift back toward their 2019 levels.
bottom_line: This is the group the Stanford data says is already being hit, and the one whose outcomes will decide the question first.

text: Small-business owners need affordable AI tools that let a few people do the work of many.
measured_by: Share of small firms reporting AI use in the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey
if_true: Adoption keeps rising but policy fights over job loss raise the cost or limit the use of the tools.
if_false: Adoption keeps rising without new restrictions.
bottom_line: This group gains from AI whether or not it costs jobs elsewhere, so its interest runs against acting on the belief rather than against the belief being true.

text: Congress and the states would fund retraining and wage insurance for displaced workers before the losses peak rather than years after.
bottom_line: Acting on the belief turns a reactive safety net into a planned one, and the estimate is the rough annual run rate of AI-attributed cuts Challenger recorded in the first half of 2026.

text: Employers would be pushed to report AI-driven headcount changes in a standard way, giving the country real data in place of press-release counts.
bottom_line: Better measurement is the one benefit both sides of this question should want, because today's fight is largely about missing data.

text: Workers in exposed occupations would lose income during the gap between losing a job and finding a new one, and public programs would carry the cost.
bottom_line: This cost follows from the belief being true regardless of what anyone does about it, and the figure is a rough estimate of a year of a lost mid-wage job's pay.

text: Two readings of government data for 2030, taken together, are a fair resolution rule for whether AI destroyed more U.S. jobs than it created by the end of 2030: the employment rate of Americans aged 25 to 54, and the change in employment in the occupations most exposed to AI compared with all other occupations.
Whether hours worked in the U.S. nonfarm business sector fall while that sector's output keeps rising is a fair measure of whether AI is replacing labor rather than adding to what workers produce.
Between the release of ChatGPT in late 2022 and the end of 2030, the number of U.S. jobs eliminated or never filled because of AI will exceed the number of U.S. jobs that exist because of AI.
Jobs that AI indirectly creates in new firms, new occupations and cheaper products will not grow fast enough by 2030 to make up for the jobs it removes in exposed occupations.

If AI is destroying more U.S. jobs than it creates, hiring of workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations such as customer service, software development and paralegal work will keep falling relative to older workers through 2027.
If lawmakers act on the belief that AI is a net job destroyer, Congress or several states will pass retraining funds, AI layoff notice rules or a tax on replaced positions by the end of 2027.
If AI destroys more U.S. jobs than it creates through 2030, the share of Americans aged 25 to 54 who are employed will be lower in 2035 than in 2025, reversing the recovery since the pandemic.

If AI removes most entry-level white-collar work over the next decade, U.S. employers will have fewer experienced mid-career workers in law, finance and software by the mid-2030s, because fewer people got the first jobs that train them.
AI will push the U.S. unemployment rate above 10 percent by the end of 2030.
AI will have eliminated half of all entry-level white-collar jobs in the United States by the end of 2030.
By the end of 2030, AI will have reduced employment of U.S. workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations, even if total U.S. employment keeps growing.
By the end of 2030, AI will have destroyed more jobs than it created in at least a few U.S. occupations, such as customer service representatives and paralegals.
Artificial general intelligence, meaning an AI that can do nearly any thinking job a person can, will exist before 2035.
bottom_line: The best measured evidence for yes is METR's finding that the length of software tasks AI can finish has doubled about every 89 days since 2024, though with wide error bars. The broadest evidence against is a survey of 2,778 researchers that gave even odds of machines beating people at every task only by 2047. The real fight is whether scaling up today's methods is enough: Epoch AI finds compute can keep growing through 2030, but 76 percent of researchers in the AAAI 2025 survey said scaling alone is unlikely to produce AGI.
hook: The best AI system could work on its own for about five hours in January 2026, and METR's data say that figure has been doubling every four to seven months.
question: Will an AI that can do nearly any thinking job a person can exist before 2035?
ask: The page most needs a reader who can argue, with a source, whether any published AI system has shown learning from experience after training ends, since that is the capability the disagree side says is missing and the agree side has not addressed.

text: The leaders of the three largest AI labs (Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind) have each said in public that AI matching human experts across most fields is likely within two to ten years.
bottom_line: Light to moderate weight: these people see unreleased systems before anyone else, but they also raise money on the claim, so their timelines should be discounted for interest.

text: Training compute for frontier models has grown about four times a year, and Epoch AI finds that power, chips, data and latency allow that pace to continue through 2030.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: compute growth has predicted capability jumps so far, but it only argues that scaling can continue, not that scaling alone reaches general intelligence.

text: METR's Time Horizon 1.1 update finds that the length of software tasks frontier models can complete with 50 percent reliability has doubled about every 196 days since 2019, about every 131 days since 2023, and about every 89 days since 2024, with the best model at 320 minutes.
bottom_line: The single most useful measured trend on the question, limited by wide confidence intervals and a task suite that is close to saturating.

text: Epoch AI's 2024 study of the four main limits on AI training (power, chip manufacturing, data and latency) concludes that training runs of 2 times 10 to the 29th floating-point operations, about 10,000 times GPT-4, are likely feasible by 2030.
bottom_line: Credible engineering analysis that scaling will not stall for physical reasons before 2030; it says nothing about whether scaling is enough.

text: The Metaculus 'weakly general AI' question (3479) will resolve yes before the end of 2029.
METR will publish a 50 percent time horizon of at least 160 human-hours (one working month) for a public model before the end of 2029.
A frontier AI system publicly passes a two-hour adversarial Turing test run by an independent group, with judges allowed to send images and audio, before the end of 2030.
An AI system designs, runs and writes up a scientific result that a peer-reviewed journal publishes without human co-authors doing the intellectual work, and the result replicates.
Adding more compute, data and incremental improvements to today's AI methods will keep producing capability gains at roughly the pace seen since 2019.

Gaps in today's AI systems such as continual learning, long-term memory and reliability are engineering problems that can be solved within a few years, not puzzles that need new scientific breakthroughs.
Most thinking jobs can be done through a computer, so an AI does not need a body or years of on-the-job experience to do nearly any of them.

Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, wrote in his October 2024 essay "Machines of Loving Grace" that AI smarter than a Nobel Prize winner in most fields could come as early as 2026, though it could also take much longer.
Sam Altman, chief executive of OpenAI, wrote in his January 2025 blog post "Reflections" that OpenAI is now confident it knows how to build AGI as it has traditionally been understood.
The Singularity Is Nearer: When We Merge with AI, Ray Kurzweil, 2024
bridge: Kurzweil restates his decades-old forecast that AI will reach human-level intelligence by 2029 and argues that steady exponential gains in computing price-performance make that date likely.
bottom_line: Light to moderate weight: his 1999 date has held up better than most, but the book argues from long-run curves rather than from tests of what current systems can and cannot do.

text: Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead, Leopold Aschenbrenner, 2024
bridge: A former OpenAI researcher counts expected gains in compute, algorithmic efficiency and removal of model limitations and concludes that AGI by 2027 is strikingly plausible.
bottom_line: Moderate weight as the clearest statement of the scaling case, discounted because it assumes the trend lines continue and the author now runs an investment fund built on that view.

text: In the largest survey of AI researchers, the median answer put a 50 percent chance of machines doing every task better and cheaper than people at 2047, not before 2035.
bottom_line: Heavy weight: 2,778 published researchers are the broadest expert base available, though their past forecasts have consistently been too slow.

text: Three quarters of the AI researchers surveyed by the AAAI in 2025 said scaling current approaches is unlikely or very unlikely to produce AGI.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the respondents are mostly academics outside the frontier labs, which is both a strength (no stake in the hype) and a weakness (less access to the newest systems).

text: Every past prediction of human-level AI within a decade, from the 1950s through the 2000s, has been wrong, which gives a base rate against any new one.
bottom_line: Light to moderate weight: the base rate is real, but past predictions were not backed by trillions of dollars of compute or by measured capability curves.

text: The 2023 Expert Survey on Progress in AI, answered by 2,778 authors of papers at top AI venues, put a 50 percent chance of high-level machine intelligence (machines doing every task better and more cheaply than people) by 2047, and of full automation of all labor by 2116.
bottom_line: The broadest expert survey on record and the strongest single piece of evidence against; its weakness is that the same survey series moved its median 13 years earlier in one year.

text: In the AAAI 2025 Presidential Panel survey of 475 AI researchers, 76 percent said that scaling up current AI approaches to produce AGI is unlikely or very unlikely.
bottom_line: Reliable as a count of what academic researchers believe; it asked about scaling alone, so it does not rule out AGI by another route before 2035.

text: No publicly announced AI system will have met the robotic assembly condition of Metaculus question 5121 by the end of 2030.
METR's measured doubling time for AI task length lengthens to more than 12 months in two consecutive annual reports.
High AI scores on written tests mostly reflect training on test-like material rather than general ability that carries over to real jobs.
Human-level AI requires abilities, such as learning on the job and understanding the physical world, that need new ideas whose arrival cannot be forecast from trend lines.
Limits on electric power, chips, money or regulation will slow the growth of AI training compute well before 2035.

Andrej Karpathy, a founding member of OpenAI, said in an October 2025 interview with Dwarkesh Patel, released as "AGI is still a decade away," that AI agents able to work like a human employee are about ten years off because they still lack continual learning and memory.
Yann LeCun, Meta's former chief AI scientist, said on the Big Technology Podcast in 2025 that people are not going to get to human-level AI by just scaling up large language models.

Gary Marcus bet Miles Brundage at the end of 2024, at 10 to 1 odds, that AI systems will not be able to perform 8 of 10 named thinking tasks, such as writing Oscar-caliber screenplays or 10,000 lines of bug-free code, by the end of 2027.
Rebooting AI: Building Artificial Intelligence We Can Trust, Gary Marcus and Ernest Davis, 2019
bridge: The authors argue that systems trained on statistical patterns lack common sense, causal reasoning and models of the world, and that scaling them will not supply those things.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: several of its specific predictions about language models aged badly, but its list of missing abilities (reliability, reasoning about the physical world) still matches the gaps critics point to.

text: On the Measure of Intelligence, François Chollet, 2019
bridge: Chollet argues that intelligence is the efficiency of acquiring new skills, not skill at known tasks, and introduces the ARC test to measure it, the line of tests where people still far outscore AI.
bottom_line: Moderate to heavy weight as the clearest definition of what benchmark scores miss, though ARC tests have been beaten faster than their author expected.

text: Patients with rare diseases need new treatments found faster.
measured_by: Number of new drugs approved by the FDA per year for rare diseases.
if_true: Rises as AI systems run the design and analysis work that now takes research teams years.
if_false: Stays near the current pace set by human researchers and trial timelines.
bottom_line: A strong interest in the belief being true, and the one most often used to justify the race.

text: AI lab employees and their investors need the capital bet on AI to pay off.
measured_by: Annual revenue of the frontier AI labs against their cumulative spending.
if_true: Revenue grows into the hundreds of billions and the spending is justified.
if_false: Spending outruns revenue and the labs cut staff or fold.
bottom_line: The most direct financial interest on the agree side, which is why their forecasts deserve a discount.

text: Early-career office workers need entry-level jobs to still exist.
measured_by: Employment of 22 to 25 year olds in AI-exposed occupations relative to less exposed peers.
if_true: Falls further from the 19 percent gap already measured.
if_false: Recovers as firms resume hiring once the current tools' limits are clear.
bottom_line: The group with the most to lose from the belief being true, and already losing.

text: Households near new data centers need stable electricity prices.
measured_by: Residential electricity price in regions with heavy data-center growth.
if_true: Rises as AI electricity demand more than doubles.
if_false: Stabilizes as data-center building slows.
bottom_line: A concrete local cost that lands regardless of whether AGI arrives, since the data centers are being built now.

text: AI that can do nearly any thinking job raises world output by several percentage points within a decade.
bottom_line: The Goldman Sachs 2023 estimate of 7 percent was for generative AI short of AGI, so a true AGI would likely exceed it, but the figure has never been tested against outcomes.

text: AI that can do the thinking work of a research scientist shortens the time to find and test new drugs.
bottom_line: Plausible and the benefit AI leaders cite most, but no AI-discovered drug has yet reached approval, so the size is unknown.

text: AI that can do nearly any thinking job removes most of the entry-level office work that young graduates use to start careers.
bottom_line: The 19 percent gap is already measured for today's AI (Stanford, August 2026), so AGI would push it further; the authors call it descriptive, not causal.

text: Data centers built for AI more than double world data-center electricity use by 2030.
bottom_line: The IEA's 945 TWh projection for 2030 is for the current build-out; a real AGI would raise demand further.

text: The length of a human task that frontier AI systems can complete with 50 percent reliability, as measured on METR's public task suite, is a fair measure of how close AI is to doing nearly any thinking job.
Measured AI capabilities have kept improving at a pace that, if it continues, reaches human level on most thinking tasks by the early 2030s.
An AI system that can do nearly any thinking job a person can do can be recognized by a public test, agreed on in advance, before 2035.
AI agents will complete multi-day software and research projects with little human supervision at the largest technology companies.
Employers will cut hiring for entry-level analyst, paralegal and junior programmer roles as AI agents take on that work.
Growth in U.S. output per worker will run well above its 2010s average as AI systems do a large share of office work.
AI systems will do most of the experimental design and data analysis behind new findings in fields such as chemistry and biology.
Artificial general intelligence, meaning an AI that can do nearly any thinking job a person can, will exist before the end of 2028.
AI systems that outperform the best human experts in nearly every field of thinking work will exist before 2035.
AI systems that can do most computer-based office tasks as well as a typical worker will exist before 2040.
Artificial general intelligence, meaning an AI that can do nearly any thinking job a person can, will be built sometime this century.
Astronauts will land on the Moon again before the end of 2028.
bottom_line: The rocket and capsule have now carried four astronauts around the Moon, so the question rests mostly on whether SpaceX's Starship lander can prove orbital refueling, which no spacecraft had done at that scale as of September 2026, and an uncrewed lunar landing, now set for 2027. NASA still targets 2028, but every crewed landing date it has announced since 2019 has slipped, and China's own goal is a landing before 2030, so no other nation is likely to fill the gap by the end of 2028.
hook: When the Artemis II crew swung around the Moon in April 2026 they traveled 252,756 miles from Earth, farther than any humans before them, yet no one has stood on the Moon since December 1972.
question: Will astronauts from any nation set foot on the Moon before the end of 2028?
ask: Add a dated, sourced row each time SpaceX's propellant transfer or uncrewed landing demonstration happens or slips, since those two milestones decide this question more than anything else.

text: NASA's Artemis II mission flew four astronauts around the Moon and brought them home safely in April 2026, so the SLS rocket and Orion capsule that would carry a landing crew to lunar orbit are already flight-proven with people aboard.
bottom_line: Strong weight: the government-built half of a landing works with crew aboard, which removes a whole class of possible delays, though the hardest piece (the lander) was never part of that flight.

text: NASA's February 2026 decision to turn Artemis III into a 2027 docking test in low Earth orbit lets crews practice docking Orion with a commercial lander close to home before anyone tries it at the Moon.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: testing in Earth orbit lowers the risk of the landing mission, but it also adds one more flight that must go well and on time before a 2028 landing can fly.

text: The US government has made a 2028 Moon landing an explicit national goal, through Executive Order 14369 of December 18, 2025 and NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman's 2026 budget testimony, which generally protects a program's money and attention.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: political priority helps keep funding steady, but presidential deadlines cannot make untested hardware ready, as the 2024 date set in 2019 showed.

text: China's announced goal of landing astronauts on the Moon before 2030 gives US leaders of both parties a strong reason to fund and defend a 2028 American landing date.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: competition historically sped up Apollo, but China's own date is after 2028, so the pressure pushes toward landing first rather than landing by 2028 specifically.

text: NASA keeping two lander companies, SpaceX and Blue Origin, under contract means a delay at one company does not automatically stop a 2028 landing.
bottom_line: Low weight: Blue Origin's crewed lander was scheduled for later missions and its uncrewed pathfinder had not flown by late 2026, so in practice the 2028 date rides mostly on SpaceX's Starship.

text: Artemis II launched on April 1, 2026 and splashed down on April 11, 2026, carrying four astronauts around the far side of the Moon to 252,756 miles from Earth, farther than any humans had traveled before.
bottom_line: Strong for what it shows: the rocket and capsule work with crew; it says nothing directly about the lander.

text: Starship Flight 14 on September 28, 2026 reached orbit for the first time and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites at about 275 km, with controlled splashdowns of both the booster and the ship.
bottom_line: Moderate: reaching orbit is a needed step toward refueling and a lunar lander, but Flights 12 and 13 earlier in 2026 both lost their boosters on landing.

text: NASA states that it continues to target the first Artemis lunar landing for 2028, a date it says has remained consistent since mid-2025.
bottom_line: Low to moderate: the agency's own target is informative, but NASA's earlier targets were stated just as firmly before they slipped.

text: SpaceX will complete a successful ship-to-ship propellant transfer between two Starships in Earth orbit by June 30, 2027.
An uncrewed Human Landing System lander will touch down intact on the Moon by December 31, 2027.
SpaceX moves enough propellant between two Starships in orbit on its first attempt for NASA to declare the refueling demonstration complete in early 2027.
The Artemis III docking test in low Earth orbit flies in 2027 on schedule and NASA reports that Orion docked with a commercial lander without major problems.
The earlier slips in the Artemis landing date came mostly from early design and rocket problems that the successful 2026 Artemis II flight has now put behind the program.
SpaceX's practice of flying, breaking and fixing Starship quickly can compress the remaining lander work (orbital refueling, an uncrewed lunar landing) into roughly two years.
NASA will shrink or simplify the first landing mission, for example with a shorter stay on the surface, rather than let the date slip past 2028.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman posted a schedule on X on March 3, 2026 listing "Early 2028: Artemis IV lunar landing" and "Late 2028: Artemis V lunar landing," committing NASA publicly to two crewed Moon landings in 2028.
President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14369, "Ensuring American Space Superiority," in December 2025, setting the return of American astronauts to the Moon by 2028 as a national goal.
Reentry: SpaceX, Elon Musk, and the Reusable Rockets that Launched a Second Space Age, Eric Berger, 2024
bridge: Berger documents how SpaceX's build, fly, break and fix approach brought the Falcon 9 and early Starship to flight faster than traditional aerospace programs, which is the main reason to expect the Starship lunar lander to close its remaining gaps in time for 2028.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a well-sourced history of SpaceX's speed, but it was written before orbital refueling was attempted and cannot show that the hardest remaining step will go as quickly.

text: Executive Order 14369, "Ensuring American Space Superiority," The White House, December 2025
bridge: The order makes a return of American astronauts to the Moon by 2028 a stated national goal, which shows the political backing a 2028 landing has from the top of the US government.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight: it shows priority and likely funding, but an order cannot finish hardware, as the 2024 landing date set in 2019 showed.

text: Every crewed Artemis landing date NASA has announced since 2019 (2024, then 2025, then September 2026, then mid-2027) has slipped, so a 2028 landing date is more likely than not to slip as well.
bottom_line: Strong weight: a program's own record is generally the best guide to its next deadline, though Artemis II flying in 2026 shows the program does eventually deliver.

text: SpaceX's Starship lander must be refueled in Earth orbit by ship-to-ship transfer of super-cold propellant, a feat no spacecraft had done at that scale as of September 2026, before it can carry astronauts to the Moon.
bottom_line: Strong weight: orbital refueling is the single biggest unproven step on the path, and every month it waits pushes the rest of the sequence closer to the 2028 deadline.

text: NASA moved SpaceX's uncrewed Starship lunar landing demonstration from 2025 to 2027, which leaves little room to find and fix a failure before a crewed landing in 2028.
bottom_line: Strong weight: a crewed landing generally follows a successful uncrewed one, so any failure in a 2027 demonstration could easily push the crewed landing past 2028.

text: China is unlikely to land astronauts on the Moon by the end of 2028, because its Long March 10 rocket, Mengzhou capsule and Lanyue lander had not flown a full mission by 2026 and China's stated target is before 2030.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it removes the only realistic backup for the belief coming true, since the resolution counts a landing by any nation, though China has generally met its space dates.

text: The first Artemis landing near the lunar south pole needs several systems that have never flown with crew (a commercial lander, new Axiom Space moonwalking suits and a new landing region) to all be ready at once, and any one of them can hold up the mission.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: projects that depend on many new parts arriving together generally slip to the pace of the slowest one, though NASA can sometimes trim the mission to fit.

text: After the Columbia accident, NASA's safety culture leads its managers to delay a crewed flight rather than launch with unresolved risks, so a political 2028 deadline is unlikely to override safety reviews.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: NASA did hold Artemis II for heat-shield analysis before it flew, which shows dates bend to safety findings rather than the other way around.

text: As of September 2023, NASA's Human Landing System program had delayed 8 of its 13 key events by at least six months, and its planned development schedule was 13 months shorter than the average NASA major project.
bottom_line: Strong: an independent audit found the lander schedule was both slipping and unusually compressed, a pattern that generally predicts further delay.

text: SpaceX's uncrewed Starship lunar landing demonstration, expected in 2025 as of January 2024, was moved to 2027 in NASA's March 3, 2026 update, and the orbital propellant transfer demonstration had not flown as of September 2026.
bottom_line: Strong: the two milestones that must come before a crewed landing were both still undone with about two years left.

text: NASA will announce by December 31, 2027 that the first Artemis crewed landing is no earlier than 2029.
No ship-to-ship propellant transfer between two Starships in orbit will have been completed by December 31, 2027.
The uncrewed Starship lunar landing demonstration fails or slips into 2028, leaving no time to repeat it before a 2028 crewed landing.
NASA's Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel or Inspector General reports that the lander, spacesuits or SLS core stage for Artemis IV cannot be ready before 2029.
A space program's own record of missed dates predicts its next deadline better than its current official schedule does.
Moving super-cold propellant from ship to ship in orbit at the scale a Starship lander needs is a genuinely new engineering problem that cannot be rushed by money or political pressure.
NASA Artemis Programs: Crewed Moon Landing Faces Multiple Challenges, U.S. Government Accountability Office, GAO-24-106256, November 2023
bridge: GAO found the lander program planned to finish development in 79 months, 13 months faster than the average NASA major project, that 8 of 13 key lander milestones had slipped by at least six months, and that SpaceX's progress on in-orbit propellant storage and transfer had been limited.
bottom_line: Strong weight: an independent audit whose warning that the landing would slip past its then-official date proved correct, though its numbers predate two years of Starship flight tests.

text: "Acting NASA chief says 2024 Moon landing no longer a 'realistic' target," Eric Berger, 2021
bridge: The article records NASA's own leadership conceding in February 2021 that a politically set landing date could not be met, the first of several public slips in the Artemis landing date.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight: it documents the pattern of slipping dates well, but one past slip says only so much about a 2028 date set with more hardware already flown.

text: Planetary scientists need fresh rock and ice samples collected by people from the lunar south pole
measured_by: Kilograms of human-collected lunar south-pole samples in NASA's curation labs
if_true: Rises from zero by 2029
if_false: Stays at zero until a later landing
bottom_line: A real need, though robotic missions can return some samples on their own.

text: US national security officials need American astronauts to reach the lunar south pole before Chinese astronauts do
measured_by: Gap in years between the first US crewed south-pole landing and China's first crewed landing
if_true: A US lead of about one to two years
if_false: The lead shrinks or China lands first
bottom_line: A widely shared priority in Washington, though the value of being first is debated.

text: Space scientists who run NASA's robotic missions need their budgets protected from being drained to hold a landing date
measured_by: NASA science mission funding in dollars a year
if_true: Under pressure while money flows to the landing
if_false: Less pressure from a landing sprint
bottom_line: A real tradeoff, though Congress sets the split and has often protected science.

text: A US landing in 2028 would put American astronauts on the lunar south pole about one to two years before China's target of a crewed landing before 2030.
bottom_line: Moderate: the lead matters for setting norms and site choices near the south pole, but China has not committed to a date earlier than 2030.

text: A 2028 landing would return the first human-collected samples from the lunar south pole, a region no Apollo crew visited.
bottom_line: Moderate: the science value is real, but the sample mass of a first two-person landing has not been published, so no figure is given.

text: A landing by 2028 would show results for Artemis spending that the NASA Inspector General estimated at about $93 billion through 2025.
bottom_line: Moderate: one landing does not repay the cost, but it turns spending into the outcome it was approved for.

text: Pressure to meet a political 2028 deadline could push managers to accept risks, as the Columbia Accident Investigation Board found schedule pressure did before the 2003 shuttle loss.
bottom_line: Moderate: the risk is documented in NASA's history, but it cannot be counted in advance, so no figure is given.

text: Concentrating NASA's budget on a 2028 landing can squeeze money for robotic science missions that have nothing to do with the Moon.
bottom_line: Moderate: the tradeoff is real in a fixed budget, but how much moves depends on yearly appropriations, so no figure is given.

text: The date SpaceX completes a ship-to-ship propellant transfer demonstration in Earth orbit is a fair measure of whether the Starship lander can be ready for a 2028 crewed landing.
Whether an uncrewed lander touches down intact on the Moon in a NASA-required demonstration by the end of 2027 is a fair measure of whether a crewed landing in 2028 is on track.
SpaceX's Starship lander or Blue Origin's Blue Moon lander will complete orbital refueling and an uncrewed lunar landing demonstration early enough to carry a crew to the Moon before the end of 2028.
NASA's Artemis III docking test in low Earth orbit, planned for 2027, will go well enough that Artemis IV can attempt a landing without first repeating the test.
A crewed Artemis IV landing in 2028 would make Congress much more likely to fully fund Artemis V and later landings in the following NASA budget.
The first rock and ice samples collected by people near the lunar south pole would arrive in NASA's curation labs within weeks of a 2028 landing.

An American landing at the lunar south pole before China's would give the United States and its Artemis Accords partners the stronger hand in setting the working rules for mining water ice on the Moon.
NASA's Artemis IV mission will land astronauts on the Moon in the first half of 2028, as NASA scheduled in March 2026.
NASA will land astronauts on the Moon twice before the end of 2028, on both Artemis IV and Artemis V.
Astronauts from some nation will land on the Moon again before the end of 2030.
NASA will launch a crewed Artemis mission meant to land on the Moon before the end of 2028, even if the landing itself happens later.
People will land on Mars before 2040.
bottom_line: The hardware is further along than ever (Starship has flown fourteen times and Artemis II carried four people around the Moon in April 2026), but the company most committed to Mars announced a delay of about five to seven years in February 2026, no government has funded a crewed landing, and only about five launch windows remain. The real fight is whether a private company's pace can break the long pattern of Mars dates slipping by a decade at a time.
hook: In February 2026, Elon Musk, the loudest champion of an early Mars landing, announced that SpaceX would delay its Mars plans by about five to seven years to build on the Moon first (ABC News and CNN, as cited by Wikipedia's "SpaceX Mars program").
question: Will any person set foot on Mars before January 1, 2040?
ask: The page most needs a sourced, independent estimate of whether a crew-capable lander can depart in the 2035 or 2037 launch window under SpaceX's revised schedule.

text: SpaceX's Starship, a fully reusable rocket designed to carry crew and cargo to Mars, has already flown fourteen integrated test flights, so the vehicle a Mars landing would need is being built and flown rather than only drawn.
bottom_line: Medium weight: real flight hardware is the strongest thing the optimistic side has, but test flights near Earth are a long way from landing people on Mars.

text: The Apollo program showed that a funded national effort can go from a presidential commitment in 1961 to people walking on another world in 1969, about eight years, which is less time than remains before 2040.
bottom_line: Medium weight: the precedent is real, but Apollo had a Cold War urgency and a budget priority that no Mars effort has today.

text: A crewed Moon base built in the late 2020s and early 2030s would test the landers, life support, refueling and surface operations that a Mars landing needs, so the 2026 shift of NASA and SpaceX toward the Moon can shorten the later path to Mars.
bottom_line: Medium weight: Moon experience generally transfers to Mars, but it also absorbs the money and attention that a Mars landing would need.

text: Even after SpaceX's February 2026 delay of about five to seven years, the company's earlier plan of crewed Mars flights around 2030 still points to a crewed attempt in the mid to late 2030s, before 2040.
bottom_line: Low to medium weight: the arithmetic works only if the new schedule holds better than every earlier schedule did.

text: Reusable rockets have cut the cost of reaching orbit enough that a private company can now pay for much of a Mars landing itself, so the landing no longer waits on a single government budget.
bottom_line: Medium weight: private money removes one old bottleneck, but the company has shown it will move its money to nearer goals.

text: Starship flew 14 integrated test flights between April 20, 2023 and September 28, 2026, nine of them counted as successes, and its booster was caught by the launch tower for the first time on October 13, 2024.
bottom_line: Shows a crew-scale Mars vehicle exists and is improving, but says nothing directly about landing it on Mars.

text: Artemis II carried four astronauts around the Moon from April 1 to April 11, 2026, reaching 252,756 miles from Earth, farther than any people had traveled before.
bottom_line: Confirms deep-space crew flight has resumed after more than 50 years, a needed step but a small fraction of a Mars round trip.

text: About eight years passed between President Kennedy's May 1961 call to land a man on the Moon and the Apollo 11 landing in July 1969.
bottom_line: Proves a crash program can land people on another world within a decade, but it is one case under unusual political conditions.

text: NASA states that it is working to send astronauts to Mars "as early as the 2030s" and illustrates its plan with a round-trip Mars mission in 2039.
bottom_line: Shows the agency still aims inside the window, but an aim stated without a funded program is weak evidence of an outcome.

text: SpaceX or another operator will complete a ship-to-ship propellant transfer in Earth orbit before the end of 2028.
At least one uncrewed crew-scale spacecraft, such as Starship, will land intact on Mars before the end of 2031.
An uncrewed Starship lands intact on Mars during the 2028-29 launch window and sends back surface data.
Congress passes a multiyear appropriation that funds a crewed Mars landing mission with a target date in the 2030s.

Elon Musk wrote in September 2024 that SpaceX planned to send its first uncrewed Starships to Mars in the 2026 launch window and to follow with crewed flights about two years later if those landed safely.
The Case for Mars: The Plan to Settle the Red Planet and Why We Must, Robert Zubrin with Richard Wagner, 1996
bridge: Zubrin's Mars Direct plan argues that people can reach Mars with rockets close to existing technology by making return fuel from the Martian air, which makes a landing an engineering and funding problem rather than a matter of waiting for new science.
bottom_line: Medium weight: the plan is detailed and influential, but its own hopeful timelines from the 1990s were never funded, which is itself a warning about Mars dates.

text: Making Humans a Multi-Planetary Species, Elon Musk, 2017
bridge: Musk lays out the SpaceX design for a fully reusable ship refueled in Earth orbit and on Mars, the same plan Starship is now being flown to test.
bottom_line: Medium weight: it is the clearest public account of the vehicle most likely to land people on Mars early, written by the person with the strongest motive to be optimistic.

text: Moon to Mars Architecture Definition Document (ESDMD-001), NASA Exploration Systems Development Mission Directorate, 2023
bridge: NASA's architecture treats lunar missions as a proving ground for the landers, habitats and life support a crewed Mars mission will need, which supports the claim that Moon work can shorten the path to Mars.
bottom_line: Low to medium weight: it shows an official plan that ends at Mars, but it is a framework without a dated, funded Mars landing.

text: Elon Musk's dates for people on Mars have slipped every time they came due, from a crew launch he called likely for 2024 in 2016, to no earlier than 2029 in 2022, to a further delay of about five to seven years announced in February 2026.
bottom_line: High weight: the person and company most committed to an early landing have the longest documented record of missing their own Mars dates.

text: A crewed Mars landing needs large ship-to-ship refueling in orbit, a crew-scale landing on Mars, life support for a round trip lasting years, and a launch back off the Martian surface, and none of these has yet been demonstrated.
bottom_line: High weight: each step is a first, and history generally shows that firsts take longer than planned.

text: No government has funded a crewed Mars landing program, and NASA's own public goal is to send astronauts to Mars only "as early as the 2030s."
bottom_line: High weight: a goal stated with "as early as" and no program budget is the kind of target that usually slips.

text: Because launch windows to Mars open only about every 26 months, a crew must leave Earth by roughly the 2037 window to land before 2040, so only about five chances remain and each slip costs more than two years.
bottom_line: High weight: the calendar is fixed by orbital mechanics, which leaves almost no room for the ordinary delays of a first-of-its-kind mission.

text: SpaceX's February 2026 decision to focus on a Moon base shows that contracts and nearer-term revenue, not Mars, set the company's schedule, so Mars is likely to keep yielding to closer goals.
bottom_line: Medium weight: one pivot is a strong signal of priorities, though a company can pivot back once the Moon work is done.

text: SpaceX's public Mars dates have moved repeatedly: a crew launch "probably in 2024" (June 2016), crewed flight no earlier than 2029 (March 2022), a 50 percent chance of uncrewed flights in the 2026 window (May 2025), and a delay of "about five to seven years" to focus on the Moon (February 9, 2026).
bottom_line: Strong evidence: four documented schedule statements, each later pushed back, from the most optimistic actor in the field.

text: An independent study for NASA found that a crewed Mars orbital mission in 2033 was not feasible under any budget scenario it examined, and that 2037 was the earliest feasible date for an orbital mission, with a landing coming later.
bottom_line: Strong for NASA-led paths, since it puts even an orbit near the edge of the window, though it predates Starship's flight record and did not model a SpaceX-led mission.

text: The radiation detector aboard the Curiosity rover measured an average of about 1.84 millisieverts per day during its cruise to Mars, which implies about 662 millisieverts for a 360-day round trip before any time on the surface.
bottom_line: A solid measurement of a real health cost; it slows a landing through safety rules rather than making one impossible.

text: As of late September 2026, Starship had reached orbit only on its fourteenth flight test, and no ship-to-ship transfer of propellant in orbit, which a Mars mission requires, had been reported.
bottom_line: Shows the vehicle is still several hard firsts away from a Mars-capable configuration with about five launch windows left.

text: No government or company will have named a crew and a launch date for a Mars landing mission departing before 2038 by the end of 2034.
SpaceX announces that its first crewed Mars flight will not launch before the 2040s.
NASA health studies conclude that radiation and other risks of a Mars round trip exceed its astronaut career limits with no practical shielding or mission design that fixes the problem in the 2030s.
A first-of-its-kind crewed Mars mission will slip the way earlier Mars dates from SpaceX and NASA have slipped.
A Moon base in the late 2020s and 2030s will absorb the money and engineering talent a Mars landing would need, rather than freeing them up.
Radiation limits and the lack of proven long-duration life support will keep agencies and companies from sending crews until well after the 2037 launch window.
Measurements of Energetic Particle Radiation in Transit to Mars on the Mars Science Laboratory, Cary Zeitlin et al., 2013
bridge: Radiation measured inside the Curiosity rover's capsule on its way to Mars implies a dose of about 662 millisieverts for a round trip's travel alone, near or above the career limits space agencies set for astronauts.
bottom_line: Medium weight: the measurement is solid, but radiation slows a landing through rules and shielding rather than making one impossible.

text: A City on Mars: Can We Settle Space, Should We Settle Space, and Have We Really Thought This Through?, Kelly Weinersmith and Zach Weinersmith, 2023
bridge: The book documents how little is known about keeping people healthy and supplied far from Earth, problems a first landing must also solve in smaller form.
bottom_line: Low to medium weight: its case is mainly against fast settlement, not against a single landing, so it bears on this belief only indirectly.

text: Planetary scientists need people on Mars to search for signs of past life faster than robotic rovers can
measured_by: Number of Martian sites sampled and samples returned per year
if_true: Rises sharply in the late 2030s as crews do fieldwork in person.
if_false: Stays at the slow pace of rovers and a robotic sample return.
bottom_line: A strong and widely shared interest, though robotic missions meet part of it at lower cost.

text: Aerospace workers in Texas, Florida and California need long-running Mars programs to keep their jobs funded
measured_by: Aerospace employment in Mars-related programs in those states
if_true: Holds steady or grows through the 2030s.
if_false: Shifts toward lunar, defense and satellite work instead of Mars hardware.
bottom_line: Real but not unique to Mars, since lunar and defense work also employs these workers.

text: Students considering engineering careers need a visible frontier goal that shows the work matters
measured_by: Engineering and physical science degree enrollments in the years around a landing
if_true: Likely ticks upward around a crewed landing in the 2030s.
if_false: Follows ordinary trends with no Mars-driven bump.
bottom_line: Plausible, but the size of any effect is uncertain.

text: Weather forecasters and farmers need NASA's Earth-observing satellites funded ahead of crewed Mars hardware
measured_by: Number and funding of Earth-observing satellite missions in NASA's budget
if_true: Could shrink if a government Mars push competes for the same budget.
if_false: Stays protected in a budget without a crewed Mars race.
bottom_line: A real competing claim on federal dollars, though Congress can fund both.

text: Geologists working on the Martian surface before 2040 could search for signs of past life far faster than rovers, which cover only a few miles a year.
bottom_line: A real scientific gain that most planetary scientists accept, though its size is hard to put a number on.

text: A crewed Mars landing program running through the 2030s would keep aerospace design and manufacturing jobs funded for more than a decade.
bottom_line: Likely real, but the same money spent elsewhere would also fund jobs, so the net gain is disputed.

text: A visible crewed landing before 2040 would draw more students into engineering and science degrees, as Apollo is often credited with doing.
bottom_line: Plausible and widely claimed, but the effect is hard to separate from other causes.

text: A crewed Mars landing program is likely to cost on the order of 500 billion dollars, money that taxpayers and investors could spend elsewhere.
bottom_line: A 2010 estimate (Taylor, The Scientific Exploration of Mars) that predates cheaper reusable rockets, so the true figure could be lower or higher.

text: Federal dollars spent racing to land crews on Mars before 2040 would compete with Earth-observing satellites that track weather, drought and climate.
bottom_line: A real trade-off in a fixed NASA budget, though private funding of a Mars landing would soften it.

text: A crewed spacecraft touching down on the surface of Mars with at least one living person aboard on or before December 31, 2039 (UTC) is a fair measure of whether people landed on Mars before 2040.
A successful uncrewed landing on Mars of a crew-scale vehicle, such as Starship, by the end of 2031 is a fair measure of whether the hardware is on pace for a crewed landing before 2040.
A demonstrated ship-to-ship transfer of propellant between two vehicles in Earth orbit by the end of 2028 is a fair measure of whether the refueling a Mars mission depends on is arriving in time.
Some government or company will commit enough money to a crewed Mars landing in the next decade to carry it from test flights to an actual crewed launch.
People will be allowed to fly on a Mars mission whose risks of death and radiation exposure are higher than current astronaut limits.
Launch pads, fuel plants and habitats left on Mars by the first landing would make later crewed trips cheaper and more frequent through the 2040s.
People will land on Mars before 2032.
A permanently occupied human base will exist on Mars before 2040.
People will land on Mars before 2050.
People will fly to Mars and orbit it, with or without landing, before 2040.
SpaceX Starship will fly a fully reusable flight, with both stages recovered and reflown, before the end of 2027.
bottom_line: The evidence is strong on what SpaceX has done (caught boosters three times, flown two of them again, and brought ships through reentry five flights running) and thin on the hard part: no Starship upper stage had been caught or flown twice as of October 2026, and booster catches have not yet been repeated on the new Block 3 design. The real question is whether the first ship catch, planned soon after Flight 15, works early enough to leave time to refurbish that ship and fly it on a reflown booster within about a year.
hook: After fourteen Starship test flights, SpaceX has caught a 230-foot Super Heavy booster with the arms of its launch tower three times, but it has never caught, or flown again, a single Starship upper stage (Wikipedia, "SpaceX Starship flight tests", October 2026).
question: Will SpaceX launch a Starship whose booster and upper stage have both flown before and been recovered, before the end of 2027?
ask: The page most needs a sourced account of how much refurbishment a Starship upper stage needs after reentry, from SpaceX, NASA or an independent engineering analysis.

text: SpaceX has already caught Super Heavy boosters with the launch tower's arms three times and flown two of those caught boosters again, so the first-stage half of a fully reused Starship flight has been shown to work.
bottom_line: Strong weight, because it is a matter of public flight record, but the booster is the easier half and the upper stage is the part that has never been recovered.

text: SpaceX took Falcon 9 from its first successful booster landing to its first reflight of a landed booster in about fifteen months, which suggests the company can turn a first recovery into a reflight well within the time left before the end of 2027.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the track record is real, but Falcon 9 never had to bring back an upper stage through orbital reentry heating.

text: Elon Musk said Starship Flight 15, set for no earlier than November 2026, would be the last flight before SpaceX tries to catch a Starship upper stage, which would leave roughly a year for a caught ship to be refurbished and flown again before the end of 2027.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a scheduled attempt is real progress, but Musk's own odds for the first catch were only 50 to 60 percent and SpaceX schedules have slipped before.

text: SpaceX builds Starship boosters and ships on an assembly line and now flies from a second tower at Starbase, so it can test catch and reflight attempts on several vehicles in parallel instead of waiting on one.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight: parallel hardware shortens the gap between attempts, but each attempt still needs a flight slot and, after any failure, a mishap review.

text: Super Heavy boosters were caught by the launch tower on Starship Flights 5 (October 13, 2024), 7 (January 16, 2025) and 8 (March 6, 2025), and the boosters caught on Flights 7 and 8 flew again on Flights 9 and 11.
bottom_line: Strong evidence that booster catch and reflight are possible, though both reflights were on the older Block 2 design.

text: Falcon 9's first successful booster landing came on December 21, 2015, and SpaceX first flew a landed booster again on March 30, 2017 (the SES-10 mission), about fifteen months later.
bottom_line: Moderate evidence by analogy: the same company has turned a first recovery into a reflight quickly before, but with a far easier stage to recover.

text: Starship upper stages made controlled ocean splashdowns on all five flights from Flight 10 (August 26, 2025) through Flight 14 (September 28, 2026), and Flight 14 was the first Starship flight to reach orbit.
bottom_line: Moderate evidence: five clean reentries in a row show the ship survives, but splashdown is not recovery and says little about how much repair a ship needs.

text: Starship upper stage S42, assigned to Flight 15, completed catch-related tests at the second Starbase launch tower on September 11 and 12, 2026.
bottom_line: Low to moderate evidence: ground tests show the catch hardware is being readied, not that a catch will work.

text: SpaceX catches or lands intact at least one Starship upper stage by June 30, 2027.
A Block 3 Super Heavy booster is caught by the launch tower and flies again before the end of 2027.
A Starship upper stage caught by the tower is shown to need only minor heat shield tile replacement before it is cleared to fly again.
SpaceX catches Block 3 Super Heavy boosters on several consecutive flights in late 2026 and early 2027.
SpaceX's past pace of turning a first recovery into a reflight, as it did with Falcon 9 boosters, is a fair guide to how fast it can turn a first Starship ship catch into a ship reflight.
The Starship heat shield problem can be solved by iterating on tiles and design over a handful of flights, rather than needing a fundamental redesign that takes years.
No serious accident, long mishap investigation, or regulatory hold will stop Starship flights for more than a few months between now and the end of 2027.
Reentry: SpaceX, Elon Musk, and the Reusable Rockets That Launched a Second Space Age, by Eric Berger (2024)
bridge: Berger traces how SpaceX went from a first Falcon 9 booster landing to routine booster reflights, the closest precedent for how fast the company turns a first recovery into regular reuse.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a well-reported history of booster reuse, but it covers a first stage that never faced orbital reentry heating, so it supports the booster half of the claim more than the ship half.

text: Liftoff: Elon Musk and the Desperate Early Days That Launched SpaceX, by Eric Berger (2021)
bridge: Berger documents how SpaceX reached orbit with Falcon 1 after three failures by testing, failing and iterating quickly, the same approach it is applying to Starship.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight: it shows the company's habit of recovering from failure, but a culture of iteration does not set a date for a specific milestone.

text: SpaceX's own forecasts for catching a Starship upper stage have already slipped by well over a year: in November 2024 Starbase general manager Kathy Lueders said the company hoped to catch a ship within six months, and as of October 2026 no ship has been caught.
bottom_line: Strong weight: it is the company's own stated timeline, measured against the record, and it shows how much ship recovery has resisted schedules.

text: No Super Heavy booster has been caught since Starship Flight 8 in March 2025, and the new Block 3 boosters failed their Gulf of Mexico landings on Flights 12 and 13, so even the booster half of full reuse has not been reliable on the current vehicle design.
bottom_line: Strong weight: a fully reused flight needs a caught Block 3 booster as well as a caught ship, and that has not been shown on the vehicle that will fly in 2027.

text: A Starship upper stage has to come through orbital reentry with its heat shield intact enough to fly again with little repair, and every ship flown so far has been recovered only from the ocean, if at all, so no one has yet shown that a ship can be refurbished quickly.
bottom_line: Moderate to strong weight: the heat shield is the hardest unsolved part of full reuse, and the Space Shuttle showed that a reusable orbiter can need long, costly work between flights.

text: Starship has flown roughly every two months in 2026, so the time left after a first ship catch attempt in late 2026 or early 2027 allows only a handful of flights to catch a ship, inspect it, and launch it again on a booster that has also flown.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it is arithmetic on the current flight rate, which could rise, but any failure and the mishap review that follows eats directly into that thin margin.

text: In November 2024 Starbase general manager Kathy Lueders said SpaceX hoped to catch a Starship upper stage within the next six months, and that catch did not occur; as of the Flight 14 launch on September 28, 2026, no Starship upper stage had been caught or flown a second time.
bottom_line: Strong evidence that ship recovery runs behind SpaceX's own schedules.

text: The first four Block 2 Starship upper stages were all lost in 2025, and Starship did not reach orbit until its fourteenth flight test.
bottom_line: Moderate evidence: a new vehicle version has needed many flights to work at all, and the ships flying in 2027 are still being revised.

text: Each Space Shuttle orbiter was designed for 100 launches or ten years of service, yet the whole fleet flew 135 missions in thirty years at a cost of about $450 million per launch in 2011.
bottom_line: Low to moderate evidence by analogy: it shows that recovering an orbital vehicle is not the same as flying it again quickly, though Starship's design and economics differ sharply.

text: Every Starship launch in 2027 uses a new, never-flown upper stage.
The first Starship upper stage catch attempt fails and destroys or badly damages the second Starbase launch tower, halting flights for months.
Inspection of a recovered Starship upper stage shows its heat shield or engine bay needs a near-rebuild before it could fly again.
Dates that SpaceX and Elon Musk give for Starship milestones are aspirational targets that have usually slipped, so a late-2027 deadline should be read against that record.
Recovering and reflying an orbital upper stage is a categorically harder problem than recovering a booster, as the Space Shuttle's costly orbiter turnarounds showed.
SpaceX's flight schedule through 2027 will be set mainly by its NASA lunar lander milestones and Starlink launches, not by a goal of proving ship reflight by a calendar date.
