Sean Duffy, as acting NASA administrator in October 2025, said publicly that SpaceX had fallen behind schedule on its Starship lunar lander and that NASA would open the Artemis III landing contract to competing companies, a public judgment that Starship's timelines were slipping.
NASA Artemis Programs: Crewed Moon Landing Faces Multiple Challenges, by the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO-24-106256, 2023)
bridge: The GAO found that SpaceX's Starship lunar lander had missed or delayed planned milestones and that its plan depends on refueling in orbit, a capability not yet shown, which suggests Starship's flight schedule will be spent on NASA milestones first.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: an independent audit of the program's schedule, though it predates the 2025 and 2026 flight campaign and does not address ship reflight directly.

text: Satellite companies and research groups need cheaper rides to orbit
measured_by: Published price per kilogram to low Earth orbit on Starship and competing rockets
if_true: Prices for heavy launches fall sharply from 2028 on as reused Starships enter service.
if_false: Prices stay near Falcon 9 levels and heavy payloads keep waiting for scarce launches.
bottom_line: The broadest interest served by full reuse, and the one with the clearest way to measure it.

text: NASA's Artemis astronauts and mission teams need a working lunar lander on schedule
measured_by: Dates of NASA's Starship lander milestones (propellant transfer test, uncrewed lunar landing demonstration) against the published plan
if_true: Refueling and lander demonstrations stay close to their 2027 dates because tanker flights are affordable.
if_false: Lander milestones slip as each refueling campaign needs many new, expended vehicles.
bottom_line: Central to the U.S. Moon program, though NASA's plans hinge on refueling more than on reuse by a fixed date.

text: Space industry workers in South Texas and Florida need steady launch work
measured_by: Starship flights per year from Starbase and Florida, and SpaceX employment at those sites
if_true: Flight counts and site employment rise through 2027 and 2028.
if_false: Flights come in bursts between long stand-downs, and hiring is uneven.
bottom_line: Real and local, but tied to Starship flying at all more than to full reuse by 2027.

text: Astronomers need dark skies free of satellite streaks
measured_by: Share of wide-field telescope images crossed by satellite streaks, as reported by observatories
if_true: The share climbs as cheap reused Starships launch large Starlink satellites in bulk.
if_false: The share grows more slowly while Starship launches stay expensive and less frequent.
bottom_line: A well-documented concern that rises with any increase in launch rate.

text: Workers on NASA's Space Launch System rocket need their program to keep flying
measured_by: Space Launch System funding in NASA's annual budget and the number of SLS flights on NASA's manifest
if_true: Pressure to cancel or cut the Space Launch System grows as a cheap reusable alternative becomes real.
if_false: The Space Launch System keeps its place as NASA's heavy rocket for crewed Moon flights.
bottom_line: A narrow but politically powerful interest whose stake runs directly against Starship's success.

text: Flying both Starship stages again would make the many tanker flights needed to refuel a lunar lander in orbit affordable, keeping NASA's Moon landing plans on track.
bottom_line: Important, because the lander depends on refueling, though NASA's schedule also depends on many things besides reuse.

text: A steady Starship reflight schedule would keep work going at Starbase in South Texas and at SpaceX's Florida launch sites.
bottom_line: Real but modest, since SpaceX builds and flies Starship whether or not full reuse arrives by 2027.

text: Full Starship reuse would make it cheap to launch many more large Starlink satellites, adding bright objects that streak through telescope images.
bottom_line: A real cost that grows with launch rate, though it follows from Starship flying often, not from reuse alone.

text: A faster Starship launch and catch schedule at Starbase would mean more road and beach closures, noise and sonic booms for people living near Boca Chica, Texas.
bottom_line: Concrete and local; its size depends on how many flights regulators allow.

text: A cheap, fully reusable Starship would weaken the case for NASA's expendable Space Launch System, which costs far more per flight, putting that program's contracts at risk.
bottom_line: A real cost to a specific group, though whether it is a cost to taxpayers is exactly what is disputed.

text: A single Starship launch, lifting off on or before December 31, 2027 (UTC), in which both the Super Heavy booster and the Starship upper stage had each flown to space before and been recovered intact (caught or landed, not fished from the sea), is a fair measure of whether SpaceX Starship flew a fully reusable flight before the end of 2027.
The number of Starship upper stages caught or landed intact by June 30, 2027 is a fair measure of whether ship reuse is on pace for a reflight in 2027.
The number of days between a Super Heavy booster's recovery and its next flight is a fair measure of how quickly SpaceX can turn Starship hardware around.
SpaceX can recover a Block 3 Super Heavy booster intact and fly it again before the end of 2027.
A Starship upper stage can come back from orbit, be caught or landed intact, and be made ready to fly again with limited repair before the end of 2027.
SpaceX will choose to spend at least one 2027 launch on a flight that pairs a reflown booster with a reflown ship, rather than using only new vehicles for its NASA and Starlink missions.

If Starship flies both stages again by the end of 2027, SpaceX will be able to fly the many tanker flights its lunar lander needs for orbital refueling at a lower cost per flight, keeping NASA's 2027 refueling and lander demonstrations closer to schedule.
If Starship flies both stages again by the end of 2027, SpaceX will begin offering Starship launches to outside satellite customers at prices below what an expendable heavy rocket can charge.

If Starship becomes fully reusable by the end of 2027, the price of sending a kilogram to low Earth orbit will fall far below Falcon 9 prices over the following decade, making very large satellites and space stations affordable to build.

If Starship becomes fully reusable by the end of 2027, competing launch companies in the United States, China and Europe will shift their programs toward fully reusable rockets within a decade or lose most heavy-launch business to SpaceX.
SpaceX will fly the same Starship upper stage at least three times before the end of 2027.
SpaceX will fly a reflown Starship upper stage within one month of its previous flight before the end of 2027.
SpaceX will catch a Starship upper stage intact with its launch tower before the end of 2027.
SpaceX Starship will fly a fully reusable flight, with both stages recovered and reflown, before the end of 2030.
The World Health Organization will declare another public health emergency of international concern before the end of 2028.
bottom_line: The WHO's record gives about a two-in-three chance of a new declaration in a window this long, and five declarations since 2019 lean higher. The record also has gaps of three to five years. The open question is whether a new threat emerges separate from the Ebola and polio emergencies already in force, and whether a WHO without U.S. funding, under a Director-General chosen in 2027, chooses to declare it.
hook: Less than five months after the WHO declared it a global emergency in May 2026, the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in Congo, which Doctors Without Borders called the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record, had passed 9,000 confirmed cases, and even that does not count toward this question.
question: Will the World Health Organization declare a new public health emergency of international concern, separate from the polio and Ebola emergencies already in force, between October 10, 2026 and the end of 2028?
ask: The page most needs a published probability from a forecasting platform or modeling group for a new WHO emergency declaration by 2028, with its method, to set beside the simple base rate here.

text: The World Health Organization has declared nine public health emergencies of international concern since April 2009, about one every 1.9 years, so a window running from October 2026 to the end of 2028 would usually contain at least one new declaration.
bottom_line: The strongest reason on the page, because it rests on the WHO's own record, though nine events is a small sample and the rate has been lumpy.

text: The pace of WHO emergency declarations has picked up, with five of the nine declared since July 2019 (Kivu Ebola, COVID-19, mpox twice, and Bundibugyo Ebola).
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a recent cluster suggests a rate above the long-run average, but five events in seven years can also be chance.

text: Outbreaks of animal-borne diseases in people have been growing more frequent for decades, which keeps feeding the WHO new candidates for an emergency declaration.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the long-term rise is documented, but part of it reflects better reporting, and most outbreaks never come close to a global emergency.

text: H5N1 bird flu now circulates in dozens of mammal species, including United States dairy cattle, and the International Health Regulations require countries to report every human case of a new influenza subtype to the WHO.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: H5N1 is the most-watched pandemic candidate, but it has not spread steadily between people in more than two decades of human cases.

text: WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has shown he is willing to declare, including declaring mpox a global emergency in July 2022 when his own emergency committee could not reach consensus.
bottom_line: Moderate weight for most of the window, but it fades after August 2027, when his second term ends and a successor takes over.

text: Mpox has already been declared a global emergency twice, in 2022 and 2024, showing that a disease whose emergency has ended can return and qualify for a new declaration.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight: it shows repeat declarations happen, but it does not show that mpox or any other disease will flare again by 2028.

text: The WHO declared nine public health emergencies of international concern between April 26, 2009 and May 17, 2026 (H1N1, polio, West African Ebola, Zika, Kivu Ebola, COVID-19, mpox in 2022, mpox in 2024, Bundibugyo Ebola), a rate that, if held constant, gives roughly a 65 to 69 percent chance of at least one new declaration in the 26.7 months from October 10, 2026 to December 31, 2028.
bottom_line: Good evidence for the starting estimate, with the caveat that a constant rate is an assumption and nine events give a wide margin of error.

text: A study of 12,102 outbreaks of 215 human infectious diseases in 219 nations from 1980 to 2013 found that the number of outbreaks and the number of distinct diseases causing them rose significantly, even after controlling for surveillance and communications, and that zoonoses made up 65 percent of the diseases.
bottom_line: Solid evidence that the pool of possible emergencies is growing, though the data end in 2013 and count outbreaks of every size.

text: A statistical study of epidemics over four centuries estimated that an epidemic as intense as COVID-19 recurs about every 129 years at present rates, and that the rate of new disease emergence could raise the yearly probability of extreme epidemics up to threefold in coming decades.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it supports a rising risk of severe epidemics, but most PHEICs are far below COVID-19 in scale, so it bears only indirectly on the next declaration.

text: The WHO counted 993 confirmed human H5N1 cases and 477 deaths from 2003 to December 2025, and the current clade 2.3.4.4b virus has become established in United States dairy cattle and has infected at least 43 mammal species.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it shows a high-fatality virus with wide animal spread, which is the setup for a declaration, but not the human spread that would trigger one.

text: WHO confirms a cluster of human-to-human transmission of H5N1 or another novel influenza A virus before the end of 2027.
A new clade of mpox or another pathogen spreads across several countries within months, as clade Ib mpox did when it reached four new countries in a single month in 2024.
The pace of WHO emergency declarations since 2009 is a fair guide to the pace between October 2026 and the end of 2028.
The WHO Director-General who takes office in August 2027 will set roughly the same bar for declaring a public health emergency of international concern as the Directors-General before.
Funding and staff cuts at the WHO will not stop it from detecting and assessing a dangerous new outbreak in time to declare.

Michael Osterholm, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota, argued in his 2017 book Deadliest Enemy, written with Mark Olshaker, that a severe influenza pandemic is coming and that the world is not prepared for it.
Global trends in emerging infectious diseases (Kate E. Jones, Nikkita G. Patel, Marc A. Levy, Adam Storeygard, Deborah Balk, John L. Gittleman and Peter Daszak, 2008)
bridge: The study counted emerging infectious disease events from 1940 to 2004, found that they rose over time even after allowing for more reporting, and found that most came from animals, which is the supply of candidates a WHO emergency declaration draws on.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a widely cited baseline for the rise in new outbreaks, but its data end in 2004 and it measures outbreaks, not WHO declarations.

text: Intensity and frequency of extreme novel epidemics (Marco Marani, Gabriel G. Katul, William K. Pan and Anthony J. Parolari, 2021)
where_found: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
bridge: The authors used centuries of outbreak records to estimate how often very deadly new epidemics occur and concluded that such events are not rare over a lifetime and that the rate of new disease emergence may be rising.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it supports a steady supply of serious outbreaks, though it says nothing about whether the WHO will formally declare any of them in a 26-month window.

text: Spillover: Animal Infections and the Next Human Pandemic (David Quammen, 2012)
bridge: Quammen explains, through case after case from Hendra to HIV, how viruses jump from animals to people and why the conditions for such jumps keep growing.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight: clear and well reported for general readers, but it is a narrative, not a forecast or a count.

text: A public health emergency of international concern is a judgment call by the WHO Director-General, not an automatic result, and WHO emergency committees have advised against declaring for serious events such as MERS and the 2016 yellow fever outbreak.
bottom_line: Strong weight: of the first nine events that got an emergency committee, three ended with no declaration, so a dangerous outbreak does not guarantee one.

text: The window from October 10, 2026 to December 31, 2028 is only about 26.7 months, and three of the eight gaps between past WHO emergency declarations ran longer than that.
bottom_line: Strong weight: it is the honest flip side of the base rate, since stretches of three to five years with no new declaration have happened before.

text: The Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in Congo and Uganda and the polio emergency are already under declaration, so their spread to new countries cannot count as another public health emergency of international concern.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the outbreak now drawing the most attention is ruled out by the resolution rule, so the belief needs a separate threat to emerge and be declared.

text: The World Health Organization lost its largest funder when the United States withdrawal took effect on January 22, 2026, and a cash-strapped agency already running an Ebola emergency may be slower to take on another.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight: a declaration itself costs little, but staff cuts can delay the detection and assessment that come before one.

text: Political backlash after COVID-19, including the United States leaving the WHO and rejecting the 2024 amendments to the International Health Regulations, has raised the political cost to the WHO of declaring a new global emergency.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight: the backlash is real, but the WHO declared mpox in 2024 and Ebola in 2026 despite it.

text: A new WHO Director-General takes office in August 2027, when Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus's second term ends, and a successor elected amid funding and political pressure may set a higher bar for emergency declarations.
bottom_line: Low weight: it is a guess about a person not yet chosen, and it affects only the last 17 months of the window.

text: Of the nine events for which WHO convened an IHR Emergency Committee through early 2020, six were declared public health emergencies of international concern and three (MERS-CoV, yellow fever in 2016, and the 2018 Equateur Ebola outbreak in Congo) were not, and the review found the criteria were often vague and applied inconsistently.
bottom_line: Strong weight: even a dangerous event that reaches a committee has failed a third of the time, so the path from outbreak to declaration is far from certain.

text: Three of the eight gaps between consecutive WHO emergency declarations since 2009 lasted longer than 26.7 months: about 60 months from H1N1 (April 2009) to polio (May 2014), about 41 months from Zika (February 2016) to Kivu Ebola (July 2019), and about 30 months from COVID-19 (January 2020) to mpox (July 2022).
bottom_line: Good evidence that a window the length of this one can pass with nothing declared; it argues for a probability well short of certain.

text: Across 993 confirmed human H5N1 cases reported since 2003, no sustained human-to-human transmission has been documented, and reported human cases fell from 81 in 2024 to 30 in 2025.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the most-feared candidate has not shown the behavior that would force a declaration, though one year's drop is weak evidence of a trend.

text: The WHO IHR Emergency Committees page lists no committee first convened on a new event after October 10, 2026.
Any emergency committee convened on a new event advises against a public health emergency of international concern and the Director-General follows that advice.
An emergency committee on a serious new multi-country outbreak in 2027 or 2028 advises against a declaration and the WHO Director-General agrees.
The WHO announces it will handle new outbreaks with regional alerts or internal grading rather than public health emergency of international concern declarations.
The cluster of WHO emergency declarations since 2019 reflects chance and the attention COVID-19 brought, more than a lasting rise in the rate of dangerous outbreaks.
Political pressure on the WHO after COVID-19 will make it reluctant to declare a new global emergency for anything short of a clear pandemic threat.
Regional bodies such as Africa CDC will increasingly handle cross-border outbreaks without the WHO declaring a public health emergency of international concern.

An analysis of International Health Regulations Emergency Committees and Public Health Emergency of International Concern Designations (Lucia Mullen, Christina Potter, Lawrence O. Gostin, Anita Cicero and Jennifer B. Nuzzo, 2020)
bridge: The authors reviewed the emergency committees the WHO had convened under the International Health Regulations and found that the criteria for a declaration were applied unevenly, so a serious outbreak does not reliably lead to one.
bottom_line: Strong weight for the disagree side's main point, that a declaration is a judgment call, though it predates the 2022, 2024 and 2026 declarations.

text: Ebola in North Kivu, DR Congo - is it an undeclared public health emergency of international concern (PHEIC)? (Oyewale Tomori, David Durrheim, Lawrence Gostin and Matthew M. Kavanagh, 2019)
bridge: The editorial asked why the WHO had not yet declared the North Kivu Ebola outbreak an emergency while it was spreading, a case where the WHO held back for months on a deadly outbreak before declaring in July 2019.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it shows the WHO can delay a declaration, which matters for a window as short as 26 months, but in that case the declaration did eventually come.

text: From PHEIC to PHECs: reclaiming Africa's agency in global health security governance (Nelson Aghogho Evaborhene, 2026)
bridge: The article argues for Africa CDC's own Public Health Emergencies of Continental Concern as a step away from overreliance on the WHO's emergency system, a path by which some cross-border outbreaks could be handled without a WHO declaration.
bottom_line: Low weight: it is an argument for what should happen, not evidence that regional declarations are replacing WHO ones.

text: Public health workers in low-income countries need international money and staff to arrive early when an outbreak crosses borders.
measured_by: Days from a WHO emergency declaration to the first release of international outbreak funding to the affected country
if_true: The measure is tested again before 2029 and shows whether funding arrives faster than in past emergencies.
if_false: The measure goes untested through 2028, and readiness is judged only by the Ebola response already under way.
bottom_line: The most direct interest: a declaration is the trigger that unlocks money for these workers.

text: Older adults and people with weak immune systems need vaccines and treatments ready before a new virus reaches them.
measured_by: Doses of vaccine or antiviral drugs stockpiled per person at highest risk, by country
if_true: Stockpiles are drawn down in a new emergency and their adequacy is tested.
if_false: Stockpiles sit unused and may expire or be cut from budgets.
bottom_line: Large in a severe emergency, small in a mild one, so its weight depends on which pathogen comes.

text: Travelers and airline crews need early, clear warning about where a dangerous outbreak is spreading.
measured_by: Days from first WHO outbreak report to published travel guidance
if_true: Travel guidance is issued for a new event before 2029.
if_false: No new emergency guidance is needed beyond that for the existing Ebola and polio emergencies.
bottom_line: Real but secondary to the health of people in outbreak zones.

text: Hotel, tour and airline workers in outbreak countries need to avoid the bookings lost to travel bans that follow an emergency declaration.
measured_by: Change in international arrivals to the affected country in the six months after a declaration
if_true: Arrivals fall in whichever country is at the center of the new emergency.
if_false: No new country suffers a declaration-driven drop in arrivals before 2029.
bottom_line: Concentrated and severe for the workers affected, which is why it shapes how fast governments report outbreaks.

text: Taxpayers in donor countries need public health money spent on likely threats rather than on standing alarms.
measured_by: Share of global health budgets held in emergency reserves versus spent on routine programs
if_true: Reserves are spent on a new emergency and the holding cost is justified.
if_false: Reserves sit idle through 2028 and critics argue the money should have gone to routine care.
bottom_line: Legitimate, though the base rate makes idle reserves the less likely outcome.

text: Poultry farmers and meat exporters need to avoid trade bans that follow an emergency declaration over bird flu.
measured_by: Value of poultry and meat exports blocked by import bans after a declaration
if_true: If the new emergency is influenza, export bans spread across affected countries.
if_false: Existing animal-health trade rules apply, without the added weight of a WHO emergency.
bottom_line: Matters only if the next emergency is an influenza, but then it matters a great deal.

text: Countries that set aside vaccines, tests and emergency money before the next declared global health emergency can start a response weeks sooner than countries that wait for the declaration.
bottom_line: Likely real and large for poorer countries, but no source on this page measures the size of the gain.

text: Preparing for another declared emergency means stocking vaccines and antiviral drugs ahead of time, which protects people most likely to die from a new virus.
bottom_line: Plausible and important, but it depends on guessing the right pathogen, which preparedness has often failed to do.

text: Treating another global health emergency as likely keeps travel advisories and border screening plans current, so travelers get clear guidance quickly.
bottom_line: Modest weight: guidance helps, but it matters less than detection at the source.

text: Money held for a global health emergency that may not come before 2029 is money not spent on routine care such as childhood vaccination and tuberculosis treatment.
bottom_line: A real trade-off, though the base rate suggests the money would more likely than not be used within the window.

text: An emergency declaration often brings travel bans and canceled bookings for the affected countries, even though the International Health Regulations discourage such restrictions.
bottom_line: Meaningful for the countries hit, and one reason some governments delay reporting outbreaks.

text: A declaration over bird flu can trigger import bans on poultry and meat from affected countries.
bottom_line: Narrow but sharp: it falls on one industry and only if an influenza emergency is declared.

text: The number of IHR Emergency Committees first convened on a new event after October 10, 2026 is a fair measure of how close the WHO is to another declaration.

The yearly count of confirmed human cases of H5N1 or another novel influenza A subtype reported to the WHO, and any cluster showing person-to-person spread, is a fair measure of pressure toward an influenza emergency.
At least one dangerous outbreak that spreads, or threatens to spread, across borders and is not already under a WHO emergency declaration will arise between October 10, 2026 and December 31, 2028.
The International Health Regulations and the WHO's power to declare an emergency under them remain in force through the end of 2028, despite the United States withdrawal from the WHO.
Within weeks of a new WHO emergency declaration, countries would receive WHO temporary recommendations on surveillance, testing, travel and trade for the declared disease.
A new WHO emergency declaration would prompt the release of outbreak money, such as the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies, to the countries first affected.

A new WHO emergency declaration before 2029 would give the amended International Health Regulations, in force since September 2025, one of their first real tests and show whether the changes speed up the response.

A new WHO emergency declaration before 2029 would raise pressure on governments to finish and ratify the WHO Pandemic Agreement adopted in May 2025 and to keep funding vaccine stockpiles and disease surveillance.
The World Health Organization will declare at least two new public health emergencies of international concern before the end of 2028.
The World Health Organization will declare a pandemic emergency under the amended International Health Regulations before the end of 2028.
The World Health Organization will declare another public health emergency of international concern before the end of 2030.
The World Health Organization will convene an International Health Regulations emergency committee for a new outbreak before the end of 2028.
A peer-reviewed mathematics journal will publish an AI-produced proof that settles one of the six open Millennium Prize Problems before the end of 2028.
bottom_line: The question is no longer whether an AI can produce a candidate Millennium proof: OpenAI released a 166-page forced Navier-Stokes blowup proof in September 2026, and the problem's author called it solved. What is thin is the path to a journal: no submission is on record, the Lean check does not match the written proof, and past long proofs took three to seven years to publish, so the fight is about refereeing speed and whether a forced blowup counts.
hook: On September 8, 2026, OpenAI said about 10,000 AI agents working for roughly 88 hours had produced a proof that the Navier-Stokes equations of fluid flow can blow up, a $1 million Millennium Prize question open since the Clay Institute posed it in 2000 (Quanta Magazine, 2026).
question: Will a peer-reviewed mathematics journal publish an AI-produced proof that settles a Millennium Prize Problem before the end of 2028?
ask: The page most needs a sourced record of whether OpenAI's "Finite Time Blowup for Navier–Stokes" has been submitted to a refereed journal, and if so which one and when.

text: Charles Fefferman's official Clay statement of the Navier-Stokes problem accepts a breakdown of smooth solutions under a smooth external force (his alternatives C and D) as a solution, so a correct forced-blowup proof like OpenAI's settles the Millennium Problem as written.
bottom_line: Strong weight: Fefferman, who wrote the problem statement, told Quanta he was thrilled the problem was solved, which answers the objection that a forced result is only a side question.

text: A machine-checked Lean formalization lets journal referees of an AI-produced proof focus on whether the formal statement matches the intended theorem, which can make refereeing faster than for a human proof of the same length.
bottom_line: Moderate weight at best: the October 2026 preprint by Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen found the Lean code and the written proof do not match line for line, so referees still have to read the written proof.

text: AI mathematics has moved from an officially graded gold-medal score at the International Mathematical Olympiad in July 2025 to a disproof of Erdős's unit distance conjecture in May 2026 to a claimed Navier-Stokes proof in September 2026, so AI systems may well produce more publishable research proofs well before the end of 2028.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the pace is real and documented, but speed of discovery says little about how fast journals referee.

text: OpenAI reported that about 10,000 AI agents working for roughly 88 hours produced its Navier-Stokes singularity proof, and that another AI model formalized it in Lean about 17 hours later.
bottom_line: Shows an AI-produced candidate proof exists today; it says nothing yet about whether the proof survives review.

text: The Annals of Mathematics published Andrew Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in volume 141, issue 3, in May 1995, about 23 months after his June 1993 lectures and about 8 months after his September 1994 repair of the gap.
bottom_line: Proves a top journal can publish a landmark proof inside the belief's window, though one case is a thin base rate.

text: Terence Tao's tracking wiki listed 18 distinct Erdős problems with a full solution produced by an AI system working on its own, as of June 30, 2026.
bottom_line: Shows AI systems are now producing correct research-level proofs routinely, though the wiki itself warns many of these problems may be obscure rather than hard.

text: A refereed mathematics journal will list OpenAI's Navier-Stokes blowup paper, or a revised version of it, as accepted or in press.
At least one group of mathematicians outside OpenAI will publish a full independent check of the written Navier-Stokes blowup proof that finds it correct.
A journal editor confirms publicly that OpenAI's Navier-Stokes blowup paper has been submitted and is under review with a referee panel.
An independent team of fluid-equation specialists publishes a line-by-line check of OpenAI's written Navier-Stokes proof and finds no gaps.
A journal paper whose proof was generated by an AI system still counts as an AI-produced proof even when, under the Leiden Declaration's rules, only humans are listed as its authors.
A proof of finite-time blowup for the Navier-Stokes equations under a smooth external force, Fefferman's alternatives C or D, settles the Millennium Problem as the Clay Institute wrote it.
OpenAI's 166-page Navier-Stokes proof, or a rival AI-produced proof, contains no gap serious enough to stop a journal from accepting it.
Charles Fefferman, who wrote the Clay Mathematics Institute's official statement of the Navier-Stokes problem, told Quanta Magazine in September 2026 that he was thrilled the problem had been solved.
Existence and Smoothness of the Navier-Stokes Equation, Charles L. Fefferman, 2000
where_found: Clay Mathematics Institute, official Millennium Prize problem description
bridge: Fefferman's official statement lists four alternatives that each count as a solution, two of which (C and D) are a smooth solution breaking down in finite time under a smooth external force, which is the kind of result OpenAI claims.
bottom_line: Strong weight on the question of what counts as settling Navier-Stokes, since it is the governing text, but no weight on whether any particular proof is correct or will be published in time.

text: Advanced version of Gemini with Deep Think officially achieves gold-medal standard at the International Mathematical Olympiad, Google DeepMind, 2025
bridge: DeepMind reported on July 21, 2025 that an advanced Gemini Deep Think model solved five of six IMO problems for 35 of 42 points, graded by IMO coordinators under student time limits, a marker of how quickly AI mathematical reasoning has advanced.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight: it documents the pace of AI progress in mathematics, but olympiad problems are short and known to be solvable, unlike a Millennium Problem.

text: Refereeing a long, new proof in mathematical analysis usually takes years, and Thomas Hales's Kepler conjecture proof took from its 1998 announcement until 2005 to appear in the Annals of Mathematics, so publishing OpenAI's 166-page Navier-Stokes proof by the end of 2028 is a tight deadline.
bottom_line: Heavy weight: the belief has about 27 months from OpenAI's September 2026 release, and the best historical comparisons for long, partly machine-dependent proofs ran far longer.

text: The Lean formalization of OpenAI's Navier-Stokes proof does not faithfully match the written proof, so the machine check does not shorten human refereeing of the 166 pages.
bottom_line: Strong weight: the mismatch is documented in a named preprint, and it removes the main reason to expect an AI proof to be refereed faster than a human one.

text: Most mathematicians who work on Navier-Stokes study the unforced equations, so journal referees and editors may decline to describe a blowup that depends on a built-in external force as settling the Millennium Problem.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: Fefferman's wording permits the forced version, but if the published paper is framed as a forced result only, whether the belief came true will be argued over.

text: OpenAI has said it will not claim the Millennium Prize and has not reported submitting its Navier-Stokes paper to any journal, so a company that already got its publicity from the announcement may never put the paper through peer review.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: no submission is on record as of October 2026, though a company could still submit, or outside mathematicians could publish a refereed version.

text: Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen found that the Lean formalization of OpenAI's Navier-Stokes blowup proof does not faithfully translate the written proof; for example, one lemma in the written proof uses four extra derivatives where the cited Lean estimate uses five.
bottom_line: Strong: it does not say the proof is wrong, but it means the written proof must be refereed by hand like any other.

text: Thomas Hales announced his Kepler conjecture proof in August 1998; after four years of work the referee panel reported in 2003 that it was only "99% certain" the proof was correct, and the Annals of Mathematics published it in 2005.
bottom_line: The closest past case of a long, computer-dependent proof, and it took about seven years to publish.

text: Grigori Perelman posted his Poincaré conjecture preprints in November 2002, March 2003 and July 2003, and the first journal accounts of the complete proof appeared in June 2006 (Cao and Zhu, Asian Journal of Mathematics) and 2008 (Kleiner and Lott, Geometry and Topology).
bottom_line: The only solved Millennium Problem took more than three years to reach journals in full, longer than the belief allows.

text: A gap will be found in the written proof in OpenAI's "Finite Time Blowup for Navier–Stokes" that OpenAI acknowledges or does not repair within six months.
A referee or outside mathematician finds an error in OpenAI's written Navier-Stokes blowup proof that the Lean formalization does not cover and that cannot be repaired.
OpenAI states that it will not submit its Navier-Stokes blowup paper to any peer-reviewed journal and no outside group takes up a refereed write-up.

Refereeing a long new proof in mathematical analysis will take about as long for an AI-produced proof as it historically has for human proofs, because a machine check that does not match the written proof saves referees little time.
A company that has already announced a Millennium-level result by press release has little reason to spend time putting the paper through journal review.

A Millennium Problem should be counted as settled only by a result that most specialists accept as answering the question they care about, which for Navier-Stokes many take to be the unforced equations.
Anders C. Hansen co-wrote an October 2026 preprint arguing that the Lean formalization of OpenAI's Navier-Stokes blowup proof does not correspond to the written proof it was meant to check.
A proof of the Kepler conjecture, Thomas C. Hales, 2005
bridge: Hales announced his computer-dependent proof in 1998, and it appeared in the Annals only in 2005 after referees reported they could not fully check the computer parts, the closest historical match to a long proof that leans on machine work.
bottom_line: Strong weight as a timeline comparison, since it shows how long refereeing of a long, machine-dependent proof has taken, though formal proof tools have improved a great deal since then.

text: Notes on Perelman's papers, Bruce Kleiner and John Lott, 2008
bridge: Grigori Perelman posted his Poincaré conjecture proof as preprints in 2002 and 2003 and never published it in a journal himself, and this detailed checked exposition appeared in a refereed journal only in 2008, showing that the one solved Millennium Problem took years to reach refereed print.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it is the only precedent for a solved Millennium Problem and it ran well past a 27-month window, but Perelman's refusal to engage with journals made his case unusually slow.

text: AI researchers need refereed, public tests of their systems' mathematical reasoning, so that claims about ability rest on checked work rather than announcements.
measured_by: Number of AI-produced research proofs published in refereed journals with AI production stated.
if_true: Rises to at least one Millennium-level refereed proof by the end of 2028.
if_false: Stays at zero Millennium-level refereed proofs, leaving AI math claims resting on company announcements and preprints.
bottom_line: A strong interest on the belief's side, since refereed publication is the test these researchers say they want.

text: Mathematicians who study fluid equations need a fast, checkable verdict on the claimed Navier-Stokes blowup, so they can build on it or set it aside.
measured_by: Months from OpenAI's September 2026 release to a refereed verdict (publication or a documented gap).
if_true: Under 28 months, ending in publication.
if_false: More than 28 months, or a verdict that the proof has an unrepaired gap.
bottom_line: Served by any clear verdict, so it favors the belief only if the proof is correct.

text: University mathematics departments need to know which AI tools produce trustworthy proofs, so they spend research and teaching money well.
measured_by: Whether a refereed journal has confirmed any AI-produced proof of a major open problem.
if_true: A confirmed case exists by 2028 that departments can point to.
if_false: No confirmed case exists, and departments must judge AI tools from smaller results.
bottom_line: A modest interest; departments benefit from clarity either way.

text: Journal referees need enough time to check long proofs line by line, so that published results can be trusted.
measured_by: Months between submission and acceptance for the AI-produced proof, and whether errors are later found.
if_true: Review is completed within roughly two years of release, a pace that raises pressure on referees.
if_false: Review runs longer than 2028, on a schedule set by checking rather than by a deadline.
bottom_line: A strong interest, since a fast publication that later fails would harm trust in both journals and AI mathematics.

text: Young mathematicians need credit and career rewards for their own discoveries, which a race to publish AI results can take from them.
measured_by: Whether the human researchers whose methods an AI proof used are credited as authors or prominently cited in the published paper.
if_true: An AI-produced paper is published while the priority dispute over human contributions remains open.
if_false: Human-authored papers by Córdoba, Martínez-Zoroa, Buckmaster, Alpöge and others have time to appear and set the record.
bottom_line: A real interest, shown by the September 2026 open letter from Fields Medalists warning that rushed AI announcements leave too little time for credit.

text: Mathematicians who use commercial AI tools on unpublished work need assurance their prompts and drafts will not be used to beat them to publication.
measured_by: Public, checkable commitments from AI companies on use of user prompts, and the number of data-use disputes raised by mathematicians.
if_true: A company's AI proof is published while data-use questions like Buckmaster's remain unverifiable from outside.
if_false: Publication waits until provenance questions are resolved or documented.
bottom_line: Moderate weight; the interest is about process, and it could be met even if a journal publishes the proof.

text: Publishing a refereed AI-produced Millennium Problem proof by 2028 would give AI developers and mathematicians a public, checked example of how to verify AI mathematics, combining a Lean formalization with human refereeing.
bottom_line: Real but narrow: one published case sets a precedent, and its value depends on the review being careful rather than fast.

text: A refereed Navier-Stokes blowup construction would let researchers on fluid equations build on a checked result instead of an unverified company manuscript.
bottom_line: Meaningful for the field; no source gives a figure for how much earlier a checked result arrives.

text: A refereed AI-produced proof would show university mathematics departments which AI tools produce trustworthy research, so they can decide what to teach and buy.
bottom_line: Plausible but indirect; departments would learn as much from a careful rejection as from a publication.

text: Publishing the AI-produced Navier-Stokes proof first can shift credit away from the human mathematicians whose methods it relied on, including Diego Córdoba, Luis Martínez-Zoroa, Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge.
bottom_line: Real and already happening: the priority dispute is public, and the four named researchers are the ones Quanta and Fortune report as affected.

text: Mathematicians who test unpublished ideas in commercial AI tools risk having those ideas reach a company's own systems first, which a published AI proof would reward.
bottom_line: Unsettled: OpenAI denies any use of Buckmaster's prompts after July 3, 2026, and outsiders cannot check either side.

text: Acceptance of an AI-produced Navier-Stokes blowup paper by a refereed journal before December 31, 2027 is a fair measure of whether the review process is on pace to finish publication by the end of 2028.

The number of independent public checks by analysts outside OpenAI that confirm the written Navier-Stokes proof correct, by June 30, 2027, is a fair measure of whether the mathematics community will accept the proof in time.
At least one AI-produced proof of one of the six open Millennium Prize Problems, such as OpenAI's September 2026 Navier-Stokes blowup proof, is correct.
A peer-reviewed mathematics journal will accept and publish an AI-produced Millennium Problem proof by December 31, 2028.
A proof whose key steps were generated by an AI system counts as AI-produced even if the published paper lists only human authors and credits them with checking and writing it up.

Within two years of an AI-produced Navier-Stokes proof being published, major mathematics journals will adopt written policies on how referees should handle proofs submitted with a machine-checked Lean formalization.

Within two years of an AI-produced Millennium Problem proof being published, the AI labs racing in mathematics will announce attempts on at least one other Millennium Problem using the same large-scale agent approach.

Within a decade of an AI-produced Millennium Problem proof being published, leading mathematics journals will routinely require a faithful formal proof, checked against the written text, for long proofs in analysis.

Within a decade of an AI-produced Millennium Problem proof being published, graduate training in mathematics will put much more weight on checking, explaining and extending machine-produced proofs than on producing long proofs by hand.
Peer-reviewed mathematics journals will publish AI-produced proofs that settle at least two of the six open Millennium Prize Problems before the end of 2028.
The Clay Mathematics Institute will award a Millennium Prize for an AI-produced proof before the end of 2030.
A peer-reviewed mathematics journal will publish an AI-produced proof that settles one of the six open Millennium Prize Problems before the end of 2032.

Most specialists in fluid dynamics will accept an AI-produced proof of finite-time blowup for the forced Navier-Stokes equations as correct before the end of 2028, whether or not a journal has published it.
H5N1 bird flu will spread from person to person in a sustained way somewhere in the world before 2030.
hook: Since 2003 the World Health Organization has confirmed more than a thousand human H5N1 infections and recorded 479 deaths among them, yet not one of those infections is known to have passed in a sustained chain from one person to the next.
question: Will H5N1 bird flu begin spreading from person to person in a sustained way somewhere in the world before 2030?
ask: The page most needs a current, sourced running count of H5N1 human cases that investigators could not link to any animal exposure, updated as WHO and national agencies report them.

text: H5N1 has infected an unusually wide range of mammals since 2024, including dairy cattle across many US states, which gives the virus far more chances to adapt to mammal hosts than it had in earlier decades.
bottom_line: Strong as a reason the risk has risen, because more mammalian replication means more rolls of the dice, though host range alone does not prove human spread will follow.

text: Laboratory work on a recent bovine H5N1 virus showed that a single change in the hemagglutinin protein can switch its binding preference toward the human-type receptors found in the airway.
bottom_line: Medium weight: it shows the receptor barrier is not large, but the experiment used an isolated protein, not a whole transmissible virus, so it is suggestive rather than decisive.

text: Serologic surveys of dairy workers found recent H5 infection in people who never reported symptoms, showing that many human exposures to H5N1 go undetected.
bottom_line: Medium to strong: undetected mild infections mean the virus gets more quiet opportunities to adapt in people than case counts suggest.

text: Influenza viruses swap whole gene segments when two strains infect the same host, and H5N1 could acquire human-adapted genes by mixing with a seasonal flu virus in a person or pig, the route by which past pandemic strains arose.
bottom_line: Strong in principle because reassortment has produced pandemics before, but it depends on a co-infection event that has not been observed for H5N1 to date.

text: Major public health bodies rate H5N1 as a leading pandemic candidate and have stockpiled H5 vaccine, reflecting a specialist judgment that sustained human spread is a realistic possibility within years.
bottom_line: Moderate: expert concern is informed but is a forecast, not evidence of the event, and preparedness spending is a precaution against a tail risk rather than a prediction it will occur.

text: A single amino acid change (Q226L) in the hemagglutinin of a 2024 bovine H5N1 virus switched its binding specificity toward human-type receptors in laboratory binding assays.
bottom_line: High-quality structural and binding work, but it tested an isolated protein, so it shows a low receptor barrier, not an actual transmissible virus.

text: Of 115 dairy workers sampled in Michigan and Colorado, 8 (7 percent, 95 percent confidence interval 3.6 to 13.1 percent) had serologic evidence of recent infection with highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5).
bottom_line: A convenience sample, not a random one, so the exact percent is uncertain, but it establishes that undetected human infections occur.

text: If H5N1 is heading toward sustained human spread, clusters of human cases with no traceable animal exposure will be reported in at least one country.
If the belief is true, at least one H5N1 isolate from a human patient will be sequenced showing both human-type receptor binding and a mammalian polymerase adaptation.
A confirmed epidemiologic report of a chain of H5N1 infection across three or more successive people who shared no common animal source would strengthen the belief.
Repeated isolation from human patients of H5N1 carrying human-receptor-switch mutations, together with efficient airborne transmission between ferrets in the laboratory, would strengthen the belief.
Holding the belief assumes that the large number of mammalian H5N1 infections now occurring meaningfully raises the odds that the virus acquires the changes needed for human-to-human spread.
Holding the belief assumes that the number of genetic changes required for efficient human spread is small enough to assemble by 2030 rather than over many decades.
Airborne Transmission of Influenza A/H5N1 Virus Between Ferrets, Sander Herfst and colleagues, 2012
bridge: The study showed that a small number of mutations, about five, let an H5N1 virus spread through the air between ferrets, the standard animal model for human respiratory spread.
bottom_line: Strong weight on the mechanism because it demonstrated that airborne spread between mammals is reachable, though the engineered virus was weakened and ferrets are not people.

text: A single mutation in bovine influenza H5N1 hemagglutinin switches specificity to human receptors, Ting-Hui Lin and colleagues, 2024
bridge: The study found that one amino acid change in the surface protein of a 2024 human H5N1 isolate switched its binding preference toward the human-type receptors found in the airway.
bottom_line: Medium weight because it tested the isolated protein and not a whole transmissible virus, and the authors warned that more changes would likely be needed for spread between people.

text: Deadliest Enemy: Our War Against Killer Germs, Michael T. Osterholm and Mark Olshaker, 2017
bridge: The book argues that a novel influenza virus is the single most likely source of a catastrophic pandemic and names avian strains like H5N1 among the leading candidates.
bottom_line: Moderate weight as informed expert argument rather than evidence of the event, useful for understanding why specialists rank flu first among pandemic threats.

text: Despite more than 1,000 reported human H5N1 infections since 2003 and decades of heavy exposure, no sustained chain of human-to-human transmission has ever been documented.
bottom_line: Strong: a long record of spillover without sustained spread is the best evidence that the barrier to human transmission is high.

text: H5N1 hemagglutinin prefers the avian-type receptors that are scarce in the human nose and throat, so the virus does not readily spread by coughs and sneezes between people.
bottom_line: Strong as the core biological reason sustained spread has not happened, though it is exactly the barrier the mutation studies probe.

text: The single-mutation receptor study modified only the isolated hemagglutinin protein, and its authors explicitly cautioned that it does not show such evolution has occurred or that a virus with only that change would spread between humans.
bottom_line: Strong against over-reading the lab result: the authors themselves limited the claim, so it does not support imminent human transmission.

text: Efficient airborne spread between people likely requires several genetic changes at once, such as human-receptor binding together with polymerase adaptations, and the chance of all of them arising and spreading together is low.
bottom_line: Medium to strong: the multi-step requirement is a real brake, though combinations can assemble over time given enough mammalian infections.

text: The United States dairy cattle outbreak produced roughly seventy mostly mild human cases with no person-to-person spread detected, even among heavily exposed workers.
bottom_line: Strong for the near term: a large natural experiment in sustained human exposure has not yet yielded human transmission.

text: Current World Health Organization and United States Centers for Disease Control assessments continue to rate sustained human-to-human transmission as unlikely and the public risk as low.
bottom_line: Moderate: these are standing judgments by the bodies closest to the data, but they describe the present state and can change quickly if the virus does.

text: Across the United States dairy outbreak, which produced about seventy human cases, no person-to-person spread has been identified to date.
bottom_line: Strong real-world evidence that even sustained, intense human exposure has not produced transmission so far.

text: If the belief is false, reported annual H5N1 human cases will remain overwhelmingly linked to direct animal exposure through the end of the decade.
If the belief is false, WHO risk assessments will keep stating that no sustained human-to-human transmission of H5N1 has been identified.
Large serologic surveys across several countries finding H5N1 antibodies only in animal-exposed people, with no secondary infections in their households, would weaken the belief.
Experimental work showing that recent H5N1 strains, even carrying receptor-switch mutations, fail to transmit by air between ferrets would weaken the belief.
Rejecting the belief assumes that the long record of more than a thousand human H5N1 infections since 2003 without sustained spread is a reliable guide to what happens before 2030.
Rejecting the belief assumes that control measures such as culling and worker protection will keep human exposure low enough to prevent the needed adaptation.
Updated joint FAO/WHO/WOAH public health assessment of recent influenza A(H5) virus events in animals and people, FAO, WHO and WOAH, 2026
where_found: World Health Organization and World Organisation for Animal Health
bridge: The three agencies assessed the global public health risk from H5 avian influenza as low as of early 2026, with no sustained human-to-human transmission detected.
bottom_line: Strong weight as the shared judgment of the bodies closest to the data, though it describes the present state and can change quickly if the virus adapts.

text: H5 Bird Flu: Current Situation, United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2025
where_found: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (cdc.gov)
bridge: The assessment reports mostly mild United States human cases from animal exposure and no detected person-to-person spread, and rates the public risk as low.
bottom_line: Moderate to strong for the near term because it reflects direct United States surveillance, though no detected spread is not proof that spread cannot start.

text: Nurses and hospital staff need enough warning and protective equipment to treat a surge of flu patients without falling sick themselves.
measured_by: Stock of fitted N95 respirators and staffed intensive care beds per capita.
if_true: Stockpiles and surge plans built in advance are drawn down to save lives.
if_false: Those stockpiles sit unused and partly expire.
bottom_line: A strong interest because frontline workers bear the first and heaviest risk in any respiratory wave.

text: Poultry and dairy workers need paid sick leave and protective gear so they can report illness without losing income.
measured_by: Share of farm workers with paid sick leave and employer-provided protective equipment.
if_true: Early reporting and protection slow onward spread from the first clusters.
if_false: The protections still reduce routine zoonotic infections and worker harm.
bottom_line: Robust interest that holds value whether or not sustained spread ever develops.

text: Parents of young children need schools and clinics to have a plan for a fast-moving respiratory outbreak.
measured_by: Share of school districts and pediatric clinics with a current outbreak response plan.
if_true: Ready plans shorten closures and protect children in a wave.
if_false: The planning effort yields little direct return.
bottom_line: Moderate interest, strongest precisely in the scenario the belief predicts.

text: Poultry farmers need to avoid mass culls and trade bans ordered on the basis of a human threat that may not materialize.
measured_by: Number of birds culled and the value of lost exports per year.
if_true: Aggressive culling and restrictions are easier to justify as a human safeguard.
if_false: Those same measures impose large losses with little human benefit.
bottom_line: A serious and concrete interest, since the costs land on producers immediately whatever the virus does later.

text: Taxpayers need public money spent where the expected benefit is highest, not locked into one pathogen that may never spread between people.
measured_by: Dollars committed to H5N1 preparedness compared with other unmet health needs.
if_true: The spending looks well targeted in hindsight.
if_false: The money could have done more good elsewhere.
bottom_line: Legitimate but partly offset because preparedness capacity can serve other respiratory threats too.

text: Small-business owners need to avoid another round of restrictions and closures triggered by a threat that proves smaller than warned.
measured_by: Days of mandated closure or capacity limits imposed in response.
if_true: Restrictions are a painful but defensible response to a real wave.
if_false: They inflict economic damage without a matching public health gain.
bottom_line: Strong interest shaped by recent experience, though it argues against overreaction more than against the forecast itself.

text: Building respirator stockpiles and hospital surge plans before an H5N1 wave would let hospitals treat a surge of patients with fewer deaths.
bottom_line: Large potential payoff if a wave comes, but the benefit is realized only in the scenario the belief describes.

text: Giving farm workers paid sick leave and protective gear would catch spillovers earlier and cut the chance of onward infection.
bottom_line: Valuable on its own terms even if sustained spread never arrives, so this benefit is fairly robust.

text: Keeping vaccines and tests ready in advance would shorten the gap between a first human cluster and an effective response.
bottom_line: High value in the bad scenario, though readiness programs carry ongoing cost whether or not the event occurs.

text: Acting on the belief can drive precautionary poultry culls and trade restrictions that impose heavy losses even if human spread never comes.
bottom_line: Real and recurring cost already seen in current outbreaks, falling hardest on producers regardless of whether human spread follows.

text: Large sustained spending focused on one pathogen diverts money and attention from other pressing health needs.
bottom_line: A genuine trade-off, though preparedness capacity often carries over to other respiratory threats, softening the loss.

text: Preparing hard for a wave that does not arrive can erode public trust and willingness to cooperate with the next warning.
bottom_line: Plausible but hard to measure, and it depends heavily on whether preparation takes the form of quiet readiness or visible restrictions.

text: A World Health Organization or national public health agency confirmation of at least one sustained chain of H5N1 human-to-human transmission (three or more successive human generations of infection with no animal source) before 1 January 2030 is a fair measure of whether the belief came true.
The number of H5N1 human cases per year that have no identified animal exposure is a fair measure of hidden person-to-person spread.
The detection in human patients of H5N1 carrying both human-type receptor binding and a mammalian polymerase adaptation is a fair measure of the virus adapting toward human spread.
H5N1 can acquire the ability to spread efficiently between people through mutation, gene swapping, or both.
The number of independent mammalian and human H5N1 infections between now and 2030 will be large enough to give rare adapting mutations real chances to occur.
If the belief is treated as likely and acted on, governments and manufacturers would expand H5 vaccine stockpiles and pre-position antiviral drugs within a year or two.
If the belief is treated as likely and acted on, surveillance of dairy herds, poultry flocks, and exposed farm workers would be stepped up and better funded in the near term.
Over a decade, if sustained human H5N1 spread does occur, the world could face a severe influenza pandemic with high illness, death, and economic disruption.

Over a decade, sustained investment in pandemic flu vaccines and surveillance driven by the H5N1 threat could leave the world better prepared for any novel flu, even if H5N1 itself never spreads between people.
H5N1 bird flu will cause a global human pandemic that kills more people than COVID-19 before 2030.
Sustained human-to-human H5N1 transmission is inevitable and will begin within the next two years.
H5N1 bird flu will cause at least one documented cluster of limited human-to-human transmission before 2030, even if it never becomes sustained.
The chance that H5N1 begins spreading between people before 2030 is high enough to justify stockpiling vaccines and expanding surveillance now.
More than one in five American adults will be taking a GLP-1 drug such as Ozempic or Wegovy by the end of 2030.
hook: In just 18 months, the share of American adults taking a GLP-1 drug doubled, from about 6% to 12%, according to KFF's November 2025 poll.
question: Will more than one in five American adults be taking a GLP-1 drug such as Ozempic or Wegovy by the end of 2030?
ask: The page most needs a prescription-based count of distinct American adults currently filling any GLP-1 drug, so the survey readings of 11% to 12% can be checked against pharmacy records.

text: The share of American adults currently taking a GLP-1 drug doubled in about 18 months, from about 6% in May 2024 to 12% in late 2025 (KFF), so the share needs to grow by less than two points a year to pass 20% by the end of 2030.
bottom_line: This deserves real weight because it rests on a measured trend confirmed by a second pollster, but drug uptake usually slows once the most eager patients are already on treatment, so a straight-line projection is the optimistic case.

text: The number of American adults who medically qualify for a GLP-1 weight-loss drug is far larger than one in five, because about 40% of U.S. adults have obesity (CDC, 2021 to 2023) and many more are overweight with a related condition.
bottom_line: Strong as a statement of potential demand: need is not the limit, but eligibility says nothing about whether people can pay for the drugs or will keep taking them.

text: The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge, which began July 1, 2026, lets eligible Medicare Part D enrollees get Wegovy, Zepbound or Foundayo for weight loss at a $50 monthly copay, opening the drugs to millions of older adults whom Medicare was previously barred from covering for weight loss.
bottom_line: Meaningful but fragile: adults 65 and over are a large group with low current use (9% in KFF's 2025 poll), yet the Bridge is scheduled to end in December 2027 and its successor is uncertain.

text: GLP-1 drugs keep gaining medical reasons to prescribe them beyond weight loss, including a 20% cut in heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular deaths among overweight adults with heart disease in the SELECT trial, plus approvals for kidney disease in diabetes and for sleep apnea.
bottom_line: Solid evidence from a large randomized trial that makes insurers more willing to pay for some patients, though each new use applies to people who are mostly already in the eligible pool.

text: About 12% of U.S. adults said they were currently taking a GLP-1 drug for weight loss, diabetes or another condition in a poll fielded October 27 to November 2, 2025, up about 6 points from May 2024, and 18% said they had ever taken one.
bottom_line: Strong for the trend so far, since Gallup separately measured weight-loss use rising from 5.8% in February 2024 to 12.4% in 2025; the poll has a margin of error of about 3 points.

text: 40.3% of U.S. adults had obesity during August 2021 to August 2023, based on measured height and weight.
bottom_line: Highly reliable measurement showing the eligible pool is about twice the 20% threshold, but it measures need, not uptake.

text: 22% of U.S. adults not currently taking a GLP-1 said they would be interested in taking one to lose weight, rising to 43% among non-users who had been told they were obese or overweight.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: stated interest shows room to grow, but only 7% of non-users said they were very interested, and interest often does not turn into a prescription.

text: A KFF or Gallup national survey fielded in 2027 will find at least 15% of U.S. adults currently taking a GLP-1 drug.
Medicare will continue covering GLP-1 drugs for weight loss after the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge ends in December 2027, through Part D or a successor program.
A large pharmacy-claims study finds that more than 30% of American adults who started a GLP-1 drug for weight loss in 2025 or later were still taking one three years later.
National prescription data show the number of distinct American adults filling a GLP-1 prescription grew by more than 15% a year in both 2026 and 2027.
Lower cash prices, daily pills and Medicare coverage will bring new American users onto GLP-1 drugs faster than existing users stop taking them.
Drug makers will be able to manufacture enough GLP-1 drugs to supply more than one in five American adults by 2030 without new shortages.
National surveys asking American adults whether they currently take a GLP-1 drug give an honest count of use, including people who buy compounded or cash-pay versions.
Poll: 1 in 8 Adults Say They Are Currently Taking a GLP-1 Drug For Weight Loss, Diabetes or Another Condition, Even as Half Say the Drugs Are Difficult to Afford (KFF Health Tracking Poll, 2025)
bridge: KFF's national poll found about 12% of U.S. adults currently taking a GLP-1 drug, roughly double its 2024 reading, and 22% of adults aged 50 to 64, which shows one age group already past the one-in-five mark.
bottom_line: High weight as the most likely resolution source and the best measure of the starting point, though one fast-rising reading does not show the pace will hold for five more years.

text: Semaglutide and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Obesity without Diabetes (A. Michael Lincoff et al., 2023)
bridge: The SELECT trial found semaglutide cut heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular deaths by about 20% in overweight adults with heart disease but without diabetes, which gives insurers and Medicare a medical reason to pay beyond weight loss.
bottom_line: Strong evidence that the drugs earn wider coverage for some patients, but it bears on why people should take them, not on how many will actually be taking them in 2030.

text: Most Americans who start a GLP-1 drug for weight loss stop within a year or two, with only about 8% of commercially insured adults without diabetes still on one three years after starting (Prime Therapeutics, 2025), so new starts largely replace dropouts instead of piling up.
bottom_line: This is the strongest reason to doubt the belief, because the share taking the drug at any moment depends as much on how long people stay on as on how many start; the caution is that persistence has been improving for newer starters.

text: Even at $149 to $350 a month, a year of GLP-1 treatment paid in cash costs about $1,800 to $4,200, which is out of reach for many of the uninsured and low-income adults who make up a large part of the eligible population.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: affordability limits cash buyers, though falling pill prices and the Medicare copay narrow the gap for some groups.

text: Only 8% of commercially insured adults without diabetes who started a GLP-1 drug for obesity were still taking one three years later, and 14% of those who started a high-potency drug such as Wegovy.
bottom_line: Strong on its face because it uses pharmacy claims rather than self-report, but it is a company analysis not published in a peer-reviewed journal and covers people who started during the 2021 to 2022 drug shortages.

text: Among 125,474 U.S. adults with overweight or obesity who started a GLP-1 drug between 2018 and 2023, 64.8% of those without type 2 diabetes and 46.5% of those with it stopped within one year.
bottom_line: Strong: a large peer-reviewed study whose direction matches Prime Therapeutics' claims data, though many who stopped later restarted (36.3% of those without diabetes within a year).

text: Every KFF or Gallup national survey fielded in 2027 will find fewer than 14% of U.S. adults currently taking a GLP-1 drug.
Fewer than 13 state Medicaid programs will cover GLP-1 drugs for obesity in 2028.
Repeated national surveys from 2026 through 2028 show the share of American adults currently taking a GLP-1 drug holding flat at roughly 11% to 13%.
A newly confirmed serious health risk from GLP-1 drugs leads the FDA to narrow who may be prescribed them for weight loss before 2030.
The high rates at which Americans stopped GLP-1 drugs in 2018 to 2023 will largely hold for people who start them after prices fell in 2025 and 2026.
The rapid rise in GLP-1 use from 2024 to 2025 came mostly from the most eager patients, so growth in the share of American adults taking the drugs will slow from here.
Employers, state Medicaid programs and Medicare will keep limiting or dropping coverage of GLP-1 drugs for weight loss through 2030 because of their cost.
Greg Justice estimated in Asterisk Magazine in July 2024 that U.S. GLP-1 supply would be enough for only about 23 million Americans by 2030, far fewer than one in five adults.
Discontinuation and Reinitiation of Dual-Labeled GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Among US Adults With Overweight or Obesity (Patricia J. Rodriguez et al., 2025)
bridge: In health records for about 125,000 U.S. adults who started semaglutide, tirzepatide or liraglutide between 2018 and 2023, most stopped within two years, and those without type 2 diabetes stopped more often and restarted less often.
bottom_line: High weight because the share taking a drug at any moment depends on how long people stay on it, though these patients started before prices fell and pills arrived.

text: How Long Til We're All on Ozempic? (Greg Justice, 2024)
bridge: Working from manufacturing capacity, insurance limits and stop rates, the article estimated enough GLP-1 supply for roughly 23 million Americans by 2030, well under one in five adults.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a careful supply-side estimate, but written in mid-2024 before the 2025 price deal, the pills and the Medicare Bridge, so some of its limits have already eased.

text: Adults with obesity need weight-loss medicine they can afford and keep taking.
measured_by: The adult obesity rate measured by CDC's National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey and Gallup's yearly obesity tracking.
if_true: The obesity rate keeps falling below Gallup's 37.0% reading for 2025.
if_false: The obesity rate stays near 37% to 40%.
bottom_line: This is the largest group with a direct stake, and the evidence that the drugs work for people who stay on them is strong.

text: Adults with heart disease or type 2 diabetes need treatments that lower their risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney failure.
measured_by: Rates of heart attack, stroke and kidney failure per 100,000 adults in CDC data.
if_true: Those rates fall faster than their pre-2024 trend.
if_false: Those rates follow their pre-2024 trend.

bottom_line: Real and already visible in 2026 coverage cuts, though states may save on obesity-related illness later.

text: Wider GLP-1 use among overweight adults with heart disease cuts heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular deaths.
bottom_line: Well supported for the trial population: the SELECT randomized trial (Lincoff et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2023) found a 20% reduction, though the benefit only applies to the patients who stay on the drug.

text: More than one in five American adults taking GLP-1 drugs would bring Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk well over $100 billion a year in U.S. sales.
bottom_line: Rough arithmetic, not a forecast: about 53 million adults (20% of the Census Bureau's roughly 267 million in 2024) times $245 a month, the government price in the November 2025 deal, times 12 months; real net prices could be lower as competition grows.

text: Americans who stop taking a GLP-1 drug regain most of the weight they lost, so millions of short courses of treatment buy little lasting benefit.
bottom_line: Supported by the STEP 1 trial extension (Wilding et al., Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, 2022), in which people regained about two-thirds of their lost weight a year after stopping semaglutide; combined with high dropout rates, this is a real cost of broad but short use.
