bottom_line: Which survey you read decides most of this question: the self-reported National Health Interview Survey already read 33.4 percent in 2024, while NHANES, which actually weighs people, read 40.3 percent in 2021 to 2023, so the belief is judged on NHANES and needs a measured drop of about five points. Uptake, falling prices and new pills point toward that drop, and measured health records show a small decline under way. The real fight is whether Americans will stay on the drugs for life, because trials show most of the weight comes back when they stop, and whether NHANES will even publish a reading for 2032 in time.
hook: By the CDC's self-reported National Health Interview Survey, American adult obesity was already 33.4 percent in 2024; by the CDC survey that actually weighs and measures people, it was 40.3 percent.
question: Will GLP-1 drugs like Wegovy, Zepbound and the new pills bring the measured share of American adults with obesity below 35 percent by 2032?
ask: The page most needs a published study that measures how many Americans who started a GLP-1 drug in 2025 or later are still taking it two or three years on.

text: Self-reported obesity among American adults fell about three percentage points between 2022 and 2025 while GLP-1 use for weight loss roughly doubled, which suggests the drugs are already moving the national number.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the drop is real in Gallup's consistent method, but it is self-reported, not peer reviewed, and cannot by itself show the drugs caused it.

text: Daily GLP-1 pills such as Eli Lilly's Foundayo (orforglipron), approved by the FDA in 2026, remove the need for weekly injections and cold storage, which should widen use among American adults who avoid needles.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: pills reach more people, but they produce somewhat less weight loss than the strongest injections, so each user moves fewer BMI points.

text: One-year persistence on GLP-1 drugs for weight loss rose sharply once the 2022 to 2024 shortages ended, so more of the Americans who start these drugs are now staying on them long enough to lose meaningful weight.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the improvement comes from a pharmacy benefit manager's press release, and long-term persistence beyond a year is still low.

text: Tirzepatide, the strongest widely used GLP-1 drug, cut body weight by about 21 percent in its main trial, enough to carry a typical trial participant from a BMI of 38 to about 30, the obesity line.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: trial results are the best case, and real-world users lose less on average because of lower doses and stopping early.

text: Gallup's National Health and Well-Being Index found self-reported adult obesity in the United States fell from 39.9 percent in 2022 to 37.0 percent in 2025, about 7.6 million fewer adults, while self-reported GLP-1 use for weight loss rose from 5.8 percent in February 2024 to 12.4 percent in 2025.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: large and consistent in method, but self-reported, not peer reviewed, and correlational.

text: Epic Research's Cosmos records, covering more than 300 million patients, show GLP-1 prescriptions rising from 1,884 to 8,819 per 100,000 U.S. adults between the second quarter of 2021 and the first quarter of 2026, while the share of adults with obesity in those records fell from 42.3 percent to 40.7 percent, mostly in the later years.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: measured BMI from clinic visits is better than self-report, but patients who see doctors are not a random sample of adults.

text: An analysis of about 16.7 million U.S. adults in Optum claims and health records found mean BMI and obesity prevalence fell in 2023 for the first time in more than a decade, with the largest drop in the South, the region with the highest GLP-1 dispensing.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: peer reviewed and measured, but the decline was small and the authors did not rule out pandemic-related causes.

text: In the SURMOUNT-1 trial of 2,539 adults with a mean BMI of 38.0, tirzepatide 15 mg reduced body weight by 20.9 percent at 72 weeks compared with 3.1 percent on placebo.
bottom_line: Strong weight on what the drug can do; weak on what the population will do, since trial adherence is far higher than real-world adherence.

text: A large claims or health record study finds that more than half of Americans who started a GLP-1 drug for obesity in 2025 or 2026 are still taking it three years later.
The first NHANES estimate after 2023 shows measured adult obesity at or below 37 percent, a drop of three points or more from 40.3 percent in 2021 to 2023.
Millions of American adults who start GLP-1 drugs will keep taking them for years, because the weight stays off only while the drugs are taken.
Many American GLP-1 users start with a BMI close enough to 30 that the weight they lose takes them out of the obese range, rather than only lowering them within it.

Gallup researchers Dan Witters and Mary Page James reported in October 2025 that U.S. adult obesity had fallen from 39.9 percent in 2022 to 37.0 percent in 2025 as GLP-1 use for weight loss more than doubled, with the biggest drops in the age groups using the drugs most.

John Brownstein and his co-authors wrote in JAMA Health Forum in December 2024 that growing use of GLP-1 drugs may be one reason the BMI of American adults in clinic records stopped rising in 2022 and dipped in 2023.
Obesity Rate Declining in U.S., Dan Witters and Mary Page James, 2025
bridge: Gallup's self-reported adult obesity rate fell from a peak of 39.9 percent in 2022 to 37.0 percent in 2025, while the share of adults using GLP-1 injections for weight loss rose from 5.8 percent in February 2024 to 12.4 percent, and the age groups with the most GLP-1 use had the largest drops.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the method is the same from year to year, so the trend is real for that survey, but the heights and weights are self-reported and the link to GLP-1 drugs is a correlation.

text: Changes in Adult Obesity Trends in the US, Benjamin Rader, Rebecca Hazan and John S. Brownstein, 2024
bridge: Mean BMI in clinic records for 16.7 million American adults rose every year through 2021, flattened in 2022 and dipped slightly in 2023 (30.24 to 30.21), with the largest drop in the South, the region with the most GLP-1 dispensing.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the BMIs are measured in clinics rather than self-reported, but the population is insured patients, the change is small, and the authors do not rule out pandemic-era causes.

text: Tirzepatide Once Weekly for the Treatment of Obesity, Ania M. Jastreboff, Louis J. Aronne, Nadia N. Ahmad and others (SURMOUNT-1), 2022
bridge: The SURMOUNT-1 randomized trial showed that tirzepatide at its top dose cut body weight by about a fifth over 72 weeks, the size of loss that can carry many people across the BMI 30 line.
bottom_line: Strong weight on what the drug can do for a person who stays on it, weak weight on what the national rate will do, because trial participants take the drug far more steadily than people in everyday life.

text: Most Americans who start a GLP-1 drug for obesity stop within a few years, and only about one in twelve was still taking one three years after starting in a large insurance claims analysis.
bottom_line: Strong weight: a drug that most people quit cannot hold a population-wide number down unless persistence improves a great deal.

text: People who stop semaglutide regain most of the weight they lost, about two-thirds within a year in the STEP 1 trial extension, so a drop in obesity built on short courses of treatment would largely reverse.
bottom_line: Strong weight: this is randomized trial evidence, and it means the national rate depends on lifelong use, not on how many people ever try the drugs.

text: Semaglutide's average weight loss of about 15 percent would move a typical trial participant from a BMI of about 38 only to about 32, so many GLP-1 users lose a lot of weight and still count as having obesity.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the 35 percent target counts heads above BMI 30, not pounds lost, so drugs mostly shift people within the obese range unless they start near the line.

text: Measured adult obesity in the United States did not fall significantly between 2013 to 2014 and 2021 to 2023 according to NHANES, and severe obesity rose, so the measured baseline has shown no decline yet.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the latest NHANES cycle ended in 2023, before the biggest growth in GLP-1 use, so it predates most of the effect being claimed.

text: Measured adult obesity was 40.3 percent in NHANES August 2021 to August 2023, with no significant change in age-adjusted prevalence since 2013 to 2014, while severe obesity rose from 7.7 percent to 9.7 percent.
bottom_line: Strong weight as the baseline: this is the measured national figure, though it predates the steepest rise in GLP-1 use.

text: One year after stopping semaglutide and lifestyle support at week 68, STEP 1 participants had regained about two-thirds of the weight they had lost, with cardiometabolic gains largely reversed.
bottom_line: Strong weight: randomized evidence that the effect depends on continued use, replicated by the tirzepatide SURMOUNT-4 withdrawal trial.

text: Before GLP-1 drugs were widely used for weight loss, a model correcting self-reported BMI with measured NHANES data projected that 48.9 percent of U.S. adults would have obesity by 2030.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight: it shows the underlying pressure is upward, but measured obesity has already run below this projection's path.

text: The NHANES 2025 to 2027 cycle will report measured adult obesity of 38 percent or higher if GLP-1 drugs will not bring national obesity below 35 percent by 2032.
The first NHANES estimate after 2023 shows measured adult obesity at 40 percent or higher despite more than one in ten adults reporting GLP-1 use.
Epic Research's Cosmos records show the adult obesity share rising again or flat for three straight years after the first quarter of 2026, even as GLP-1 prescriptions keep climbing.

The recent declines in self-reported and clinic-record obesity in the United States reflect reporting habits, who visits doctors, or pandemic after-effects more than real weight loss across the population.
Obesity and Severe Obesity Prevalence in Adults: United States, August 2021 to August 2023, Samuel D. Emmerich, Cheryl D. Fryar, Bryan Stierman and Cynthia L. Ogden, 2024
where_found: National Center for Health Statistics, NCHS Data Brief No. 508
bridge: CDC's measured survey found 40.3 percent of American adults with obesity in 2021 to 2023, no significant change in age-adjusted obesity since 2013 to 2014, and severe obesity rising from 7.7 to 9.7 percent.
bottom_line: Strong weight as the baseline the belief must beat, since it is the only national survey that weighs and measures people, though its fieldwork ended before the largest growth in GLP-1 use.

text: Weight regain and cardiometabolic effects after withdrawal of semaglutide: The STEP 1 trial extension, John P. H. Wilding, Rachel L. Batterham, Melanie Davies and others, 2022
bridge: Participants who lost 17.3 percent of their weight on semaglutide over 68 weeks regained 11.6 percentage points within a year of stopping, about two-thirds of what they had lost.
bottom_line: Strong weight: it is randomized trial evidence that a national drop in obesity holds only as long as people keep taking the drugs.

text: National-level and state-level prevalence of overweight and obesity among children, adolescents, and adults in the USA, 1990-2021, and forecasts up to 2050, GBD 2021 US Obesity Forecasting Collaborators, 2024
bridge: The Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation's forecast projects American adult obesity continuing to rise for decades, the trend a GLP-1-driven decline would have to reverse.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it sets out how strong the upward pressure has been, but its data end in 2021 and cannot account for the drugs' recent spread.

text: Bringing measured U.S. adult obesity from about 40 percent to below 35 percent would mean roughly 14 million fewer American adults with obesity, using Gallup's estimate that a 2.9 point drop equals about 7.6 million people.
bottom_line: High importance if it happens, since obesity drives diabetes, heart disease and joint problems, though BMI below 30 is a line, not a cure.

text: A falling obesity rate would reduce the number of American adults who later develop type 2 diabetes and need lifelong diabetes care.
bottom_line: Plausible and important, but Gallup found diagnosed diabetes at a record 13.8 percent in 2025, so the payoff has not yet shown up.

text: Covering GLP-1 drugs for obesity in Medicare would add about $35 billion in net federal spending from 2026 to 2034 by CBO's 2024 estimate, before the later price cuts.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the estimate predates the $245 Medicare price, so the true cost is likely lower but still large.

text: Keeping the U.S. obesity rate low with GLP-1 drugs requires lifelong use, which at Medicare's negotiated price of $245 a month costs about $2,940 per user each year.
bottom_line: Moderate to high weight: the cost repeats every year for every user, and stopping brings most of the weight back.

text: Gastrointestinal side effects lead a minority of GLP-1 users to stop treatment, with 4.5 percent of semaglutide users in the STEP 1 trial quitting for stomach problems compared with 0.8 percent on placebo.
bottom_line: Low to moderate weight: most side effects are mild, but they shrink the share of people who can stay on the drugs.

The share of new GLP-1 users for weight loss still taking the drug two years after starting is a fair measure of whether the drugs can hold the national obesity rate down rather than produce short-lived losses.

Any fall in measured American adult obesity by 2032 will be caused mainly by GLP-1 drugs rather than by diet, aging, bariatric surgery or a change in who takes part in the survey.
